sources.quote:
1. 1. Purpose
This clause, 4.1 Underwriting Standards, establishes the foundational principles and criteria for credit underwriting within the
wholesale banking division of the institution. As a synthetic demonstration document, it is designed to reflect industry best
practices while ensuring alignment with the parent policy CP-Wholesale-v4.2. The purpose of this clause is to define the
minimum standards for evaluating the creditworthiness of wholesale clients, ensuring that all credit exposures are underwritten
with a consistent, risk-aware, and compliant approach.
The underwriting standards outlined herein are intended to balance the institution’s risk appetite with its strategic objectives. By
adhering to these standards, the bank aims to mitigate credit risk, maintain portfolio quality, and ensure regulatory compliance.
This clause applies to all wholesale credit exposures, including but not limited to term loans, revolving credit facilities, letters of
credit, and derivative transactions.
A core objective of this clause is to ensure that all credit decisions are supported by thorough analysis, robust documentation,
and clear accountability. The standards are designed to be scalable, allowing for the evaluation of both large corporate clients
and smaller wholesale entities. The policy emphasizes the importance of a disciplined underwriting process, which includes the
assessment of financial strength, industry risk, management quality, and collateral adequacy.
This clause also serves as a reference for internal auditors, regulators, and external stakeholders to understand the bank’s
approach to wholesale credit underwriting. It is critical that all personnel involved in the credit process adhere to these
standards to maintain the integrity and reputation of the institution. Any deviations from these standards must be justified,
documented, and approved through the appropriate governance channels.
Finally, this clause is part of a broader credit policy framework and should be read in conjunction with other relevant policies,
such as CP-Wholesale-v4.2, which provides overarching guidance on wholesale credit risk management. The standards herein
are subject to periodic review to ensure they remain relevant and effective in addressing emerging risks and market conditions.

2. 2. Scope
The scope of this clause, 4.1 Underwriting Standards, encompasses all wholesale credit exposures originated, renewed, or
amended by the bank. Wholesale credit exposures are defined as those extended to corporate entities, financial institutions,
sovereigns, and other non-retail counterparties with an aggregate exposure of USD 1,000,000 or more. This threshold ensures
that the underwriting standards are applied consistently across the bank’s wholesale portfolio.
The clause applies to all business lines and geographic regions where the bank operates, unless explicitly exempted by the
Global Credit Policy Committee. Exemptions must be documented and justified based on local regulatory requirements or
unique market conditions. All personnel involved in the underwriting process, including relationship managers, credit analysts,
and approval authorities, are required to comply with the standards outlined in this clause.
The underwriting standards cover the entire lifecycle of a credit exposure, from initial due diligence and approval to ongoing
monitoring and renewal. This includes the evaluation of new credit requests, amendments to existing facilities, and the annual
or event-driven reviews of creditworthiness. The standards are also applicable to the underwriting of derivative transactions,
trade finance, and other non-traditional credit products offered to wholesale clients.
For the purposes of this clause, wholesale clients are categorized into three tiers based on their annual revenue: Tier 1 (USD 1
billion and above), Tier 2 (USD 250 million to USD 999 million), and Tier 3 (USD 1 million to USD 249 million). The underwriting
requirements, including the depth of analysis and approval thresholds, are tailored to the risk profile of each tier. Higher-risk
industries, such as commodities trading or highly leveraged sectors, may be subject to additional underwriting scrutiny.
This clause does not apply to retail or small business lending, which are governed by separate credit policies. However, it is
acknowledged that certain wholesale clients may have retail or small business subsidiaries. In such cases, the underwriting of
exposures to these subsidiaries must be evaluated in the context of the parent company’s overall creditworthiness and the
bank’s aggregate exposure to the group.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data

 4.1 Underwriting Standards
CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose
This clause, 4.1 Underwriting Standards, establishes the foundational principles and criteria for credit underwriting within the
wholesale banking division of the institution. As a synthetic demonstration document, it is designed to reflect industry best
practices while ensuring alignment with the parent policy CP-Wholesale-v4.2. The purpose of this clause is to define the
minimum standards for evaluating the creditworthiness of wholesale clients, ensuring that all credit exposures are underwritten
with a consistent, risk-aware, and compliant approach.
The underwriting standards outlined herein are intended to balance the institution’s risk appetite with its strategic objectives. By
adhering to these standards, the bank aims to mitigate credit risk, maintain portfolio quality, and ensure regulatory compliance.
This clause applies to all wholesale credit exposures, including but not limited to term loans, revolving credit facilities, letters of
credit, and derivative transactions.
A core objective of this clause is to ensure that all credit decisions are supported by thorough analysis, robust documentation,
and clear accountability. The standards are designed to be scalable, allowing for the evaluation of both large corporate clients
and smaller wholesale entities. The policy emphasizes the importance of a disciplined underwriting process, which includes the
assessment of financial strength, industry risk, management quality, and collateral adequacy.
This clause also serves as a reference for internal auditors, regulators, and external stakeholders to understand the bank’s
approach to wholesale credit underwriting. It is critical that all personnel involved in the credit process adhere to these
standards to maintain the integrity and reputation of the institution. Any deviations from these standards must be justified,
documented, and approved through the appropriate governance channels.
Finally, this clause is part of a broader credit policy framework and should be read in conjunction with other relevant policies,
such as CP-Wholesale-v4.2, which provides overarching guidance on wholesale credit risk management. The standards herein
are subject to periodic review to ensure they remain relevant and effective in addressing emerging risks and market conditions.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope
The scope of this clause, 4.1 Underwriting Standards, encompasses all wholesale credit exposures originated, renewed, or
amended by the bank. Wholesale credit exposures are defined as those extended to corporate entities, financial institutions,
sovereigns, and other non-retail counterparties with an aggregate exposure of USD 1,000,000 or more. This threshold ensures
that the underwriting standards are applied consistently across the bank’s wholesale portfolio.
The clause applies to all business lines and geographic regions where the bank operates, unless explicitly exempted by the
Global Credit Policy Committee. Exemptions must be documented and justified based on local regulatory requirements or
unique market conditions. All personnel involved in the underwriting process, including relationship managers, credit analysts,
and approval authorities, are required to comply with the standards outlined in this clause.
The underwriting standards cover the entire lifecycle of a credit exposure, from initial due diligence and approval to ongoing
monitoring and renewal. This includes the evaluation of new credit requests, amendments to existing facilities, and the annual
or event-driven reviews of creditworthiness. The standards are also applicable to the underwriting of derivative transactions,
trade finance, and other non-traditional credit products offered to wholesale clients.
For the purposes of this clause, wholesale clients are categorized into three tiers based on their annual revenue: Tier 1 (USD 1
billion and above), Tier 2 (USD 250 million to USD 999 million), and Tier 3 (USD 1 million to USD 249 million). The underwriting
requirements, including the depth of analysis and approval thresholds, are tailored to the risk profile of each tier. Higher-risk
industries, such as commodities trading or highly leveraged sectors, may be subject to additional underwriting scrutiny.
This clause does not apply to retail or small business lending, which are governed by separate credit policies. However, it is
acknowledged that certain wholesale clients may have retail or small business subsidiaries. In such cases, the underwriting of
exposures to these subsidiaries must be evaluated in the context of the parent company’s overall creditworthiness and the
bank’s aggregate exposure to the group.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 3

3. 3. Governance and Roles
The governance framework for underwriting standards is designed to ensure clear accountability, segregation of duties, and
independent oversight. The Global Credit Policy Committee (GCPC) is the ultimate authority responsible for the approval and
periodic review of this clause. The GCPC delegates day-to-day oversight to the Wholesale Credit Risk Division, which is
responsible for implementing and enforcing the underwriting standards.
The Wholesale Credit Risk Division is led by the Chief Credit Officer (CCO) for Wholesale Banking, who reports directly to the
GCPC. The CCO is responsible for ensuring that all underwriting activities adhere to the standards outlined in this clause and
that any exceptions are properly escalated and documented. The division includes regional credit officers, industry specialists,
and portfolio managers who provide subject-matter expertise and support to the business lines.
Relationship managers (RMs) are the primary point of contact for wholesale clients and are responsible for originating credit
requests. RMs must conduct initial due diligence and prepare credit applications in accordance with the underwriting standards.
Credit analysts, who report independently to the Wholesale Credit Risk Division, are responsible for performing detailed
financial and risk assessments. Their role includes validating the information provided by RMs, identifying key risk factors, and
recommending credit ratings and facility structures.
Approval authorities are assigned based on the risk profile and size of the credit exposure. The approval matrix, as outlined in
Section 6 of this clause, defines the thresholds for delegated approvals. For exposures exceeding USD 50 million, approval
must be obtained from a credit committee, which includes representatives from the Wholesale Credit Risk Division, business
lines, and independent risk functions. The credit committee’s decision is final and must be documented in the credit file.
Independent review functions, including Internal Audit and Compliance, are responsible for testing adherence to the
underwriting standards. These functions conduct periodic audits and reviews to ensure that the standards are applied
consistently and that any deviations are appropriately managed. Findings from these reviews are reported to the GCPC and
senior management for remediation and process improvements.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 4

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
The underwriting criteria outlined in this section define the qualitative and quantitative factors that must be evaluated to assess
the creditworthiness of wholesale clients. The criteria are designed to provide a comprehensive view of the borrower’s ability
and willingness to repay its obligations. The evaluation must include an assessment of the borrower’s financial strength,
industry risk, management quality, competitive position, and collateral adequacy.
Financial strength is evaluated through a detailed analysis of the borrower’s historical and projected financial statements. Key
metrics include leverage ratios (e.g., Debt/EBITDA, Total Debt/Total Capital), coverage ratios (e.g., Interest Coverage, Fixed
Charge Coverage), liquidity ratios (e.g., Current Ratio, Quick Ratio), and profitability trends. For Tier 1 and Tier 2 clients, a
minimum Interest Coverage Ratio of 2.5x and a maximum Leverage Ratio of 4.0x are required for investment-grade ratings.
Sub-investment-grade clients may be approved with lower thresholds, but these must be justified by compensating factors such
as strong collateral or industry leadership.
Industry risk is assessed using the bank’s internal industry risk rating framework, which categorizes industries into five risk tiers:
Low, Moderate-Low, Moderate, Moderate-High, and High. Industries in the High-risk tier, such as cryptocurrency or speculative
real estate, require additional underwriting scrutiny, including higher capital allocations and more frequent reviews. The industry
risk assessment must consider macroeconomic trends, regulatory changes, and competitive dynamics that could impact the
borrower’s ability to service its debt.
Management quality is evaluated through direct interactions with the borrower’s senior management, as well as third-party
assessments such as credit reports and industry analyses. Key factors include the experience and track record of the
management team, the quality of financial reporting, and the borrower’s corporate governance practices. For privately held
companies, the assessment must also consider the ownership structure and the alignment of interests between shareholders
and creditors.
Collateral adequacy is determined based on the type, quality, and liquidity of the assets pledged as security. The bank’s
collateral valuation policies must be followed, and haircuts must be applied based on the asset class and market conditions. For
example, accounts receivable are typically valued at 80% of their face value, while inventory may be valued at 50% or less,
depending on its liquidity. Unsecured exposures are permitted but are subject to stricter underwriting criteria and higher pricing.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 5

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
Quantitative limits are established to ensure that credit exposures remain within the bank’s risk appetite and regulatory
constraints. These limits are applied at various levels, including individual borrowers, industry sectors, geographic regions, and
product types. The limits are designed to prevent excessive concentration risk and to ensure diversification across the
wholesale portfolio.
The bank’s aggregate wholesale credit exposure to a single borrower or borrower group must not exceed 15% of the bank’s
Tier 1 capital, as defined by regulatory guidelines. For Tier 1 clients, the maximum exposure is capped at USD 500 million,
unless approved by the GCPC. For Tier 2 clients, the cap is USD 200 million, and for Tier 3 clients, it is USD 50 million.
Exposures exceeding these thresholds require a detailed concentration risk analysis and approval from the CCO for Wholesale
Banking.
Industry sector limits are set to prevent over-exposure to any single industry. The bank’s aggregate exposure to a single
industry sector must not exceed 25% of the total wholesale portfolio. Industries with higher risk ratings, such as High or
Moderate-High, are subject to lower limits. For example, the aggregate exposure to the commodities trading sector is capped at
10% of the wholesale portfolio. Sector limits are monitored monthly, and breaches must be reported to the GCPC within five
business days.
Geographic limits are applied to manage country risk and ensure diversification across regions. The bank’s aggregate exposure
to a single country must not exceed 20% of the total wholesale portfolio. For countries with a sovereign credit rating below
BBB-, the limit is reduced to 10%. Exposures to countries subject to international sanctions or with significant political instability
are prohibited unless explicitly approved by the GCPC.
Product-type limits are established to manage the risk associated with different credit products. For example, the aggregate
exposure to derivative transactions must not exceed 15% of the wholesale portfolio. Similarly, the exposure to unsecured credit
facilities is capped at 30% of the portfolio. These limits are designed to ensure that the bank’s risk profile remains balanced and
that no single product type dominates the portfolio.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 6

6. 6. Approval Authorities and Escalation Paths
Approval authorities are delegated based on the risk profile, size, and complexity of the credit exposure. The approval matrix
ensures that higher-risk or larger exposures receive appropriate levels of scrutiny and oversight. The matrix is structured to
align with the bank’s risk appetite and regulatory expectations, and it is reviewed annually by the GCPC.
For Tier 3 clients with exposures up to USD 10 million, approval authority is delegated to the regional credit officer. Exposures
between USD 10 million and USD 50 million require approval from the regional credit committee, which includes
representatives from the Wholesale Credit Risk Division and the business line. For Tier 2 clients, exposures up to USD 50
million require regional credit committee approval, while exposures between USD 50 million and USD 200 million require
approval from the global credit committee.
Tier 1 clients and exposures exceeding USD 200 million require approval from the GCPC. The GCPC meets monthly to review
large or complex credit requests and ensures that all material risks are identified and mitigated. In urgent cases, the CCO for
Wholesale Banking may grant interim approval, but this must be ratified by the GCPC at its next scheduled meeting.
Escalation paths are clearly defined to ensure that any credit request that does not meet the underwriting standards or exceeds
delegated authorities is promptly escalated to the appropriate level. For example, if a credit analyst identifies a material
weakness in a borrower’s financial position that was not addressed in the initial application, the request must be escalated to
the regional credit officer for further review. Similarly, if a relationship manager proposes a structure that deviates from the
bank’s standard terms, the request must be escalated to the global credit committee.
All approvals and escalations must be documented in the credit file, including the rationale for the decision, any conditions or
covenants imposed, and the names of the approving authorities. The credit file must also include evidence of compliance with
the underwriting standards, such as financial statements, industry analyses, and collateral valuations. Failure to obtain the
required approvals or to document the decision-making process may result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination
of employment.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 7

7. 7. Monitoring and Ongoing Review
Ongoing monitoring is a critical component of the underwriting process, ensuring that the bank’s credit exposures remain
consistent with the initial underwriting assessment. The Wholesale Credit Risk Division is responsible for establishing and
maintaining a robust monitoring framework that includes financial covenant tracking, credit rating reviews, and early warning
indicators.
Financial covenants are tailored to the borrower’s risk profile and are designed to provide early warning of potential credit
deterioration. Common covenants include minimum Interest Coverage Ratios, maximum Leverage Ratios, and minimum net
worth requirements. Covenant compliance is monitored quarterly, and breaches must be investigated and reported to the
appropriate credit committee within 10 business days. Persistent or material covenant breaches may trigger a review of the
borrower’s credit rating or the imposition of additional restrictions on the facility.
Credit ratings are assigned to all wholesale borrowers using the bank’s internal rating methodology, which is aligned with
regulatory expectations. Ratings are reviewed at least annually, or more frequently if there are significant changes in the
borrower’s financial condition, industry risk, or management quality. The rating review process includes a reassessment of all
underwriting criteria, as well as an evaluation of the borrower’s performance relative to its peers. Downgrades in credit ratings
must be approved by the regional or global credit committee, depending on the size of the exposure.
Early warning indicators are used to identify potential credit issues before they result in a default or loss. These indicators may
include deteriorating financial performance, negative news coverage, changes in management, or adverse industry trends. The
Wholesale Credit Risk Division maintains a watchlist of borrowers exhibiting early warning signs, and these borrowers are
subject to enhanced monitoring, including more frequent financial reporting and site visits.
The monitoring framework also includes portfolio-level reviews to identify emerging risks or concentrations. The Wholesale
Credit Risk Division conducts quarterly portfolio reviews, which are presented to the GCPC. These reviews include an analysis
of credit quality trends, industry and geographic concentrations, and the effectiveness of the underwriting standards. The results
of the portfolio reviews are used to refine the underwriting criteria and quantitative limits as needed.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 8

8. 8. Exceptions and Waivers
Exceptions to the underwriting standards may be granted in limited circumstances, provided that they are justified, documented,
and approved through the appropriate governance channels. Exceptions are not to be granted routinely and must be supported
by a compelling business case or risk mitigation factors. The bank’s policy is to minimize exceptions to maintain the integrity
and consistency of the underwriting process.
An exception may be considered if the borrower’s financial metrics fall slightly below the minimum thresholds but are
compensated by other strengths, such as a strong market position, high-quality collateral, or a long-standing relationship with
the bank. For example, a borrower with an Interest Coverage Ratio of 2.0x (below the 2.5x threshold) may be approved if it has
a dominant market share in a stable industry and pledges liquid collateral with a conservative haircut.
The process for requesting an exception begins with the relationship manager, who must submit a formal exception request to
the regional credit officer. The request must include a detailed rationale for the exception, an assessment of the compensating
factors, and an analysis of the incremental risk to the bank. The regional credit officer reviews the request and, if deemed
appropriate, escalates it to the regional or global credit committee for approval.
Waivers of financial covenants are treated as exceptions and must follow the same approval process. Covenant waivers are
typically granted for temporary or technical breaches that are not indicative of a broader credit deterioration. For example, a
borrower may request a waiver for a one-time capital expenditure that temporarily increases its Leverage Ratio. Waivers must
be time-bound and include a corrective action plan to bring the borrower back into compliance.
All exceptions and waivers must be documented in the credit file and reported to the GCPC on a quarterly basis. The report
must include the number of exceptions granted, the types of exceptions, the rationale for each, and the incremental risk
assumed by the bank. The GCPC reviews the report to ensure that exceptions are being managed appropriately and that the
overall risk profile of the portfolio remains within the bank’s risk appetite.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 9

9. 9. Reporting and Documentation
Accurate and comprehensive reporting and documentation are essential to the integrity of the underwriting process. The bank
maintains a centralized credit file for each wholesale borrower, which serves as the official record of all underwriting activities,
approvals, monitoring, and exceptions. The credit file must be complete, up-to-date, and accessible to all relevant stakeholders,
including relationship managers, credit analysts, and auditors.
The credit file must include all documents and analyses used to support the underwriting decision, such as financial statements,
industry reports, management assessments, and collateral valuations. For new credit requests, the file must also include the
credit application, approval memorandum, and any exception or waiver requests. For existing exposures, the file must be
updated with the results of ongoing monitoring, including covenant compliance reports, credit rating reviews, and early warning
indicators.
The bank’s credit reporting framework includes regular and ad hoc reports to ensure transparency and accountability. Monthly
reports are generated for the regional credit committees, summarizing new credit approvals, amendments, covenant breaches,
and exceptions. Quarterly reports are provided to the GCPC, including portfolio-level trends, credit quality metrics, and the
results of the monitoring framework. Ad hoc reports are prepared as needed for specific requests from senior management,
regulators, or auditors.
The approval memorandum is a critical component of the credit file and must be prepared for all new credit requests,
amendments, and annual reviews. The memorandum must include a summary of the borrower’s business and financial profile,
the proposed facility structure, the underwriting analysis, and the rationale for the approval decision. It must also document any
conditions or covenants imposed, as well as the names and signatures of the approving authorities.
Documentation standards are enforced through periodic audits conducted by Internal Audit and Compliance. These audits
assess the completeness and accuracy of the credit files, as well as adherence to the reporting requirements. Findings from the
audits are reported to the GCPC and must be addressed through corrective action plans. Failure to maintain adequate
documentation may result in the suspension of delegated approval authorities or other disciplinary actions.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 10

10. 10. Policy Review and Maintenance
This clause, 4.1 Underwriting Standards, is subject to periodic review to ensure that it remains relevant, effective, and aligned
with the bank’s risk appetite and regulatory expectations. The GCPC is responsible for overseeing the review process, which is
conducted at least annually or more frequently if there are significant changes in the bank’s strategy, risk profile, or the external
environment.
The review process includes an assessment of the policy’s effectiveness in mitigating credit risk, as well as an evaluation of its
consistency with industry best practices and regulatory requirements. The Wholesale Credit Risk Division is responsible for
conducting the review and presenting its findings to the GCPC. The review must include an analysis of credit quality trends, the
frequency and nature of exceptions, and feedback from business lines and independent review functions.
As part of the review, the GCPC may solicit input from external stakeholders, such as regulators, auditors, or industry peers, to
benchmark the bank’s underwriting standards against those of its peers. The GCPC may also commission independent studies
or consultations to identify areas for improvement. The results of the review are documented in a formal report, which includes
recommendations for updates or enhancements to the policy.
Updates to the policy must be approved by the GCPC and communicated to all relevant stakeholders, including relationship
managers, credit analysts, and approval authorities. The updated policy is then incorporated into the bank’s policy management
system, and training is provided to ensure that all personnel are aware of the changes. The effective date of the updated policy
is clearly communicated, and a transition period may be granted for existing exposures to comply with new requirements.
In addition to the annual review, the policy may be updated on an ad hoc basis to address emerging risks or regulatory
changes. For example, if a new regulatory capital framework is introduced, the underwriting standards may need to be adjusted
to reflect the new requirements. Similarly, if the bank identifies a new industry or product type that presents unique risks, the
policy may be updated to include specific underwriting criteria for that segment. All ad hoc updates must follow the same
approval and communication process as the annual review.

1. 1. Purpose
The purpose of this clause, 4.2 Leverage Limits, is to establish a structured framework for assessing, approving, and monitoring
leverage exposure across the bank’s wholesale lending portfolio. This clause operates under the parent policy
CP-Wholesale-v4.2 and is designed to ensure that leverage levels remain within acceptable risk parameters, aligning with the
bank’s risk appetite and regulatory expectations. By defining clear leverage limits, the bank aims to mitigate the risk of
over-leveraged counterparties, which could lead to financial distress and potential credit losses.
Leverage limits are a critical component of the bank’s credit risk management strategy, as they provide a quantitative basis for
evaluating the financial health and stability of wholesale clients. Excessive leverage can amplify losses during economic
downturns, increase the likelihood of default, and expose the bank to systemic risks. This clause ensures that leverage is
measured consistently, monitored proactively, and managed through predefined thresholds and escalation paths.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data and is intended for illustrative purposes only. It does not reflect the actual policies,
procedures, or risk appetites of any real financial institution. All thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are fictional
and should not be interpreted as binding or actionable in a real-world context.
The policy is grounded in the principle that leverage must be evaluated not only in isolation but also in the context of the
borrower’s overall financial profile, industry dynamics, and macroeconomic conditions. By integrating leverage limits into the
broader credit assessment framework, the bank ensures a holistic approach to risk management, balancing growth objectives
with prudential safeguards.
This clause applies to all wholesale lending activities, including but not limited to corporate loans, revolving credit facilities, term
loans, and other forms of credit exposure. It is designed to be flexible enough to accommodate varying risk profiles while
maintaining rigorous standards for leverage assessment. The policy is reviewed annually to ensure its continued relevance and
effectiveness in addressing emerging risks.

2. 2. Scope
This clause, 4.2 Leverage Limits, applies to all wholesale credit exposures managed by the bank, including but not limited to
corporate entities, financial institutions, and other non-retail counterparties. The scope encompasses all forms of leverage,
whether structural (e.g., debt-to-equity ratios) or operational (e.g., short-term borrowing relative to liquidity). The policy is global
in nature and applies uniformly across all jurisdictions where the bank operates, subject to local regulatory adjustments where
necessary.
The scope explicitly includes all credit facilities extended by the bank, such as term loans, revolving credit facilities, letters of
credit, and other forms of off-balance-sheet exposures that may contribute to a counterparty’s leverage. It also covers
leveraged buyouts (LBOs), acquisition financing, and other transactions where leverage is a material consideration in the credit
decision.
Exclusions from this clause include retail lending, consumer credit, and other non-wholesale products, which are governed by
separate policies tailored to their unique risk characteristics. Additionally, intra-group exposures and transactions with sovereign
entities may be subject to specialized frameworks, as deemed appropriate by the bank’s risk governance bodies.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data and does not represent the actual scope of any real financial institution’s credit
policies. The definitions and boundaries outlined herein are illustrative and should not be relied upon for real-world
decision-making.
The policy is designed to be comprehensive, ensuring that no material leverage exposure falls outside its purview. However,
the bank retains the discretion to apply additional controls or exemptions on a case-by-case basis, provided such decisions are
appropriately documented, justified, and approved by the relevant governance bodies. Any exemptions must be reported in the
bank’s exception tracking system and reviewed quarterly.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 1
 4.2 Leverage Limits
CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose
The purpose of this clause, 4.2 Leverage Limits, is to establish a structured framework for assessing, approving, and monitoring
leverage exposure across the bank’s wholesale lending portfolio. This clause operates under the parent policy
CP-Wholesale-v4.2 and is designed to ensure that leverage levels remain within acceptable risk parameters, aligning with the
bank’s risk appetite and regulatory expectations. By defining clear leverage limits, the bank aims to mitigate the risk of
over-leveraged counterparties, which could lead to financial distress and potential credit losses.
Leverage limits are a critical component of the bank’s credit risk management strategy, as they provide a quantitative basis for
evaluating the financial health and stability of wholesale clients. Excessive leverage can amplify losses during economic
downturns, increase the likelihood of default, and expose the bank to systemic risks. This clause ensures that leverage is
measured consistently, monitored proactively, and managed through predefined thresholds and escalation paths.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data and is intended for illustrative purposes only. It does not reflect the actual policies,
procedures, or risk appetites of any real financial institution. All thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are fictional
and should not be interpreted as binding or actionable in a real-world context.
The policy is grounded in the principle that leverage must be evaluated not only in isolation but also in the context of the
borrower’s overall financial profile, industry dynamics, and macroeconomic conditions. By integrating leverage limits into the
broader credit assessment framework, the bank ensures a holistic approach to risk management, balancing growth objectives
with prudential safeguards.
This clause applies to all wholesale lending activities, including but not limited to corporate loans, revolving credit facilities, term
loans, and other forms of credit exposure. It is designed to be flexible enough to accommodate varying risk profiles while
maintaining rigorous standards for leverage assessment. The policy is reviewed annually to ensure its continued relevance and
effectiveness in addressing emerging risks.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope
This clause, 4.2 Leverage Limits, applies to all wholesale credit exposures managed by the bank, including but not limited to
corporate entities, financial institutions, and other non-retail counterparties. The scope encompasses all forms of leverage,
whether structural (e.g., debt-to-equity ratios) or operational (e.g., short-term borrowing relative to liquidity). The policy is global
in nature and applies uniformly across all jurisdictions where the bank operates, subject to local regulatory adjustments where
necessary.
The scope explicitly includes all credit facilities extended by the bank, such as term loans, revolving credit facilities, letters of
credit, and other forms of off-balance-sheet exposures that may contribute to a counterparty’s leverage. It also covers
leveraged buyouts (LBOs), acquisition financing, and other transactions where leverage is a material consideration in the credit
decision.
Exclusions from this clause include retail lending, consumer credit, and other non-wholesale products, which are governed by
separate policies tailored to their unique risk characteristics. Additionally, intra-group exposures and transactions with sovereign
entities may be subject to specialized frameworks, as deemed appropriate by the bank’s risk governance bodies.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data and does not represent the actual scope of any real financial institution’s credit
policies. The definitions and boundaries outlined herein are illustrative and should not be relied upon for real-world
decision-making.
The policy is designed to be comprehensive, ensuring that no material leverage exposure falls outside its purview. However,
the bank retains the discretion to apply additional controls or exemptions on a case-by-case basis, provided such decisions are
appropriately documented, justified, and approved by the relevant governance bodies. Any exemptions must be reported in the
bank’s exception tracking system and reviewed quarterly.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 3

3. 3. Governance
Governance for the 4.2 Leverage Limits clause is vested in the bank’s Credit Risk Committee (CRC), which is responsible for
overseeing the implementation, monitoring, and periodic review of this policy. The CRC delegates operational responsibility to
the Wholesale Credit Risk team, which ensures day-to-day adherence to the leverage limits and escalates any breaches or
exceptions to the CRC for resolution.
The Chief Credit Officer (CCO) holds ultimate accountability for the policy’s effectiveness and compliance. The CCO is
supported by the Head of Wholesale Credit Risk, who ensures that the leverage limits are applied consistently across all
business lines and that any deviations are promptly addressed. Regional Credit Officers (RCOs) are responsible for local
implementation, ensuring alignment with global standards while accounting for jurisdiction-specific nuances.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data, and the roles and responsibilities described herein are fictional. They are provided
solely for the purpose of illustrating a typical governance structure for a wholesale credit policy.
The governance framework includes a three-tiered approval hierarchy for leverage limit breaches. Tier 1 breaches, defined as
deviations of up to 10% above the approved limit, may be approved by the relevant RCO. Tier 2 breaches, exceeding 10% but
not more than 20%, require approval from the Head of Wholesale Credit Risk. Tier 3 breaches, exceeding 20%, must be
escalated to the CRC for resolution, with the CCO’s explicit approval required.
The bank’s Internal Audit function conducts an independent review of the leverage limits policy at least annually, assessing its
effectiveness, compliance, and alignment with the bank’s risk appetite. Audit findings are presented to the CRC and the bank’s
Board Risk Committee (BRC) for action. Additionally, the policy is subject to ad-hoc reviews triggered by significant market
events, regulatory changes, or material breaches.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 4

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
The underwriting criteria for leverage limits are designed to ensure that all wholesale credit exposures are evaluated against a
consistent set of financial and non-financial metrics. The primary leverage ratios considered include Total Debt to EBITDA, Net
Debt to EBITDA, Debt to Equity, and Interest Coverage Ratio. These metrics are calculated using the most recent audited
financial statements or, where applicable, management accounts that have been subject to internal validation.
For corporate borrowers, the bank applies a baseline leverage limit of 4.0x Total Debt to EBITDA for investment-grade clients
and 3.0x for non-investment-grade clients. These thresholds may be adjusted based on industry-specific risk factors, with more
conservative limits applied to cyclical or high-volatility sectors such as commodities, real estate, and leveraged finance. The
bank’s sector specialists provide input on industry benchmarks to ensure that limits are both competitive and prudent.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data, and the thresholds and criteria outlined are illustrative. They do not reflect the
actual underwriting standards of any real financial institution and should not be used for real-world credit decisions.
In addition to quantitative metrics, the underwriting process incorporates qualitative assessments, such as the borrower’s
management quality, market position, and strategic direction. The bank’s relationship managers are required to provide a
detailed rationale for any leverage limit adjustments, supported by evidence such as industry reports, peer comparisons, and
stress-testing results.
The underwriting criteria are reviewed annually by the Wholesale Credit Risk team in consultation with the bank’s Industry Risk
and Quantitative Analytics groups. Updates to the criteria are approved by the CRC and communicated to all relevant
stakeholders. Any material changes to the underwriting standards are subject to a 90-day transition period to allow for portfolio
adjustments.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 5

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
The quantitative leverage limits under this clause are structured to provide a clear and actionable framework for credit
decision-making. The bank employs a tiered approach to leverage limits, with thresholds varying by credit rating, industry, and
transaction type. For investment-grade corporate borrowers, the maximum permitted Total Debt to EBITDA ratio is 4.5x, while
for non-investment-grade borrowers, the limit is capped at 3.5x. These limits are subject to further adjustments based on the
borrower’s cash flow stability, asset quality, and access to liquidity.
For leveraged finance transactions, including LBOs and acquisition financing, the bank imposes stricter limits. The maximum
Total Debt to EBITDA ratio for such transactions is 6.0x for senior debt and 7.0x for total debt, including mezzanine financing.
These limits are designed to reflect the higher risk inherent in leveraged transactions and are supplemented by additional
covenants, such as minimum interest coverage ratios of 1.5x and debt service coverage ratios of 1.2x.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data, and the quantitative limits described are fictional. They are provided for illustrative
purposes only and do not represent the actual leverage thresholds of any real financial institution.
The bank also applies dynamic leverage limits that adjust based on macroeconomic conditions. During periods of economic
expansion, the bank may allow for a 0.5x increase in the standard leverage limits, subject to CRC approval. Conversely, during
economic downturns or periods of heightened volatility, the bank may impose a 0.5x reduction in leverage limits to account for
increased risk. These adjustments are communicated to all business lines and are effective immediately upon approval.
Quantitative limits are monitored continuously through the bank’s credit risk management system, which automatically flags any
breaches or approaching limits. Relationship managers are required to provide a corrective action plan for any breach within 5
business days, with escalation to senior management if the breach is not resolved within 30 days.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 6

6. 6. Approval Authorities
Approval authorities for leverage limit exceptions are clearly defined to ensure accountability and consistency in
decision-making. The bank operates a delegated authority framework, where approval levels are determined by the magnitude
of the leverage limit breach, the credit rating of the borrower, and the overall risk profile of the transaction.
For Tier 1 breaches (up to 10% above the approved limit), the relevant Regional Credit Officer (RCO) has the authority to
approve exceptions, provided that the borrower’s credit rating is investment-grade and the transaction does not involve
leveraged finance. The RCO must document the rationale for the exception, including mitigating factors such as strong cash
flow coverage, collateral quality, or strategic importance to the bank.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data, and the approval authorities and thresholds described are fictional. They are
provided solely for the purpose of illustrating a typical approval hierarchy in a wholesale credit policy.
Tier 2 breaches (10% to 20% above the approved limit) require approval from the Head of Wholesale Credit Risk. Such
approvals are subject to additional scrutiny, including a review of the borrower’s financial projections, stress-testing results, and
industry outlook. The Head of Wholesale Credit Risk may also require the involvement of the bank’s Industry Risk team to
assess sector-specific risks.
Tier 3 breaches (exceeding 20% above the approved limit) must be escalated to the Credit Risk Committee (CRC) for
resolution. The CRC’s approval is required, along with the explicit sign-off of the Chief Credit Officer (CCO). Tier 3 exceptions
are rare and typically reserved for transactions of strategic importance or where the bank has a unique risk mitigation
advantage, such as strong collateral or guarantees. All Tier 3 exceptions are subject to quarterly review by the CRC to ensure
ongoing compliance and risk management.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 7

7. 7. Monitoring and Controls
Monitoring and controls are critical to ensuring compliance with the leverage limits outlined in this clause. The bank employs a
multi-layered monitoring framework, combining automated system checks with manual oversight to identify and address
leverage limit breaches promptly.
The bank’s credit risk management system automatically calculates leverage ratios for all wholesale exposures on a daily basis,
using the most recent financial data available. The system generates alerts for any breaches of approved leverage limits, as
well as for exposures approaching within 10% of their limits. These alerts are distributed to the relevant relationship managers,
credit officers, and risk teams via a centralized dashboard.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data, and the monitoring processes described are illustrative. They do not reflect the
actual control mechanisms of any real financial institution and should not be relied upon for real-world applications.
In addition to automated monitoring, the Wholesale Credit Risk team conducts a monthly review of all leverage limit breaches
and near-breaches. This review includes an assessment of the root causes of the breaches, the effectiveness of corrective
actions, and any emerging trends that may indicate systemic issues. The findings are reported to the CRC and the Chief Credit
Officer, with recommendations for policy adjustments or additional controls where necessary.
The bank also conducts quarterly stress tests on its wholesale portfolio to evaluate the potential impact of adverse scenarios on
leverage ratios. These stress tests incorporate macroeconomic shocks, such as GDP contractions, interest rate spikes, and
industry-specific downturns. The results are used to inform the bank’s risk appetite and may trigger adjustments to leverage
limits or additional capital allocations for high-risk exposures.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 8

8. 8. Exception Management
Exception management under this clause is designed to ensure that any deviations from the established leverage limits are
identified, documented, and resolved in a timely and controlled manner. The bank’s exception management framework is
governed by the principle that exceptions should be rare, justified, and subject to rigorous oversight.
All leverage limit exceptions must be logged in the bank’s centralized exception tracking system, which captures details such as
the borrower’s name, the nature and magnitude of the breach, the approval authority, and the rationale for the exception. The
system also tracks the status of corrective action plans and the timeline for resolution. Exceptions are categorized by severity,
with Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 classifications aligning with the approval authority hierarchy.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data, and the exception management processes described are fictional. They are
provided for illustrative purposes only and do not represent the actual practices of any real financial institution.
For each exception, the relationship manager is required to develop a corrective action plan within 5 business days of
identification. The plan must outline specific steps to bring the exposure back within the approved leverage limits, as well as the
timeline for implementation. Corrective actions may include requesting additional collateral, restructuring the facility, or reducing
the exposure through partial repayment or asset sales.
Exceptions that remain unresolved for more than 30 days are escalated to the next level of approval authority. For example, a
Tier 1 exception that is not resolved within 30 days is escalated to the Head of Wholesale Credit Risk for review. The CRC
receives a quarterly report on all outstanding exceptions, including their age, status, and the effectiveness of corrective actions.
Persistent or recurring exceptions may trigger a review of the underlying leverage limits or the bank’s risk appetite for the
affected sector or borrower.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 9

9. 9. Reporting
Reporting is a key component of the bank’s leverage limits framework, providing transparency and accountability to
stakeholders at all levels of the organization. The bank employs a structured reporting hierarchy, with information tailored to the
needs of different audiences, from front-line relationship managers to the bank’s executive leadership and board.
At the operational level, relationship managers receive daily alerts and weekly reports on leverage limit breaches and
near-breaches for their respective portfolios. These reports include details on the magnitude of the breach, the approval status
of any exceptions, and the progress of corrective action plans. The Wholesale Credit Risk team consolidates this information
into a monthly report for regional credit officers, highlighting trends, recurring issues, and areas requiring attention.
This clause is synthetic demonstration data, and the reporting processes described are illustrative. They do not reflect the
actual reporting practices of any real financial institution and should not be used for real-world decision-making.
The CRC receives a comprehensive quarterly report on leverage limits, which includes an overview of all breaches, exceptions,
and corrective actions across the wholesale portfolio. The report also provides an analysis of leverage trends by industry,
region, and credit rating, as well as the results of stress tests and their implications for the bank’s risk appetite. The CRC uses
this information to assess the effectiveness of the leverage limits policy and to identify any emerging risks that may require
policy adjustments.
The bank’s Board Risk Committee (BRC) receives an annual report on leverage limits, summarizing the key findings from the
CRC’s quarterly reviews, as well as any material changes to the policy or its implementation. The BRC report also includes a
high-level assessment of the bank’s leverage exposure relative to its risk appetite and regulatory expectations. Additionally, the
bank’s external auditors may request leverage limit reports as part of their annual review of the bank’s credit risk management
framework.

10. 10. Policy Review and Updates
The 4.2 Leverage Limits clause is subject to regular review to ensure its continued relevance, effectiveness, and alignment with
the bank’s risk appetite and regulatory requirements. The policy review process is overseen by the Credit Risk Committee
(CRC) and involves input from a range of stakeholders, including the Wholesale Credit Risk team, Industry Risk, Quantitative
Analytics, and Internal Audit.
The policy is reviewed at least annually, with the CRC conducting a comprehensive assessment of its performance, including
an evaluation of leverage limit breaches, the effectiveness of corrective actions, and the adequacy of the quantitative
thresholds. The review also considers changes in the bank’s risk appetite, as well as developments in the regulatory landscape,
such as updates to Basel III or other relevant frameworks.

2. 2. Scope
Clause 4.3 Tenor Limits applies to all wholesale banking activities conducted by the bank, including its domestic and
international operations. The scope of this clause encompasses all credit facilities extended to corporate clients, financial
institutions, and other wholesale counterparties, regardless of the jurisdiction or currency of the transaction.
The policy is binding on all business units, including Corporate Banking, Investment Banking, Trade Finance, and Treasury, as
well as support functions such as Risk Management, Compliance, and Internal Audit. Each unit is responsible for ensuring that
its activities comply with the tenor limits and procedures outlined in this clause.
Exclusions from this policy include retail banking products, consumer lending, and credit card facilities, which are governed by
separate policies tailored to their unique risk profiles. Additionally, intra-group transactions and exposures to sovereign entities
may be subject to customized tenor limits as approved by the Group Risk Committee.
The synthetic demonstration data within this clause includes hypothetical tenor thresholds, such as a maximum tenor of 10
years for term loans to investment-grade corporates and a maximum tenor of 5 years for non-investment-grade corporates.
These thresholds are illustrative and designed to demonstrate how tenor limits might be structured in a real-world scenario.
All exceptions to the scope of this policy must be documented and approved by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) or their designated
delegate. Such exceptions will be subject to enhanced monitoring and reporting to ensure that any deviations from the standard
tenor limits do not introduce unacceptable levels of risk to the bank.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 1
 4.3 Tenor Limits
CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose
The purpose of Clause 4.3 Tenor Limits under the Parent Policy CP-Wholesale-v4.2 is to establish a structured framework for
managing the tenor of credit exposures extended to wholesale clients. This clause ensures that the bank’s credit risk appetite is
aligned with the tenor of obligations assumed, thereby mitigating the potential for liquidity mismatches, concentration risk, and
long-term exposure to adverse market conditions. By defining clear tenor limits, the bank aims to balance its commitment to
supporting client needs with prudent risk management practices.
Tenor limits are critical in ensuring that the bank’s assets and liabilities are appropriately matched, reducing the risk of liquidity
shortfalls that could arise from an overconcentration of long-term lending without corresponding long-term funding. This clause
provides the necessary guidelines to underwriters, credit analysts, and relationship managers to assess and approve credit
facilities with tenors that are consistent with the bank’s strategic objectives and risk tolerance.
The synthetic nature of this document is emphasized to clarify that while the policy is designed to reflect real-world banking
practices, it is intended solely for demonstration and testing purposes. All thresholds, roles, and procedures outlined herein are
illustrative and should not be interpreted as binding or reflective of any actual financial institution’s policies.
This clause operates in conjunction with other sections of CP-Wholesale-v4.2, particularly those addressing credit risk
assessment, collateral requirements, and portfolio diversification. Together, these policies form a cohesive risk management
framework that supports the bank’s wholesale banking activities while safeguarding its financial stability.
The tenor limits defined in this clause are applicable to all wholesale credit exposures, including but not limited to term loans,
revolving credit facilities, letters of credit, and other forms of committed and uncommitted credit. The policy ensures that
tenor-related decisions are made with a full understanding of their implications on the bank’s risk profile and capital adequacy.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope
Clause 4.3 Tenor Limits applies to all wholesale banking activities conducted by the bank, including its domestic and
international operations. The scope of this clause encompasses all credit facilities extended to corporate clients, financial
institutions, and other wholesale counterparties, regardless of the jurisdiction or currency of the transaction.
The policy is binding on all business units, including Corporate Banking, Investment Banking, Trade Finance, and Treasury, as
well as support functions such as Risk Management, Compliance, and Internal Audit. Each unit is responsible for ensuring that
its activities comply with the tenor limits and procedures outlined in this clause.
Exclusions from this policy include retail banking products, consumer lending, and credit card facilities, which are governed by
separate policies tailored to their unique risk profiles. Additionally, intra-group transactions and exposures to sovereign entities
may be subject to customized tenor limits as approved by the Group Risk Committee.
The synthetic demonstration data within this clause includes hypothetical tenor thresholds, such as a maximum tenor of 10
years for term loans to investment-grade corporates and a maximum tenor of 5 years for non-investment-grade corporates.
These thresholds are illustrative and designed to demonstrate how tenor limits might be structured in a real-world scenario.
All exceptions to the scope of this policy must be documented and approved by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) or their designated
delegate. Such exceptions will be subject to enhanced monitoring and reporting to ensure that any deviations from the standard
tenor limits do not introduce unacceptable levels of risk to the bank.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 3

3. 3. Governance
The governance framework for Clause 4.3 Tenor Limits is designed to ensure accountability, transparency, and adherence to
the bank’s risk management principles. Oversight of this clause rests with the Group Credit Committee (GCC), which is
responsible for approving any changes to the tenor limits and ensuring their alignment with the bank’s overall risk appetite.
The Credit Risk Management (CRM) department is tasked with the day-to-day administration of this policy, including the
development of procedures, the provision of guidance to business units, and the monitoring of compliance with tenor limits.
CRM is also responsible for conducting periodic reviews of the policy’s effectiveness and recommending adjustments as
necessary.
Business units are required to designate a Tenor Limit Officer (TLO) who will serve as the primary point of contact for all
matters related to this clause. The TLO is responsible for ensuring that all credit proposals submitted by their unit comply with
the tenor limits and that any exceptions are properly escalated and documented.
The governance structure includes a three-tiered approval process for tenor limit exceptions. Tier 1 exceptions, which involve
minor deviations from the standard limits, may be approved by the TLO in consultation with CRM. Tier 2 exceptions, which
involve moderate deviations, require the approval of the Business Unit Head and the CRO. Tier 3 exceptions, which involve
significant deviations, must be approved by the GCC.
Audit and compliance functions are independent of the business units and CRM, ensuring objective oversight of the policy’s
implementation. Internal Audit conducts annual reviews of the tenor limit compliance, while Compliance monitors adherence to
regulatory requirements and internal policies.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 4

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
The underwriting criteria for tenor limits are designed to ensure that the tenor of any credit facility is commensurate with the
borrower’s creditworthiness, the purpose of the facility, and the bank’s risk appetite. The primary factors considered in
determining the appropriate tenor include the borrower’s financial strength, cash flow stability, industry risk, and the economic
environment.
For investment-grade corporates, the maximum tenor for term loans is set at 10 years, provided that the borrower demonstrates
strong and stable cash flows, a low leverage ratio, and a history of prudent financial management. For non-investment-grade
corporates, the maximum tenor is limited to 5 years, reflecting the higher risk of default and the need for more frequent credit
reviews.
The purpose of the credit facility also plays a critical role in determining the tenor. For example, working capital facilities typically
have shorter tenors, often not exceeding 3 years, as they are intended to support short-term liquidity needs. In contrast, project
finance facilities may have longer tenors, up to 15 years, to align with the long-term nature of the underlying assets and cash
flows.
Underwriters are required to conduct a thorough analysis of the borrower’s ability to service debt over the proposed tenor. This
analysis includes stress testing the borrower’s financials under various scenarios, such as economic downturns,
industry-specific shocks, and changes in interest rates. The results of these stress tests must be documented in the credit
proposal and reviewed by CRM.
Collateral and other credit enhancements may influence the tenor limits. For instance, facilities that are fully secured by
high-quality collateral may qualify for longer tenors, as the bank’s risk is mitigated by the presence of the collateral. However,
the tenor must still be consistent with the bank’s overall risk appetite and the borrower’s ability to generate sufficient cash flows
to service the debt.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 5

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
Clause 4.3 Tenor Limits establishes quantitative thresholds to guide the structuring of credit facilities and ensure consistency
across the bank’s wholesale portfolio. These limits are designed to balance the bank’s risk appetite with its commitment to
supporting client needs and are applied based on the borrower’s credit rating, industry, and the type of facility.
For term loans, the maximum tenor is 10 years for borrowers rated BBB- or higher by a recognized credit rating agency. For
borrowers rated below BBB-, the maximum tenor is 5 years. These limits are designed to reflect the higher probability of default
and the increased volatility in cash flows associated with lower-rated borrowers.
Revolving credit facilities are subject to a maximum tenor of 5 years, regardless of the borrower’s credit rating. This limit reflects
the short-term nature of these facilities and the need for regular reassessment of the borrower’s creditworthiness. Exceptions to
this limit may be granted for facilities that are fully secured by high-quality collateral, subject to approval by the GCC.
Trade finance facilities, including letters of credit and bank guarantees, are typically limited to a maximum tenor of 1 year.
However, for long-term trade finance transactions, such as those supporting infrastructure projects, the tenor may be extended
up to 5 years, provided that the underlying transaction is supported by robust cash flows and adequate collateral.
The bank also imposes aggregate tenor limits on its wholesale portfolio to prevent excessive concentration in long-term
exposures. For example, no more than 30% of the bank’s total wholesale credit portfolio may have a tenor exceeding 5 years.
This limit is monitored on a quarterly basis by CRM, and any breaches must be reported to the GCC for remediation.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 6

6. 6. Approvals
The approval process for tenor limits is designed to ensure that all credit facilities are structured in accordance with the bank’s
risk appetite and that any deviations from the standard limits are properly justified, documented, and approved by the
appropriate authority. The process is tiered based on the size of the facility, the borrower’s credit rating, and the extent of the
deviation from the standard limits.
For standard credit facilities that comply with the tenor limits outlined in this clause, approval authority rests with the Business
Unit Head, provided that the facility size does not exceed the unit’s delegated authority. Facilities that exceed the unit’s
delegated authority or involve non-standard tenors require approval from CRM and, in some cases, the GCC.
Tier 1 exceptions, which involve minor deviations from the standard tenor limits (e.g., extending the tenor of a term loan to a
non-investment-grade borrower by up to 1 year), may be approved by the TLO in consultation with CRM. The TLO must
document the rationale for the exception, including the borrower’s financial strength, the purpose of the facility, and any
mitigating factors such as collateral or guarantees.
Tier 2 exceptions, which involve moderate deviations (e.g., extending the tenor of a term loan to a non-investment-grade
borrower by more than 1 year but not exceeding 3 years), require the approval of the Business Unit Head and the CRO. The
credit proposal must include a detailed analysis of the borrower’s ability to service the debt over the extended tenor, as well as
an assessment of the impact on the bank’s risk profile.
Tier 3 exceptions, which involve significant deviations (e.g., extending the tenor of a term loan to a non-investment-grade
borrower by more than 3 years or exceeding the aggregate portfolio limits), must be approved by the GCC. These exceptions
are subject to enhanced due diligence, including independent validation of the borrower’s financial projections and stress
testing under severe economic scenarios.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 7

7. 7. Monitoring
Monitoring of tenor limits is a critical component of the bank’s credit risk management framework, ensuring that the portfolio
remains aligned with the bank’s risk appetite and that any emerging risks are identified and addressed in a timely manner. CRM
is responsible for the ongoing monitoring of tenor limits, with support from the business units and Independent Risk Control
(IRC).
The monitoring process includes regular reviews of the bank’s wholesale credit portfolio to ensure compliance with the tenor
limits outlined in this clause. CRM conducts monthly reviews of new credit facilities to verify that they adhere to the approved
tenor limits and that any exceptions have been properly documented and approved.
In addition to compliance monitoring, CRM conducts quarterly reviews of the bank’s aggregate tenor exposure to assess
whether the portfolio remains within the established limits. These reviews include an analysis of the distribution of tenors across
different credit ratings, industries, and geographic regions, as well as an assessment of the potential impact of macroeconomic
trends on the portfolio’s risk profile.
Business units are responsible for monitoring the tenor of individual credit facilities within their portfolios. This includes tracking
the remaining tenor of each facility, assessing the borrower’s ongoing ability to service the debt, and identifying any early
warning signs of potential credit deterioration. Any facilities approaching their maturity date must be reviewed at least 12
months in advance to determine whether they should be renewed, restructured, or allowed to mature.
The monitoring process also includes the use of automated tools and dashboards to track tenor limits and exceptions in real
time. These tools provide alerts for any breaches of the tenor limits, as well as for facilities that are approaching their maturity
dates or exhibiting signs of increased risk. CRM is responsible for investigating and resolving any alerts in a timely manner, in
coordination with the relevant business units.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 8

8. 8. Exceptions
Exceptions to the tenor limits outlined in Clause 4.3 are permitted under specific circumstances, provided that they are justified
by the borrower’s creditworthiness, the purpose of the facility, and the bank’s strategic objectives. All exceptions must be
documented, approved by the appropriate authority, and subject to enhanced monitoring and reporting.
The most common justification for an exception is the presence of strong mitigating factors, such as high-quality collateral,
third-party guarantees, or the borrower’s demonstrated ability to generate stable and predictable cash flows over the extended
tenor. Exceptions may also be granted for facilities that support strategic transactions, such as large-scale infrastructure
projects or long-term trade finance deals, where the bank has a strong commercial interest.
The process for requesting an exception begins with the submission of a credit proposal by the business unit, which includes a
detailed rationale for the exception, an analysis of the borrower’s financial strength, and an assessment of the impact on the
bank’s risk profile. The proposal must also include a plan for monitoring the facility and mitigating any additional risks introduced
by the extended tenor.
Once submitted, the proposal is reviewed by CRM, which assesses the justification for the exception and the adequacy of the
risk mitigants. CRM may request additional information or analysis from the business unit before making a recommendation.
For Tier 1 and Tier 2 exceptions, CRM’s recommendation is forwarded to the TLO or the Business Unit Head and CRO,
respectively, for approval. For Tier 3 exceptions, the recommendation is forwarded to the GCC.
All approved exceptions are documented in the bank’s exception register, which is maintained by CRM and reviewed by the
GCC on a quarterly basis. The register includes details of the exception, the rationale for approval, the mitigating factors, and
the enhanced monitoring and reporting requirements. Exceptions are also subject to post-approval audits by Internal Audit to
ensure compliance with the approved terms and conditions.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 9

9. 9. Reporting
Reporting is a key control mechanism for ensuring transparency and accountability in the management of tenor limits. The
bank’s reporting framework for Clause 4.3 Tenor Limits is designed to provide timely and accurate information to senior
management, the GCC, and other stakeholders, enabling them to monitor compliance, assess risk exposures, and make
informed decisions.
CRM is responsible for preparing and distributing a monthly Tenor Limit Compliance Report, which provides a summary of all
new credit facilities approved during the month, including their tenors, borrower credit ratings, and any exceptions granted. The
report also highlights any breaches of the tenor limits and the actions taken to remediate them.
In addition to the monthly compliance report, CRM prepares a quarterly Tenor Risk Exposure Report, which provides a
comprehensive analysis of the bank’s aggregate tenor exposure. This report includes a breakdown of the portfolio by tenor,
credit rating, industry, and geographic region, as well as an assessment of the potential impact of macroeconomic trends on the
portfolio’s risk profile. The report also includes a summary of all active exceptions and their status.
Business units are required to prepare and submit a monthly Tenor Monitoring Report to CRM, detailing the status of all credit
facilities within their portfolios, including their remaining tenors, any early warning signs of credit deterioration, and the results of
their ongoing monitoring activities. This information is used by CRM to update the bank’s central credit registry and to identify
any emerging risks.
The GCC receives a dedicated Tenor Limit Exception Report on a quarterly basis, which provides a detailed review of all
exceptions approved during the quarter, including the rationale for each exception, the mitigating factors, and the enhanced
monitoring and reporting requirements. The report also includes an assessment of the overall effectiveness of the tenor limit
policy and any recommendations for improvements or adjustments.

CP-Wholesale-v4.2 §4.3 | Synthetic policy data
Page 10

10. 10. Review
Clause 4.3 Tenor Limits is subject to regular review to ensure that it remains aligned with the bank’s risk appetite, market
conditions, and regulatory requirements. The review process is designed to assess the policy’s effectiveness, identify any gaps
or deficiencies, and recommend adjustments as necessary to enhance the bank’s credit risk management framework.
The policy is reviewed annually by CRM, in consultation with the business units, Compliance, and Internal Audit. The annual
review includes an assessment of the policy’s adherence to regulatory requirements, its alignment with industry best practices,
and its effectiveness in managing tenor-related risks. The review also considers feedback from business units and other
stakeholders on the policy’s practicality and any challenges encountered in its implementation.
In addition to the annual review, the policy is subject to ad hoc reviews in response to significant changes in the bank’s risk
appetite, market conditions, or regulatory environment. For example, a material deterioration in economic conditions or a
change in the bank’s strategic priorities may prompt a review of the tenor limits to ensure that they remain appropriate and
effective.
The review process includes a comprehensive analysis of the bank’s tenor exposure and the performance of facilities with
non-standard tenors. This analysis assesses whether the existing limits and exceptions have contributed to the bank’s risk
profile in a manner consistent with its risk appetite and whether any adjustments are needed to better align the policy with the
bank’s objectives.
The results of the review are documented in a Tenor Limit Policy Review Report, which is presented to the GCC for approval.
The report includes a summary of the review’s findings, any recommended changes to the policy, and a plan for implementing
those changes. Once approved by the GCC, the updated policy is communicated to all relevant stakeholders, and training is
provided as necessary to ensure that the changes are effectively implemented.

This Policy is a subordinate clause
of the Parent Policy CP-Wholesale-v4.2. It establishes the framework for the structuring, negotiation, documentation, and
monitoring of covenant packages applicable to wholesale credit exposures.

2. 2. Scope and Definitions
This Policy applies to all wholesale credit exposures, including but not limited to bilateral loans, syndicated facilities, revolving
credit agreements, term loans, and other structured credit products. It covers all jurisdictions in which the Bank operates, unless
superseded by local regulatory requirements or specific legal constraints.
For the purposes of this Policy, the term 'covenant' refers to any condition or requirement stipulated in a credit agreement that
the borrower must fulfill. Covenants are classified into two primary categories: (1) Financial Covenants, which are quantitative
measures of the borrower’s financial health, and (2) Non-Financial Covenants, which are qualitative or operational conditions
that the borrower must meet.
Financial Covenants include, but are not limited to, the following: (a) Maximum Leverage Ratio (Total Debt/EBITDA), (b)
Minimum Interest Coverage Ratio (EBITDA/Interest Expense), (c) Minimum Debt Service Coverage Ratio (Net Operating
Income/Total Debt Service), and (d) Minimum Net Worth. These covenants are designed to ensure the borrower maintains a
financial position consistent with the Bank’s risk assessment at the time of approval.
Non-Financial Covenants may include requirements such as the maintenance of adequate insurance coverage, compliance
with all applicable laws and regulations, restrictions on additional indebtedness, limitations on asset disposals, and obligations
to provide periodic financial statements and other reporting. These covenants are critical for mitigating operational and legal
risks associated with the borrower’s activities.
The term 'Covenant Package' refers to the collective set of financial and non-financial covenants agreed upon between the
Bank and the borrower, as documented in the credit agreement. The Covenant Package must be approved by the relevant
credit authority in accordance with the Bank’s delegation of authority framework, as outlined in Parent Policy
CP-Wholesale-v4.2.
