extracted.name: RAROC Methodology and Calculation Formula
extracted.source_quote:
4. 4. RAROC Methodology and Calculation
The RAROC for each credit exposure is calculated using the bank’s internal economic profit model, which adjusts nominal
returns for risk, cost of capital, and operational expenses. The formula for RAROC is defined as: RAROC = (Risk-Adjusted
Revenue - Expected Loss - Operating Costs) / Economic Capital. Risk-Adjusted Revenue reflects the net interest income and
fees associated with the exposure, adjusted for credit spreads and other risk premiums.
Economic Capital is determined using the bank’s internal capital allocation model, which assigns capital to each exposure
based on its risk characteristics, including probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), and exposure at default (EAD).
The model incorporates both systematic and idiosyncratic risk factors and is calibrated to a 99.9% confidence interval over a
one-year horizon, in line with Basel III standards.
Expected Loss is calculated as the product of PD, LGD, and EAD, representing the average annual loss expected from the
exposure. Operating Costs include all direct and indirect expenses associated with originating, servicing, and monitoring the
credit exposure, such as underwriting fees, legal costs, and administrative overhead. These costs are allocated to individual
exposures based on their complexity and resource requirements.
The bank employs a tiered RAROC floor structure, with minimum thresholds varying by asset class, risk rating, and tenure. For
example, investment-grade corporate exposures are subject to a minimum RAROC floor of 12%, while sub-investment-grade
exposures require a floor of 18%. Commercial real estate exposures are assigned a floor of 15%, reflecting their higher volatility
and illiquidity risk. These thresholds are reviewed annually by the CPC and adjusted based on changes in the bank’s cost of
capital, risk appetite, or market conditions.
All RAROC calculations must be performed using the bank’s approved modeling tools and validated by the CRM department.
Manual overrides or adjustments to the model inputs are prohibited unless explicitly approved by the CRO. The methodology
and assumptions underlying the RAROC calculations are documented in the bank’s Model Risk Management Policy, which is
referenced in this document.

extracted.name: Reporting and Transparency Framework
extracted.source_quote:
9. 9. Reporting and Transparency
The bank maintains a comprehensive reporting framework to ensure transparency and accountability in the application of
RAROC floors. Monthly RAROC compliance reports are generated by the CRM department and distributed to Business Unit
Heads, the CPC, and the CRO. These reports include a summary of all exposures by asset class, risk rating, and RAROC
performance, as well as a detailed breakdown of exceptions and their status.
The monthly reports also highlight trends in RAROC performance, such as deteriorating or improving segments, and provide an
analysis of the drivers behind these trends. This includes changes in market conditions, credit spreads, or the bank’s cost of
capital. The reports are designed to facilitate proactive risk management and to inform strategic decisions regarding portfolio
composition and risk appetite.
Quarterly, the CRM department prepares a more detailed RAROC Performance Review, which is presented to the CPC and the
Board Risk Committee. This review includes an assessment of the bank’s overall RAROC performance, a comparison against
peer benchmarks, and an evaluation of the effectiveness of the RAROC floors in achieving the bank’s risk-adjusted return
objectives. The review also identifies any emerging risks or opportunities for improvement.
In addition to internal reporting, the bank includes RAROC metrics in its external disclosures, such as the annual report and
pillar 3 regulatory filings. These disclosures provide stakeholders with insight into the bank’s risk-adjusted performance and its
adherence to internal policies. The bank is committed to maintaining the confidentiality of client-specific information while
ensuring transparency in its aggregate RAROC performance.
Ad-hoc reporting is also available upon request from senior management, regulators, or other stakeholders. The CRM
department is responsible for ensuring that all reports are accurate, timely, and aligned with the bank’s data governance
standards. Any discrepancies or errors in reporting must be investigated and corrected promptly, with root cause analysis
conducted to prevent recurrence.

extracted.name: Policy Review and Amendments Mandate
extracted.source_quote:
10. 10. Policy Review and Amendments
This policy is subject to annual review by the CPC to ensure its continued relevance, effectiveness, and alignment with the
bank’s strategic objectives and risk appetite. The review process includes an assessment of the policy’s performance against its
stated objectives, an evaluation of emerging risks and market developments, and a benchmarking exercise against industry
best practices.
Amendments to the policy, including adjustments to RAROC floors or changes to governance structures, must be approved by
the CPC and, where material, by the Board Risk Committee. Proposed amendments are typically developed by the CRM
department in consultation with relevant stakeholders, including Business Units, Finance, and Risk Control. The CRM
department is responsible for conducting impact assessments to evaluate the potential effects of proposed changes on the
bank’s credit portfolio and economic profit.
The policy review process also includes a retrospective analysis of exceptions and waivers granted under the policy, with a
focus on identifying any patterns or systemic issues. This analysis informs recommendations for policy enhancements, such as
the introduction of new asset class-specific floors, adjustments to escalation paths, or revisions to the RAROC calculation
methodology.
In addition to the annual review, the CPC may initiate an interim review of the policy in response to significant changes in the
bank’s risk profile, cost of capital, or external regulatory environment. Such reviews are conducted on an expedited basis, with
amendments implemented as soon as practicable. All changes to the policy are communicated to relevant stakeholders through
formal policy updates, training sessions, and internal memoranda.
This synthetic policy is designed to be a living document, evolving in response to the dynamic nature of the banking industry
and the bank’s strategic priorities. The CPC is committed to ensuring that the policy remains a robust and effective tool for
managing risk-adjusted returns, while also fostering a culture of continuous improvement and innovation in credit risk
management.

10. 10. Policy Review and Amendments
This policy is subject to annual review by the CPC to ensure its continued relevance, effectiveness, and alignment with the
bank’s strategic objectives and risk appetite. The review process includes an assessment of the policy’s performance against its
stated objectives, an evaluation of emerging risks and market developments, and a benchmarking exercise against industry
best practices.
Amendments to the policy, including adjustments to RAROC floors or changes to governance structures, must be approved by
the CPC and, where material, by the Board Risk Committee. Proposed amendments are typically developed by the CRM
department in consultation with relevant stakeholders, including Business Units, Finance, and Risk Control. The CRM
department is responsible for conducting impact assessments to evaluate the potential effects of proposed changes on the
bank’s credit portfolio and economic profit.
The policy review process also includes a retrospective analysis of exceptions and waivers granted under the policy, with a
focus on identifying any patterns or systemic issues. This analysis informs recommendations for policy enhancements, such as
the introduction of new asset class-specific floors, adjustments to escalation paths, or revisions to the RAROC calculation
methodology.
In addition to the annual review, the CPC may initiate an interim review of the policy in response to significant changes in the
bank’s risk profile, cost of capital, or external regulatory environment. Such reviews are conducted on an expedited basis, with
amendments implemented as soon as practicable. All changes to the policy are communicated to relevant stakeholders through
formal policy updates, training sessions, and internal memoranda.
This synthetic policy is designed to be a living document, evolving in response to the dynamic nature of the banking industry
and the bank’s strategic priorities. The CPC is committed to ensuring that the policy remains a robust and effective tool for
managing risk-adjusted returns, while also fostering a culture of continuous improvement and innovation in credit risk
management.

 1.1 RAROC Floors
PRC-v1.7 §1.1 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose and Objectives
This synthetic demonstration document, titled '1.1 RAROC Floors,' establishes the Risk-Adjusted Return on Capital (RAROC)
floors for credit transactions under the parent policy PRC-v1.7. The purpose of this policy is to ensure that all credit exposures
generate returns commensurate with their risk, aligning with the bank’s strategic objectives of sustainable profitability and
risk-adjusted performance optimization. By setting explicit RAROC floors, the bank aims to prevent the erosion of economic
value through suboptimal risk-taking and to foster a culture of disciplined credit origination and portfolio management.
The primary objective of this policy is to define minimum acceptable RAROC thresholds for various credit asset classes,
ensuring that each transaction or portfolio segment contributes positively to the bank’s economic profit. These thresholds are
designed to account for the cost of capital, expected losses, and operational expenses, thereby reflecting the true economic
value of credit activities. The policy also seeks to harmonize risk appetite across business units by providing a consistent
framework for evaluating creditworthiness and pricing risk.
This document is synthetic and intended for demonstration purposes only. It does not reflect the actual policies, thresholds, or
practices of any real financial institution. All numerical values, roles, and processes described herein are fictional and designed
to illustrate a comprehensive credit policy framework.
The RAROC floors established in this policy serve as a critical control mechanism to mitigate the risk of adverse selection and
to ensure that credit extensions are only made when they meet or exceed the bank’s hurdle rates. This aligns with the broader
goal of maintaining a robust and resilient credit portfolio that can withstand economic downturns while delivering consistent
shareholder value. The policy is integral to the bank’s enterprise-wide risk management framework and supports compliance
with internal governance standards and external regulatory expectations.
Additionally, this policy aims to promote transparency and accountability in credit decision-making by requiring explicit
justification for any deviations from the established RAROC floors. Such deviations must be supported by rigorous analysis and
approved through defined escalation paths, ensuring that exceptions are rare, well-documented, and aligned with the bank’s
strategic priorities.

PRC-v1.7 §1.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope and Applicability
This policy applies to all credit exposures originated, renewed, or managed by the bank, including but not limited to corporate
loans, commercial real estate financing, project finance, and structured credit products. It encompasses both new transactions
and the periodic review of existing exposures to ensure continued compliance with RAROC floors. The policy is binding on all
business units, risk management functions, and support departments involved in credit underwriting, pricing, and monitoring.
The scope of this policy includes all jurisdictions in which the bank operates, unless superseded by local regulatory
requirements or more stringent internal policies. In such cases, the higher of the two standards must be applied. The policy is
designed to be scalable, accommodating the diverse risk profiles of the bank’s global portfolio while maintaining consistency in
the application of RAROC principles.
Exclusions from this policy are limited to credit exposures explicitly exempted by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) or the Credit
Policy Committee (CPC), provided such exemptions are documented and justified. Typical exclusions may include sovereign
exposures, interbank placements, or transactions subject to government guarantees, where risk-adjusted returns are evaluated
under separate frameworks.
The policy is applicable to all personnel involved in credit-related activities, including relationship managers, credit analysts, risk
officers, and senior management. Compliance with this policy is a mandatory requirement for all credit approvals, and
non-adherence may result in the rejection of proposals or escalation to higher authorities for review.
For the purposes of this synthetic demonstration, the policy assumes a hypothetical global banking institution with a diverse
credit portfolio. The applicability of RAROC floors is extended to all material credit exposures, regardless of size or complexity,
to ensure a uniform standard of risk-adjusted performance across the organization.

PRC-v1.7 §1.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 3

3. 3. Governance and Roles
The governance framework for this policy is overseen by the Credit Policy Committee (CPC), which is responsible for its
approval, periodic review, and amendment. The CPC is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) and includes representatives
from Credit Risk, Finance, Business Units, and Independent Risk Control. The committee meets quarterly to assess the
effectiveness of the policy and to approve any proposed changes to RAROC floors or related thresholds.
The implementation of this policy is the responsibility of the Credit Risk Management (CRM) department, which is tasked with
ensuring that all credit exposures adhere to the established RAROC floors. CRM is also responsible for developing
methodologies, tools, and training programs to support the consistent application of the policy across the bank. The Head of
CRM reports directly to the CRO and provides regular updates on policy compliance and exceptions.
Business Unit Heads are accountable for ensuring that their respective teams adhere to the policy and that all credit proposals
submitted for approval meet the minimum RAROC requirements. They are also responsible for escalating any potential
breaches or exceptions to the CRM department for review and approval. Relationship managers and credit analysts are
required to incorporate RAROC calculations into their credit assessments and to document any deviations from the policy.
The Finance department plays a critical role in providing the cost of capital and other financial inputs required for RAROC
calculations. It is also responsible for validating the economic profit models used to determine RAROC and for ensuring that the
policy’s thresholds are aligned with the bank’s overall financial objectives. The Internal Audit function conducts periodic reviews
of the policy’s implementation to verify compliance and to identify any gaps or areas for improvement.
For this synthetic policy, the governance structure is designed to reflect industry best practices, with clear segregation of duties
and escalation paths. All roles and responsibilities are documented in the bank’s broader Credit Policy Framework, which this
document supplements.

PRC-v1.7 §1.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 4

4. 4. RAROC Methodology and Calculation
The RAROC for each credit exposure is calculated using the bank’s internal economic profit model, which adjusts nominal
returns for risk, cost of capital, and operational expenses. The formula for RAROC is defined as: RAROC = (Risk-Adjusted
Revenue - Expected Loss - Operating Costs) / Economic Capital. Risk-Adjusted Revenue reflects the net interest income and
fees associated with the exposure, adjusted for credit spreads and other risk premiums.
Economic Capital is determined using the bank’s internal capital allocation model, which assigns capital to each exposure
based on its risk characteristics, including probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), and exposure at default (EAD).
The model incorporates both systematic and idiosyncratic risk factors and is calibrated to a 99.9% confidence interval over a
one-year horizon, in line with Basel III standards.
Expected Loss is calculated as the product of PD, LGD, and EAD, representing the average annual loss expected from the
exposure. Operating Costs include all direct and indirect expenses associated with originating, servicing, and monitoring the
credit exposure, such as underwriting fees, legal costs, and administrative overhead. These costs are allocated to individual
exposures based on their complexity and resource requirements.
The bank employs a tiered RAROC floor structure, with minimum thresholds varying by asset class, risk rating, and tenure. For
example, investment-grade corporate exposures are subject to a minimum RAROC floor of 12%, while sub-investment-grade
exposures require a floor of 18%. Commercial real estate exposures are assigned a floor of 15%, reflecting their higher volatility
and illiquidity risk. These thresholds are reviewed annually by the CPC and adjusted based on changes in the bank’s cost of
capital, risk appetite, or market conditions.
All RAROC calculations must be performed using the bank’s approved modeling tools and validated by the CRM department.
Manual overrides or adjustments to the model inputs are prohibited unless explicitly approved by the CRO. The methodology
and assumptions underlying the RAROC calculations are documented in the bank’s Model Risk Management Policy, which is
referenced in this document.

PRC-v1.7 §1.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 5

5. 5. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
This policy establishes the following RAROC floors for the bank’s primary credit asset classes, which serve as the minimum
acceptable thresholds for new originations and portfolio reviews. For Corporate Loans, the RAROC floor is set at 12% for
investment-grade (IG) exposures (rated BBB- or higher) and 18% for non-investment-grade (NIG) exposures (rated BB+ or
lower). Exceptions to these floors require approval from the Head of CRM and the relevant Business Unit Head.
Commercial Real Estate (CRE) exposures are subject to a RAROC floor of 15%, reflecting the higher risk and illiquidity
associated with this asset class. Within CRE, sub-segments such as development loans and speculative construction financing
are assigned a higher floor of 20% due to their elevated risk profiles. The RAROC for CRE exposures must be calculated at
both the individual loan and portfolio levels to ensure compliance with the policy.
For Project Finance, the RAROC floor is set at 16%, accounting for the long-term, non-recourse nature of these exposures and
the complexity of their cash flow structures. Structured Credit Products, including collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) and
credit derivatives, are subject to a floor of 22%, reflecting their leverage, complexity, and potential for tail risk. These thresholds
are applied to both the underlying assets and the tranched structures.
Retail and Small Business Lending portfolios are evaluated on an aggregate basis, with a minimum RAROC floor of 10% for the
entire portfolio. Individual loans within these portfolios are not required to meet the floor, provided the overall portfolio RAROC
exceeds the threshold. However, any sub-portfolio or segment exhibiting a RAROC below 8% must be flagged for review and
remediation by the CRM department.
The RAROC floors are dynamic and subject to adjustment based on macroeconomic conditions, changes in the bank’s cost of
capital, or shifts in strategic priorities. The CPC conducts a comprehensive review of the thresholds annually, with interim
adjustments permitted in response to material changes in the risk environment. All adjustments must be documented and
communicated to relevant stakeholders.

PRC-v1.7 §1.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 6

6. 6. Approval Authorities and Escalation Paths
Approval authorities for credit transactions are delegated based on the size, complexity, and RAROC compliance of the
exposure. For transactions meeting or exceeding the RAROC floors, approval authority is delegated to the Business Unit Head
for exposures up to USD 50 million. Exposures between USD 50 million and USD 200 million require approval from the
Regional Credit Committee (RCC), while those exceeding USD 200 million must be approved by the Global Credit Committee
(GCC).
Transactions that do not meet the RAROC floors are subject to an escalation process, beginning with the Business Unit Head,
who must provide a detailed justification for the deviation. If the Business Unit Head approves the exception, it must be
escalated to the Head of CRM for review. The Head of CRM has the authority to approve exceptions for exposures up to USD

50 million, provided the deviation does not exceed 2% below the RAROC floor.
For exceptions exceeding 2% below the RAROC floor or for exposures between USD 50 million and USD 200 million, approval
must be obtained from the RCC. The RCC evaluates the justification, the mitigating factors, and the potential impact on the
bank’s risk-adjusted returns. Exceptions for exposures above USD 200 million or deviations exceeding 5% below the RAROC
floor require approval from the GCC, with the CRO holding veto power over any such decisions.
All exceptions must be documented in the bank’s Credit Exception Log, which captures the rationale, approval authority, and
any conditions or mitigants imposed. The log is reviewed monthly by the CRM department to identify trends, systemic issues, or
potential areas of concern. Repeated exceptions for a particular business unit or asset class may trigger a targeted review by
the CPC.
In cases where a transaction’s RAROC is below the floor due to strategic considerations, such as relationship banking or
cross-sell opportunities, the Business Unit must provide a cost-benefit analysis demonstrating the overall economic value to the
bank. Such analyses are subject to independent validation by the Finance department and must be approved by the CRO.

PRC-v1.7 §1.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 7

7. 7. Monitoring and Compliance
The CRM department is responsible for the ongoing monitoring of RAROC compliance across the bank’s credit portfolio. This
includes the periodic recalculation of RAROC for existing exposures to ensure that they continue to meet or exceed the
established floors. Monitoring is conducted at least quarterly for all material exposures, with more frequent reviews required for
high-risk or non-compliant transactions.
The bank employs a automated monitoring system that flags any exposure falling below its RAROC floor, triggering an
immediate alert to the relevant relationship manager and risk officer. The system also generates exception reports for
distribution to the CRM department, Business Unit Heads, and the CPC. These reports include details on the magnitude of the
deviation, the duration of non-compliance, and any corrective actions taken.
For exposures that breach their RAROC floors, the relationship manager is required to develop a remediation plan within 30
days of identification. The plan must outline the steps to restore compliance, such as repricing the exposure, reducing the risk
weight, or exiting the position. The remediation plan must be approved by the Head of CRM and tracked to completion. Failure
to restore compliance within 90 days may result in the forced sale or write-down of the exposure.
The CRM department conducts annual independent reviews of a sample of exposures to validate the accuracy of RAROC
calculations and the effectiveness of monitoring controls. These reviews are documented in a report to the CPC, which includes
findings, recommendations, and any required policy or process adjustments. The Internal Audit function also includes RAROC
compliance in its annual audit plan, with findings reported to the Board Risk Committee.
In addition to internal monitoring, the bank’s RAROC floors and compliance processes are subject to review by external
regulators as part of their supervisory examinations. The bank is committed to demonstrating the robustness of its RAROC
framework and its adherence to the policy through transparent reporting and evidence of effective controls.

PRC-v1.7 §1.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 8

8. 8. Exceptions and Waivers
Exceptions to the RAROC floors are permitted only under exceptional circumstances and must be fully justified, documented,
and approved through the escalation paths outlined in Section 6. Exceptions are categorized as either temporary or permanent,
with temporary exceptions granted for a maximum period of 12 months, subject to renewal. Permanent exceptions are rare and
require a compelling strategic rationale, such as a government-mandated lending program or a long-term relationship with a
systemic client.
The justification for an exception must include a detailed analysis of the exposure’s risk-adjusted returns, the reasons for the
deviation, and the expected timeline for compliance. For temporary exceptions, the justification must also outline the specific
actions that will be taken to restore compliance, such as repricing, risk mitigation, or portfolio restructuring. The analysis must
be supported by evidence, such as market data, client financials, or third-party risk assessments.
The approval of exceptions is contingent on the implementation of compensating controls or mitigants to reduce the risk of the
exposure. These may include enhanced monitoring, additional collateral, guarantees, or hedging strategies. The CRM
department is responsible for validating the effectiveness of these mitigants and ensuring that they are reflected in the RAROC
calculation.
All exceptions are recorded in the Credit Exception Log, which is maintained by the CRM department and reviewed monthly by
the CPC. The log includes the date of the exception, the exposure details, the magnitude of the deviation, the approval
authority, the justification, and the status of any remediation actions. Exceptions that remain unresolved for more than 90 days
are escalated to the CRO for review.
The bank reserves the right to reject or unwind any exposure that fails to meet its RAROC floor without an approved exception.
In such cases, the Business Unit is responsible for absorbing any losses or costs associated with the unwinding. Repeated or
systemic exceptions may result in the suspension of delegation authorities or other disciplinary actions, as determined by the
CPC.

PRC-v1.7 §1.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 9

9. 9. Reporting and Transparency
The bank maintains a comprehensive reporting framework to ensure transparency and accountability in the application of
RAROC floors. Monthly RAROC compliance reports are generated by the CRM department and distributed to Business Unit
Heads, the CPC, and the CRO. These reports include a summary of all exposures by asset class, risk rating, and RAROC
performance, as well as a detailed breakdown of exceptions and their status.
The monthly reports also highlight trends in RAROC performance, such as deteriorating or improving segments, and provide an
analysis of the drivers behind these trends. This includes changes in market conditions, credit spreads, or the bank’s cost of
capital. The reports are designed to facilitate proactive risk management and to inform strategic decisions regarding portfolio
composition and risk appetite.
Quarterly, the CRM department prepares a more detailed RAROC Performance Review, which is presented to the CPC and the
Board Risk Committee. This review includes an assessment of the bank’s overall RAROC performance, a comparison against
peer benchmarks, and an evaluation of the effectiveness of the RAROC floors in achieving the bank’s risk-adjusted return
objectives. The review also identifies any emerging risks or opportunities for improvement.
In addition to internal reporting, the bank includes RAROC metrics in its external disclosures, such as the annual report and
pillar 3 regulatory filings. These disclosures provide stakeholders with insight into the bank’s risk-adjusted performance and its
adherence to internal policies. The bank is committed to maintaining the confidentiality of client-specific information while
ensuring transparency in its aggregate RAROC performance.
Ad-hoc reporting is also available upon request from senior management, regulators, or other stakeholders. The CRM
department is responsible for ensuring that all reports are accurate, timely, and aligned with the bank’s data governance
standards. Any discrepancies or errors in reporting must be investigated and corrected promptly, with root cause analysis
conducted to prevent recurrence.

2. 2. Scope and Applicability
The Spread Grid under Clause 1.2 of Parent Policy PRC-v1.7 applies to all credit exposures originated, renewed, or amended
by the bank, including but not limited to corporate loans, commercial real estate financing, project finance, and fixed-income
securities. It covers both new transactions and the repricing of existing exposures, ensuring that all credit decisions are aligned
with the bank’s risk-based pricing framework.
Geographically, this policy is applicable to all jurisdictions in which the bank operates, unless local regulations or market
practices explicitly conflict with its provisions. In such cases, local credit policies must be harmonized with this Spread Grid to
the greatest extent possible, and any deviations must be documented and approved by the Group Risk Committee. This
synthetic document is designed to demonstrate how such harmonization might be structured in practice.
The Spread Grid is mandatory for all business units involved in credit origination, including Commercial Banking, Investment
Banking, and Treasury. It also applies to risk management functions responsible for monitoring portfolio spreads and ensuring
compliance with the policy. Third-party vendors or partners involved in credit transactions on behalf of the bank must adhere to
equivalent standards or provide evidence of comparable risk-based pricing frameworks.
Exposures exempt from the Spread Grid include interbank placements, sovereign debt, and transactions explicitly covered by
separate, specialized pricing policies (e.g., derivatives or structured products). However, even for exempt exposures, the
underlying principles of risk-based pricing and spread determination outlined in this document should be considered where
applicable. Exemptions must be clearly documented and justified in the credit approval memorandum.
The policy is effective immediately upon issuance and supersedes all prior versions of the Spread Grid. All existing credit
exposures must be reviewed against this policy within 180 days of its effective date to ensure compliance. Any gaps identified
during this review must be addressed through repricing, additional collateral, or other risk mitigation measures, as approved by
the relevant credit authority.

 1.2 Spread Grid
PRC-v1.7 §1.2 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose and Objectives
This synthetic demonstration document, titled 'Clause 1.2 Spread Grid' (Document 14 of 20), is a component of the Parent
Credit Policy PRC-v1.7. Its purpose is to establish a structured framework for determining and applying credit spreads across
various risk categories, ensuring consistency, transparency, and alignment with the bank’s risk appetite. The Spread Grid
serves as a quantitative tool to standardize the assessment of credit risk premiums, facilitating objective decision-making in
lending and investment activities.
The primary objective of the Spread Grid is to provide a clear, scalable methodology for assigning credit spreads based on
predefined risk parameters, including borrower creditworthiness, collateral quality, industry sector, and economic conditions. By
standardizing these spreads, the bank aims to mitigate subjective biases in pricing, enhance portfolio diversification, and
maintain compliance with regulatory capital requirements. This document is synthetic and intended solely for demonstration
purposes to illustrate policy structure and content.
The Spread Grid is designed to support the bank’s broader credit strategy by ensuring that risk-based pricing is applied
uniformly across all business units. It enables credit officers to quickly determine appropriate spreads for new and existing
exposures, reducing the time and complexity associated with manual assessments. The grid is periodically reviewed and
updated to reflect changes in market conditions, regulatory expectations, and the bank’s internal risk models.
This policy applies to all credit exposures, including loans, bonds, and other fixed-income instruments, and is binding for all
personnel involved in credit underwriting, risk management, and portfolio monitoring. Adherence to the Spread Grid is
mandatory unless an exception is formally approved through the governance processes outlined in Section 9. Non-compliance
with the grid may result in mispricing of risk, potential losses, and regulatory scrutiny.
The Spread Grid is not a substitute for professional judgment but rather a tool to enhance it. Credit officers are expected to use
the grid as a starting point and adjust spreads where justified by additional qualitative factors, such as relationship history,
strategic considerations, or unique transaction structures. All deviations from the grid must be documented, justified, and
approved in accordance with the bank’s delegation of authority.

PRC-v1.7 §1.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope and Applicability
The Spread Grid under Clause 1.2 of Parent Policy PRC-v1.7 applies to all credit exposures originated, renewed, or amended
by the bank, including but not limited to corporate loans, commercial real estate financing, project finance, and fixed-income
securities. It covers both new transactions and the repricing of existing exposures, ensuring that all credit decisions are aligned
with the bank’s risk-based pricing framework.
Geographically, this policy is applicable to all jurisdictions in which the bank operates, unless local regulations or market
practices explicitly conflict with its provisions. In such cases, local credit policies must be harmonized with this Spread Grid to
the greatest extent possible, and any deviations must be documented and approved by the Group Risk Committee. This
synthetic document is designed to demonstrate how such harmonization might be structured in practice.
The Spread Grid is mandatory for all business units involved in credit origination, including Commercial Banking, Investment
Banking, and Treasury. It also applies to risk management functions responsible for monitoring portfolio spreads and ensuring
compliance with the policy. Third-party vendors or partners involved in credit transactions on behalf of the bank must adhere to
equivalent standards or provide evidence of comparable risk-based pricing frameworks.
Exposures exempt from the Spread Grid include interbank placements, sovereign debt, and transactions explicitly covered by
separate, specialized pricing policies (e.g., derivatives or structured products). However, even for exempt exposures, the
underlying principles of risk-based pricing and spread determination outlined in this document should be considered where
applicable. Exemptions must be clearly documented and justified in the credit approval memorandum.
The policy is effective immediately upon issuance and supersedes all prior versions of the Spread Grid. All existing credit
exposures must be reviewed against this policy within 180 days of its effective date to ensure compliance. Any gaps identified
during this review must be addressed through repricing, additional collateral, or other risk mitigation measures, as approved by
the relevant credit authority.

PRC-v1.7 §1.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 3

3. 3. Governance and Responsibilities
The governance of the Spread Grid is overseen by the Credit Policy Committee (CPC), which is responsible for its
development, approval, and periodic review. The CPC delegates the day-to-day administration of the grid to the Credit Risk
Management (CRM) department, which ensures that the grid remains aligned with the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory
requirements, and market conditions. This synthetic policy demonstrates how governance roles might be structured in a
real-world scenario.
The Chief Risk Officer (CRO) holds ultimate accountability for the integrity and effectiveness of the Spread Grid. The CRO is
supported by the Head of Credit Risk, who oversees the implementation of the grid across all business units and ensures that
any deviations are properly escalated and resolved. Business unit heads are responsible for ensuring that their teams adhere to
the grid and that all credit decisions are documented in accordance with the policy.
The Credit Underwriting team is responsible for applying the Spread Grid to individual transactions and ensuring that spreads
are consistent with the borrower’s risk profile. Underwriters must document the rationale for any adjustments to the grid,
including qualitative factors or market conditions, and obtain the necessary approvals. The Risk Analytics team supports the
grid by providing data-driven insights, such as historical default rates, loss given default (LGD) estimates, and macroeconomic
scenarios.
Internal Audit is responsible for independently validating compliance with the Spread Grid through periodic reviews and testing.
Audit findings, including instances of non-compliance or control weaknesses, must be reported to the CPC and addressed
through corrective action plans. The Compliance department ensures that the grid aligns with regulatory expectations, such as
Basel III capital requirements and local banking regulations.
The Spread Grid is reviewed at least annually by the CRM department, with input from business units, risk analytics, and
compliance. Ad hoc reviews may be triggered by significant changes in market conditions, regulatory requirements, or the
bank’s risk appetite. All updates to the grid must be approved by the CPC and communicated to relevant stakeholders through
formal policy memos and training sessions.

PRC-v1.7 §1.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 4

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria and Inputs
The Spread Grid is populated using a combination of quantitative and qualitative inputs to ensure that credit spreads reflect the
true risk of each exposure. Quantitative inputs include the borrower’s credit rating (internal or external), financial ratios (e.g.,
leverage, interest coverage, debt service coverage ratio), and collateral quality. For corporate borrowers, the grid incorporates
metrics such as EBITDA margin, free cash flow, and liquidity ratios, while for commercial real estate, it considers loan-to-value
(LTV) ratios and debt yield.
Qualitative inputs are equally critical and may adjust the base spread derived from quantitative factors. These include industry
risk (e.g., cyclicality, regulatory exposure), management quality, competitive positioning, and macroeconomic trends. For
example, a borrower in a high-risk industry (e.g., oil and gas) may receive a higher spread adjustment, even if its financial ratios
are strong. Similarly, a borrower with a proven track record of prudent financial management may qualify for a lower spread.
The Spread Grid categorizes borrowers into risk buckets based on their probability of default (PD) and loss given default (LGD).
PD is derived from internal credit models or external ratings (e.g., Moody’s, S&P, or Fitch), while LGD is estimated based on
historical recovery rates and collateral coverage. The grid maps these inputs to a base spread, which is then adjusted for
tenure, currency, and other transaction-specific factors. For demonstration purposes, this synthetic policy assumes a base
spread range of 100 to 500 basis points, with adjustments of up to ±200 basis points.
Collateral plays a pivotal role in spread determination. The grid assigns collateral quality scores (e.g., 1 to 5, with 1 being the
highest quality) based on factors such as liquidity, volatility, and legal enforceability. For instance, cash collateral or government
bonds may receive a score of 1, resulting in a lower spread adjustment, while real estate or inventory may receive a score of 3
or 4, leading to a higher adjustment. The grid also accounts for the seniority of the claim, with senior secured debt receiving a
lower spread than subordinated or unsecured debt.
All inputs used to populate the Spread Grid must be supported by verifiable evidence, such as audited financial statements,
third-party valuations, or internal risk assessments. Underwriters are required to document the sources of their inputs and justify
any subjective adjustments. The use of outdated or unreliable data is strictly prohibited and may result in the rejection of the
credit application or disciplinary action.

PRC-v1.7 §1.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 5

5. 5. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
The Spread Grid establishes quantitative limits to ensure that credit spreads remain within acceptable ranges based on the
bank’s risk appetite. The base spread for each risk bucket is determined by the borrower’s PD and LGD, as follows: Low Risk
(PD < 1%, LGD < 20%): 100–150 bps; Moderate Risk (PD 1–3%, LGD 20–40%): 150–300 bps; High Risk (PD 3–5%, LGD
40–60%): 300–400 bps; Very High Risk (PD > 5%, LGD > 60%): 400–500 bps. These ranges are synthetic and for
demonstration purposes only.
Adjustments to the base spread are capped to prevent excessive risk-taking or mispricing. For example, qualitative adjustments
for industry risk or management quality cannot exceed ±100 bps for Low and Moderate Risk buckets, ±150 bps for High Risk,
and ±200 bps for Very High Risk. Similarly, collateral adjustments are limited to ±50 bps for scores 1–2 and ±100 bps for scores
3–5. The total spread (base + adjustments) must not fall below the minimum threshold of 100 bps or exceed the maximum
threshold of 700 bps without explicit approval from the CPC.
Tenure adjustments are applied to reflect the increased risk of longer-duration exposures. For example, spreads for exposures
with a tenure of 1–3 years may receive a 0–25 bps adjustment, while those with a tenure of 3–5 years may receive a 25–50 bps
adjustment, and those exceeding 5 years may receive a 50–100 bps adjustment. These adjustments are cumulative with other
qualitative and collateral adjustments but are subject to the same caps.
Currency risk is another critical factor in spread determination. Exposures denominated in currencies with high volatility or
limited liquidity (e.g., emerging market currencies) may receive an additional spread adjustment of up to 50 bps. The CRM
department maintains a list of approved currencies and their associated risk premiums, which is reviewed quarterly.
Transactions in unapproved currencies require CPC approval.
The Spread Grid includes a hard stop rule: any transaction with a total spread exceeding 700 bps must be escalated to the CPC
for review, regardless of the borrower’s risk profile. Similarly, transactions with spreads below 100 bps must be justified by
exceptional collateral quality or other mitigating factors and approved by the Head of Credit Risk. These thresholds are
designed to prevent both excessive risk-taking and uneconomic pricing.

PRC-v1.7 §1.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 6

6. 6. Approval Authorities and Delegation
Approval authorities for Spread Grid adjustments are delegated based on the size of the exposure, the risk bucket, and the
magnitude of the spread adjustment. For Low and Moderate Risk exposures with total spreads within the standard range
(100–500 bps), approval authority is delegated to the Business Unit Head or their designated Credit Officer. Adjustments within
the permitted qualitative or collateral ranges (up to ±100 bps) do not require additional approvals but must be documented in
the credit memorandum.
For High Risk exposures (300–400 bps base spread) or adjustments exceeding ±100 bps, approval must be obtained from the
Regional Credit Committee (RCC). The RCC is composed of senior credit officers, risk managers, and business unit
representatives and meets bi-weekly to review such requests. Very High Risk exposures (400–500 bps base spread) or
adjustments exceeding ±150 bps require approval from the Group Credit Committee (GCC), which convenes monthly.
Transactions with total spreads exceeding 500 bps or adjustments exceeding ±200 bps must be escalated to the Credit Policy
Committee (CPC) for final approval. The CPC’s decision is binding and must be documented in the minutes of its meetings. In
urgent cases, the CRO may grant provisional approval, subject to ratification by the CPC at its next scheduled meeting. All
provisional approvals must be communicated to the CPC within 5 business days.
Delegated authorities are subject to periodic review by Internal Audit and the CRM department to ensure that they remain
appropriate given the bank’s risk profile and market conditions. Any misuse of delegated authority, such as approving spreads
outside the permitted ranges without proper justification, may result in the revocation of delegation rights and disciplinary action.
The bank maintains a central register of all delegated authorities, which is updated quarterly.
For transactions involving related parties, insiders, or conflicts of interest, the Spread Grid approval process is subject to
additional controls. Such transactions must be escalated to the next higher level of authority (e.g., from RCC to GCC) and
reviewed by the Compliance department to ensure adherence to the bank’s conflict-of-interest policy. All related-party
transactions must be reported to the Board Risk Committee on a quarterly basis.

PRC-v1.7 §1.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 7

7. 7. Monitoring and Compliance
The CRM department is responsible for monitoring compliance with the Spread Grid through a combination of automated
controls and manual reviews. Automated controls are embedded in the bank’s credit origination and pricing systems to flag
transactions that fall outside the permitted spread ranges or lack the required approvals. These controls generate alerts that are
escalated to the relevant business unit and risk management for resolution.
Manual reviews are conducted on a sample basis to validate the accuracy of inputs and the appropriateness of adjustments.
The CRM department selects a minimum of 10% of all new and renewed exposures for detailed review each quarter, with a
focus on High and Very High Risk transactions. Reviews assess whether the spreads are consistent with the borrower’s risk
profile, the quality of documentation, and the adherence to approval authorities. Findings are reported to the CPC and business
unit heads.
Portfolio-level monitoring is performed to identify trends or anomalies in spread application. The CRM department tracks
metrics such as the average spread by risk bucket, the frequency of adjustments, and the distribution of spreads across
business units. Significant deviations from expected patterns (e.g., a business unit consistently applying spreads at the lower
end of the range for High Risk exposures) trigger targeted reviews and potential remediation actions.
Compliance with the Spread Grid is also validated through Internal Audit’s annual review of the credit underwriting process.
Audit tests include verifying that spreads are calculated correctly, that adjustments are justified and approved, and that
exceptions are properly documented and escalated. Audit findings are reported to the CPC and the Board Risk Committee, with
corrective actions tracked until completion.
The bank’s Whistleblower Policy encourages employees to report any suspected violations of the Spread Grid or other credit
policies. Reports can be made anonymously through the bank’s ethics hotline and are investigated by the Compliance
department. Retaliation against whistleblowers is strictly prohibited and may result in disciplinary action, up to and including
termination.

PRC-v1.7 §1.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 8

8. 8. Exceptions and Escalation Paths
Exceptions to the Spread Grid are permitted only in limited circumstances and must be formally documented, justified, and
approved. An exception is defined as any transaction where the total spread falls outside the permitted range (100–700 bps) or
where adjustments exceed the caps specified in Section 5. Exceptions may arise due to unique transaction structures, strategic
considerations, or market dislocations that temporarily distort risk-based pricing.
The escalation path for exceptions depends on the magnitude of the deviation and the risk profile of the transaction. For
spreads between 500–700 bps or adjustments exceeding ±150 bps, the request must be escalated to the GCC for approval.
For spreads below 100 bps or above 700 bps, or adjustments exceeding ±200 bps, the request must be escalated to the CPC.
The escalation must include a detailed justification, supported by evidence such as market comparables, third-party valuations,
or stress-testing results.
The justification for an exception must address the following: (1) the specific circumstances warranting the deviation; (2) the
impact on the bank’s risk profile and capital requirements; (3) the mitigating factors (e.g., collateral, guarantees, or covenants);
and (4) the expected financial return relative to the risk. The request must also include a comparison to the Spread Grid’s base
spread and an explanation of why the standard adjustments are insufficient.
Once an exception is approved, it must be documented in the credit approval memorandum and entered into the bank’s
exception tracking system. The system monitors the performance of excepted exposures and flags any deterioration in credit
quality or compliance with covenants. Exceptions are subject to enhanced monitoring, including quarterly reviews by the CRM
department and annual validation by Internal Audit.
The CPC reviews all active exceptions at least semi-annually to assess whether the justifications remain valid and whether the
exposures continue to perform as expected. Exceptions that no longer meet the approval criteria must be repriced or unwound,
unless a new exception request is submitted and approved. The CPC may also impose additional controls, such as higher
capital charges or more frequent reporting, on excepted exposures.

PRC-v1.7 §1.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 9

9. 9. Reporting and Transparency
The bank maintains a comprehensive reporting framework to ensure transparency and accountability in the application of the
Spread Grid. The CRM department generates a monthly Spread Grid Compliance Report, which is distributed to the CPC,
business unit heads, and Internal Audit. The report includes metrics such as the number of transactions priced within the grid,
the frequency and magnitude of adjustments, the number of exceptions, and the average spread by risk bucket and business
unit.
The monthly report also highlights any control failures, such as transactions lacking required approvals or documentation, and
tracks the resolution of these issues. Business units are required to provide explanations for any material deviations from the
grid and to outline corrective actions. The CPC reviews the report to identify systemic issues or trends that may require policy
updates or additional training.
Quarterly, the CRM department produces a Spread Grid Performance Report, which analyzes the financial impact of the grid on
the bank’s portfolio. This report includes an assessment of the spreads’ effectiveness in compensating for credit losses, the
contribution of spreads to net interest margins, and the sensitivity of the portfolio to changes in market conditions. The report is
presented to the Board Risk Committee and used to inform strategic decisions, such as risk appetite adjustments or capital
allocation.
Annually, the bank publishes a summary of its Spread Grid framework in its Pillars 1 and 3 disclosures under Basel III. The
disclosure includes the methodology for determining spreads, the range of spreads applied to different risk buckets, and the
governance processes for approvals and exceptions. This transparency is intended to provide regulators, investors, and other
stakeholders with confidence in the bank’s risk management practices.
Ad hoc reporting is triggered by significant events, such as a breach of the bank’s risk appetite statement, a material change in
market conditions, or a regulatory inquiry. In such cases, the CRM department works with the affected business units to
produce a detailed analysis of the event’s impact on the Spread Grid and the broader credit portfolio. The findings are reported
to the CPC and, where necessary, to the Board of Directors.

PRC-v1.7 §1.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 10

10. 10. Policy Review and Maintenance
The Spread Grid is subject to periodic review to ensure that it remains relevant, effective, and aligned with the bank’s risk
appetite and regulatory expectations. The CRM department conducts a comprehensive review of the grid at least annually, with
input from business units, risk analytics, compliance, and Internal Audit. The review assesses the grid’s performance in
predicting credit losses, its consistency with market practices, and its compliance with regulatory requirements.
The annual review includes a validation of the quantitative inputs and thresholds used in the grid. The CRM department tests
the grid’s calibration by comparing actual default rates and loss severities to the predicted PD and LGD values. If the grid is
found to be miscalibrated (e.g., actual losses exceed expected losses for a given risk bucket), the thresholds or inputs are
adjusted accordingly. The review also considers feedback from underwriters and business units on the practicality and usability
of the grid.
Ad hoc reviews are conducted in response to material changes in the bank’s operating environment. For example, a significant
economic downturn, a new regulatory capital framework, or a merger or acquisition may necessitate an interim review of the
grid. The CPC has the authority to mandate such reviews and to fast-track updates to the grid if warranted. All ad hoc reviews
must be completed within 90 days of the triggering event.
Updates to the Spread Grid are approved by the CPC and communicated to all stakeholders through formal policy memos,
training sessions, and updates to the bank’s policy management system. The CRM department is responsible for ensuring that
all business units and risk functions are aware of the changes and have the necessary tools and training to implement them.
The effective date of updates is typically 30 days after approval, allowing time for systems updates and staff training.
The bank maintains a version control system for the Spread Grid, with each update assigned a unique version number and
effective date. The system tracks all changes, including the rationale for updates, the stakeholders consulted, and the approvals
obtained. This ensures transparency and accountability in the policy maintenance process. The current version of the Spread
Grid, as demonstrated in this synthetic document, is PRC-v1.7, Clause 1.2, effective as of the date of this policy.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 1
 2.1 CRE Sub-sector Limits
SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose
This document, titled '2.1 CRE Sub-sector Limits,' is a synthetic demonstration policy designed to establish clear, actionable
guidelines for Commercial Real Estate (CRE) sub-sector exposure limits within the bank’s credit portfolio. The purpose of this
policy is to ensure that the bank’s CRE lending activities remain aligned with its risk appetite, regulatory requirements, and
strategic objectives. By defining sub-sector limits, the bank aims to mitigate concentration risk, enhance portfolio diversification,
and maintain financial stability.
The policy provides a structured framework for identifying, assessing, and managing exposure to specific CRE sub-sectors,
such as office, retail, industrial, multifamily, and hospitality. Each sub-sector presents unique risk characteristics, and this policy
ensures that the bank’s exposure to any single sub-sector does not exceed predefined thresholds, thereby reducing the
potential for significant losses due to sector-specific downturns.
This synthetic policy is intended for internal use and demonstration purposes only. It reflects industry best practices and
hypothetical scenarios to illustrate how a bank might structure its CRE sub-sector limits. The thresholds, roles, and processes
outlined herein are fictional and should not be interpreted as actual bank policies or commitments.
The policy also serves as a tool for training and internal audits, enabling staff to understand the importance of sub-sector limits
in credit risk management. By adhering to these guidelines, the bank can demonstrate its commitment to prudent lending
practices and regulatory compliance, even in a simulated environment.
Finally, this document supports the parent policy, SEC-CRE-v2.0, by providing granular details on sub-sector limits, ensuring
consistency and coherence across the bank’s credit risk management framework. It is designed to be reviewed and updated
periodically to reflect changes in market conditions, regulatory expectations, or the bank’s strategic priorities.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope
This synthetic policy applies to all CRE lending activities conducted by the bank, including but not limited to originations,
renewals, refinancings, and acquisitions of CRE loans. It covers all business units, subsidiaries, and geographic regions where
the bank operates, ensuring a uniform approach to managing CRE sub-sector exposure across the organization.
The policy is specifically focused on sub-sector limits within the CRE portfolio. Sub-sectors are defined as distinct categories of
CRE properties, each with its own risk profile. For the purposes of this policy, the primary sub-sectors include office, retail,
industrial, multifamily, hospitality, and specialized real estate (e.g., healthcare, education, or data centers). Each sub-sector is
subject to individual exposure limits as outlined in Section 5: Quantitative Limits.
Excluded from this policy are residential mortgage lending, consumer lending, and non-real estate commercial lending. While
these areas may have their own concentration risk policies, they are not addressed within this document. Additionally, this
policy does not apply to the bank’s investment portfolio or proprietary trading activities, which are governed by separate risk
management frameworks.
The policy is binding for all employees, contractors, and third-party vendors involved in CRE lending activities. Compliance with
this policy is mandatory, and deviations must be approved through the formal exception process described in Section 8:
Exceptions. Failure to adhere to the policy may result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination of employment or
contract.
This synthetic policy is designed to be scalable and adaptable to the bank’s evolving business needs. As such, it may be
supplemented by additional guidelines or procedures tailored to specific regions, business units, or product types, provided they
do not conflict with the core principles outlined herein.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 3

3. 3. Governance
The governance framework for this synthetic CRE Sub-sector Limits policy is designed to ensure accountability, transparency,
and effective oversight. Ultimate responsibility for the policy rests with the Bank’s Board of Directors, which delegates
day-to-day oversight to the Credit Risk Committee (CRC). The CRC is responsible for approving the policy, monitoring its
implementation, and ensuring alignment with the bank’s overall risk appetite.
The Chief Credit Officer (CCO) serves as the primary executive accountable for the policy’s execution. The CCO is supported
by the CRE Risk Management Team, which is tasked with developing, maintaining, and enforcing the policy. This team reports
directly to the CCO and provides regular updates to the CRC on the policy’s effectiveness, compliance, and any emerging risks.
At the operational level, the CRE Underwriting Team is responsible for applying the sub-sector limits during the loan approval
process. Underwriters must ensure that all new CRE loans comply with the policy’s thresholds and escalate any potential
breaches to the CRE Risk Management Team for review. The Underwriting Team is also responsible for maintaining accurate
records of sub-sector exposures and providing data to support monitoring and reporting activities.
Internal Audit plays a critical role in validating the policy’s effectiveness through periodic reviews and assessments. Audits are
conducted at least annually to ensure compliance with the policy, the accuracy of exposure reporting, and the adequacy of
controls. Findings from these audits are reported to the CRC and the Board of Directors, with corrective actions tracked to
completion.
This synthetic governance structure is designed to mirror real-world best practices, ensuring that roles and responsibilities are
clearly defined and that there are multiple layers of oversight to prevent and address potential issues. The governance
framework is reviewed annually to ensure it remains fit for purpose and aligned with the bank’s strategic objectives.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 4

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
The underwriting criteria outlined in this synthetic policy are designed to ensure that all CRE loans adhere to the bank’s risk
appetite and sub-sector limits. Underwriters must evaluate each loan application against a set of qualitative and quantitative
criteria, which include but are not limited to borrower creditworthiness, property cash flow, loan-to-value (LTV) ratios, debt
service coverage ratios (DSCR), and sub-sector exposure.
For borrower creditworthiness, underwriters must assess the financial strength, experience, and track record of the borrower or
sponsoring entity. This includes a review of financial statements, credit history, and prior project performance. Borrowers must
demonstrate the ability to service debt obligations under stress scenarios, with a minimum DSCR of 1.25x for most sub-sectors.
Higher DSCR thresholds may be required for higher-risk sub-sectors, such as hospitality, where a minimum of 1.40x may apply.
Property-level underwriting must include a thorough analysis of the property’s cash flow, occupancy rates, tenant quality, and
market position. For office and retail properties, underwriters must evaluate lease rollover risk, tenant concentration, and the
property’s ability to attract and retain tenants. Industrial properties require an assessment of location, accessibility, and demand
drivers, while multifamily properties must demonstrate stable occupancy and rental income.
LTV ratios are capped at 70% for most sub-sectors, with stricter limits of 60% for higher-risk sub-sectors such as hospitality or
specialized real estate. Exceptions to these limits require approval from the CRE Risk Management Team and must be justified
by compensating factors, such as strong borrower credit or exceptional property cash flow.
Underwriters are also responsible for ensuring that the loan complies with the sub-sector exposure limits defined in Section 5. If
a loan approval would cause the bank’s exposure to a sub-sector to exceed its limit, the underwriter must escalate the request
to the CRE Risk Management Team for further review and potential exception processing.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 5

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
This synthetic policy establishes quantitative limits for CRE sub-sector exposures to mitigate concentration risk and ensure
portfolio diversification. The limits are expressed as a percentage of the bank’s total CRE portfolio and are designed to prevent
over-exposure to any single sub-sector. The following thresholds apply: Office: 25%, Retail: 20%, Industrial: 20%, Multifamily:
25%, Hospitality: 10%, and Specialized Real Estate: 10%.
Sub-sector exposure is calculated as the aggregate outstanding loan balance for all loans secured by properties within a given
sub-sector, divided by the total outstanding balance of the CRE portfolio. The CRE Risk Management Team is responsible for
monitoring these exposures on a monthly basis and reporting any breaches or potential breaches to the Credit Risk Committee.
In addition to sub-sector limits, the policy imposes concentration limits for individual loans within a sub-sector. No single loan
may exceed 10% of the bank’s total CRE portfolio, and no single borrower or related group of borrowers may account for more
than 15% of the total CRE portfolio. These limits are designed to prevent excessive exposure to any single asset or borrower.
The policy also includes a buffer zone for sub-sector limits. If exposure to a sub-sector reaches 90% of its limit, the CRE Risk
Management Team must notify the Credit Risk Committee and implement a watchlist for that sub-sector. New loans in a
sub-sector on the watchlist require additional scrutiny and approval from the CCO or their delegate.
Quantitative limits are reviewed annually by the CRE Risk Management Team and may be adjusted based on changes in
market conditions, regulatory requirements, or the bank’s risk appetite. Any proposed changes to the limits must be approved
by the Credit Risk Committee and documented in a policy amendment.
For the purposes of this synthetic policy, all quantitative thresholds are hypothetical and designed to illustrate how a bank might
structure its CRE sub-sector limits. Actual limits in a real-world scenario would be tailored to the bank’s specific risk profile and
strategic objectives.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 6

6. 6. Approvals
The approval process for CRE loans under this synthetic policy is designed to ensure that all transactions comply with the
bank’s underwriting criteria, sub-sector limits, and risk appetite. Approval authority is delegated based on loan size, complexity,
and risk profile, with higher-risk or larger loans requiring approval from more senior levels of management.
Loans with an outstanding balance of up to $5 million may be approved by a designated CRE Underwriting Manager, provided
they comply with all policy criteria, including sub-sector limits. Loans between $5 million and $20 million require approval from
the Regional Credit Officer (RCO), while loans exceeding $20 million must be approved by the Chief Credit Officer (CCO) or
their delegate.
Loans that would cause the bank’s exposure to a sub-sector to exceed its quantitative limit require approval from the CRE Risk
Management Team, in addition to the standard underwriting approval. The CRE Risk Management Team must conduct a
thorough review of the loan’s risk profile, the current exposure to the sub-sector, and the potential impact on the bank’s
portfolio. If the loan is approved, it must be classified as an exception and reported to the Credit Risk Committee.
The approval process also includes a secondary review for loans with complex structures, such as those involving multiple
properties, cross-collateralization, or non-recourse financing. These loans must be reviewed by the CRE Risk Management
Team, regardless of size, to ensure compliance with the policy and to assess any additional risks.
All approvals must be documented in the bank’s loan origination system, with clear evidence of compliance with the policy’s
criteria. Approval records must include the names and titles of the approving authorities, the date of approval, and any
conditions or stipulations attached to the approval. This documentation is subject to internal audit and regulatory review.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 7

7. 7. Monitoring
Monitoring is a critical component of this synthetic policy, ensuring that the bank’s CRE sub-sector exposures remain within
established limits and that any emerging risks are identified and addressed promptly. The CRE Risk Management Team is
responsible for overseeing the monitoring process, which includes both automated and manual reviews of the portfolio.
Automated monitoring is conducted on a monthly basis, with the bank’s risk management system generating reports on
sub-sector exposures, concentration ratios, and compliance with quantitative limits. These reports are distributed to the CRE
Risk Management Team, the Credit Risk Committee, and senior management. Any breaches or potential breaches of
sub-sector limits are flagged for immediate review.
In addition to automated monitoring, the CRE Risk Management Team conducts quarterly manual reviews of the CRE portfolio.
These reviews include a deep dive into the performance of each sub-sector, an assessment of market trends, and an evaluation
of the bank’s exposure to high-risk assets or borrowers. The findings from these reviews are presented to the Credit Risk
Committee and used to inform strategic decisions.
The policy also requires ongoing monitoring of individual loans within each sub-sector. Loan officers are responsible for tracking
the performance of their assigned loans, including financial covenants, occupancy rates, and debt service coverage. Any
deterioration in a loan’s performance must be escalated to the CRE Risk Management Team for further action, which may
include risk rating downgrades, watchlist placement, or workout strategies.
Monitoring activities are subject to internal audit to ensure their effectiveness and accuracy. The Internal Audit Team conducts
at least one audit per year focused on the CRE portfolio, with a particular emphasis on compliance with sub-sector limits and
the adequacy of monitoring controls. Audit findings and recommendations are tracked to completion by the CRE Risk
Management Team.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 8

8. 8. Exceptions
This synthetic policy recognizes that there may be circumstances where deviations from the established sub-sector limits or
underwriting criteria are justified. However, exceptions are granted only under strict conditions and with appropriate oversight to
ensure that the bank’s risk exposure remains within acceptable parameters.
An exception may be requested when a loan opportunity presents significant strategic value to the bank, such as a high-profile
client relationship, a unique market opportunity, or a transaction that aligns with the bank’s long-term goals. Exceptions may
also be considered for loans that demonstrate compensating factors, such as exceptionally strong borrower credit, superior
property cash flow, or robust collateral coverage.
The exception process begins with the submission of a formal request by the originating loan officer or underwriter to the CRE
Risk Management Team. The request must include a detailed justification for the exception, an analysis of the loan’s risk profile,
and an assessment of the impact on the bank’s sub-sector exposure. The CRE Risk Management Team reviews the request
and may consult with other stakeholders, such as the Regional Credit Officer or the Chief Credit Officer, as needed.
If the exception is approved, it must be documented in the bank’s exception log, which is maintained by the CRE Risk
Management Team. The log includes the date of approval, the names and titles of the approving authorities, the terms of the
exception, and any conditions or mitigating actions required. Exceptions are also reported to the Credit Risk Committee on a
quarterly basis for ongoing oversight.
Exceptions are subject to a sunset clause, meaning they are valid only for a specified period, typically not exceeding 12 months.
At the end of this period, the loan must either be brought into compliance with the policy or re-approved as an exception. The
CRE Risk Management Team is responsible for tracking exception expirations and ensuring timely renewals or corrections.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 9

9. 9. Reporting
Reporting is a key control mechanism under this synthetic policy, providing transparency and accountability for the bank’s CRE
sub-sector exposures. The CRE Risk Management Team is responsible for generating and distributing a suite of reports to
stakeholders at various levels of the organization, ensuring that all relevant parties are informed of the portfolio’s status and any
emerging risks.
Monthly reports are generated for the Credit Risk Committee and senior management, summarizing the bank’s exposure to
each CRE sub-sector, compliance with quantitative limits, and any breaches or potential breaches. These reports include trend
analysis, highlighting changes in sub-sector exposures over time and comparing actual exposures to the policy’s thresholds.
The reports also provide a forward-looking view, identifying upcoming loan maturities, renewals, and potential new originations
that could impact sub-sector limits.
Quarterly reports are prepared for the Board of Directors, providing a high-level overview of the CRE portfolio’s performance,
risk profile, and compliance with the policy. These reports include a summary of exception activity, monitoring findings, and any
material changes in market conditions or regulatory requirements that could affect the bank’s CRE lending strategy.
Ad-hoc reports may be generated as needed to support specific requests from regulators, auditors, or senior management.
These reports are tailored to the needs of the requestor and may include detailed analyses of specific sub-sectors, borrowers,
or properties. The CRE Risk Management Team is responsible for ensuring that all ad-hoc reports are accurate, timely, and
consistent with the policy’s requirements.
All reports generated under this policy are subject to internal controls to ensure their accuracy and completeness. The CRE
Risk Management Team conducts a pre-distribution review of each report to verify that the data is correct, the analysis is
sound, and the conclusions are supported by the underlying information. Reports are archived in the bank’s document
management system for a minimum of seven years to support audit and regulatory review.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 10

10. 10. Review
This synthetic policy is subject to periodic review to ensure that it remains relevant, effective, and aligned with the bank’s
strategic objectives, risk appetite, and regulatory requirements. The review process is designed to be comprehensive, involving
input from multiple stakeholders and a thorough assessment of the policy’s performance and adequacy.
The policy is reviewed annually by the CRE Risk Management Team, which evaluates its effectiveness in managing sub-sector
concentration risk, the appropriateness of the quantitative limits, and the adequacy of the governance, underwriting, monitoring,
and reporting frameworks. The review includes an assessment of market conditions, regulatory developments, and industry
best practices to identify any necessary updates or enhancements.
As part of the annual review, the CRE Risk Management Team solicits feedback from key stakeholders, including the Credit
Risk Committee, the Chief Credit Officer, Regional Credit Officers, and the Internal Audit Team. This feedback is used to
identify areas where the policy may be unclear, overly restrictive, or insufficiently rigorous. The team also conducts a
benchmarking exercise, comparing the bank’s sub-sector limits and practices against those of peer institutions and industry
standards.
If the annual review identifies the need for material changes to the policy, the CRE Risk Management Team drafts a policy
amendment and submits it to the Credit Risk Committee for approval. Material changes may include adjustments to quantitative
limits, revisions to underwriting criteria, or modifications to the governance framework. Minor changes, such as clarifications or
updates to references, may be implemented by the CRE Risk Management Team without formal approval but are documented
in the policy’s change log.
In addition to the annual review, the policy is subject to ad-hoc reviews in response to significant events or changes in the
bank’s operating environment. Such events may include a material breach of sub-sector limits, a regulatory examination finding,
a change in the bank’s risk appetite, or a strategic shift in the bank’s CRE lending business. Ad-hoc reviews follow the same
process as the annual review but are conducted on an expedited timeline to address the specific issue or opportunity.
The results of each review, including any changes made to the policy, are documented in a review report and presented to the
Credit Risk Committee and the Board of Directors. The report includes a summary of the review process, key findings, and the
rationale for any changes. This ensures transparency and accountability in the policy’s evolution over time.
