 2.2 Construction Guidance
SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose and Applicability
This document, titled '2.2 Construction Guidance,' is a synthetic demonstration policy derived from the parent policy
SEC-CRE-v2.0. It establishes the framework for evaluating, approving, and managing credit exposures related to construction
financing within the bank. The purpose of this policy is to ensure that construction lending activities are conducted in a manner
consistent with the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory requirements, and industry best practices. This policy applies to all business
units, employees, and third parties involved in the origination, underwriting, administration, and monitoring of construction loans.
Construction lending presents unique risks, including cost overruns, delays, and market volatility, which require specialized
underwriting and monitoring. This policy provides clear guidelines to mitigate these risks while supporting the bank’s strategic
objectives in the construction sector. It is designed to align with the bank’s broader credit risk management framework, ensuring
consistency in decision-making and risk assessment across all construction-related credit exposures.
The policy is applicable to all construction loan types, including but not limited to commercial real estate development,
residential subdivision financing, and infrastructure projects. It covers both direct lending and participations in syndicated
construction facilities. Exclusions include permanent financing arrangements, which are governed by separate policies under
SEC-CRE-v2.0.
This document is synthetic and intended for demonstration purposes only. It does not reflect the actual policies, procedures, or
practices of any real financial institution. All thresholds, roles, and requirements outlined herein are fictional and designed to
illustrate a comprehensive credit policy framework for construction lending.
Compliance with this policy is mandatory for all employees involved in construction lending activities. Failure to adhere to the
guidelines set forth in this document may result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination of employment.
Additionally, non-compliance may expose the bank to heightened regulatory scrutiny, financial losses, or reputational damage.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope and Definitions
The scope of this policy encompasses all construction loan activities, from initial application through final disbursement and
conversion to permanent financing or repayment. It applies globally across all jurisdictions where the bank operates, unless
superseded by local regulatory requirements. The policy governs the actions of relationship managers, credit analysts,
underwriters, risk managers, and senior leadership involved in the construction lending process.
For the purposes of this policy, 'construction lending' is defined as any financing arrangement where the primary use of
proceeds is the development, expansion, or rehabilitation of real estate assets. This includes both speculative and pre-sold
projects, as well as phased developments. The policy distinguishes between 'hard costs' (e.g., labor, materials) and 'soft costs'
(e.g., permits, architectural fees), both of which are subject to specific underwriting and disbursement controls.
Key definitions include: (1) 'Loan-to-Cost (LTC) Ratio': The ratio of the loan amount to the total estimated project cost,
expressed as a percentage. (2) 'Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio': The ratio of the loan amount to the appraised value of the
completed project. (3) 'Stabilized Occupancy': The occupancy rate at which a project is expected to generate sufficient cash
flow to cover debt service. (4) 'Contingency Reserve': A designated portion of the loan proceeds held back to cover unexpected
cost overruns.
The policy also defines roles and responsibilities, including the 'Relationship Manager,' who serves as the primary point of
contact for the borrower; the 'Credit Underwriter,' responsible for assessing the creditworthiness of the borrower and the viability
of the project; and the 'Construction Risk Officer,' who oversees compliance with this policy and reports to the Chief Credit
Officer.
All terms used in this policy are consistent with the bank’s internal glossary and regulatory definitions. Where conflicts arise, the
most conservative interpretation shall prevail. This section ensures that all stakeholders have a shared understanding of the
terminology and concepts critical to construction lending.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 3

3. 3. Governance and Oversight
Governance for construction lending is structured to ensure accountability, transparency, and alignment with the bank’s risk
appetite. The Chief Credit Officer (CCO) retains ultimate responsibility for the approval and oversight of this policy. The
Construction Lending Committee (CLC), a subcommittee of the bank’s Credit Risk Committee, is tasked with reviewing and
approving all construction loan requests exceeding $10 million in exposure.
The CLC is composed of senior representatives from Credit Risk, Real Estate Lending, Legal, Compliance, and Finance. It
meets bi-weekly to review pending applications, monitor portfolio performance, and address emerging risks. Decisions of the
CLC are documented in minutes, which are retained for a minimum of seven years and made available to regulators upon
request.
Day-to-day oversight of construction lending activities is delegated to the Construction Risk Officer (CRO), who reports directly
to the CCO. The CRO is responsible for ensuring adherence to this policy, conducting periodic audits of construction loan
portfolios, and escalating material deviations or risks to the CLC. The CRO also maintains a watchlist of high-risk projects,
which is reviewed quarterly by the CLC.
Independent validation of compliance with this policy is performed annually by the bank’s Internal Audit function. Audit findings
are reported to the CCO and the Board’s Risk Committee, with corrective actions tracked to completion. Additionally, the bank’s
Compliance department conducts semi-annual reviews to ensure alignment with regulatory expectations, including those
outlined in the Interagency Guidelines for Real Estate Lending.
This governance structure is designed to foster a culture of risk awareness and accountability. All employees involved in
construction lending are required to complete annual training on this policy, with completion records maintained by Human
Resources. Failure to complete training may result in restrictions on an employee’s authority to participate in construction
lending activities.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 4

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
Underwriting for construction loans must adhere to stringent criteria to ensure the borrower’s financial capacity and the project’s
feasibility. The bank requires a minimum FICO score of 700 for individual borrowers or a minimum credit rating of BBB- for
corporate borrowers. For project-specific underwriting, the borrower must demonstrate a track record of successfully completing
at least three similar projects within the past five years, with no material defaults or cost overruns exceeding 10% of the original
budget.
The Loan-to-Cost (LTC) ratio for construction loans shall not exceed 80% for commercial projects or 85% for residential
projects. For speculative developments, the LTC ratio is capped at 70%. The Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio, based on the appraised
value of the completed project, must not exceed 65% for commercial properties or 75% for residential properties. These
thresholds are designed to provide a buffer against cost overruns and market downturns.
Borrowers are required to contribute a minimum of 20% of the total project cost as equity, which must be injected prior to the
first disbursement of loan funds. Equity contributions may include cash, land (valued at no more than 50% of its appraised
value), or other unencumbered assets acceptable to the bank. The bank will not recognize sweat equity or future profits as valid
forms of equity contribution.
A comprehensive feasibility study must be submitted as part of the loan application, prepared by an independent third-party
consultant approved by the bank. The study must include detailed market analysis, pro forma financial projections, and
sensitivity analysis for key variables such as construction costs, absorption rates, and interest rates. The bank reserves the
right to commission its own feasibility study at the borrower’s expense if deemed necessary.
All construction loans must be supported by a first-priority lien on the property being developed, as well as personal or
corporate guarantees from the borrower. Additional collateral, such as assignments of contracts or letters of credit, may be
required at the discretion of the underwriter. The bank will not proceed with any construction loan without a valid, enforceable
security interest in place.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 5

5. 5. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
This policy establishes quantitative limits to control the bank’s exposure to construction lending risks. The maximum exposure
for any single construction loan is $50 million, unless approved by the CLC and the CCO. Aggregate exposure to construction
lending shall not exceed 25% of the bank’s total loan portfolio at any time. Additionally, the bank’s exposure to any single
borrower or borrower group for construction purposes is limited to 15% of the bank’s Tier 1 capital.
For speculative construction projects, the bank imposes a sub-limit of $25 million per loan and 10% of the total loan portfolio.
Speculative projects are defined as those where less than 50% of the units or space are pre-sold or pre-leased at the time of
loan closing. Projects exceeding these thresholds require additional approvals, including a unanimous vote by the CLC and
written justification from the Relationship Manager.
The bank maintains a contingency reserve requirement of 10% of the total project cost for all construction loans. This reserve is
held in a separate escrow account and released only upon completion of the project or as approved by the Construction Risk
Officer. In the event of cost overruns, the borrower is required to inject additional equity to cover the shortfall before any reserve
funds are released.
Interest rate risk is managed through the use of fixed-rate loans or interest rate caps for variable-rate construction loans. The
maximum allowable interest rate for construction loans is the bank’s prime rate plus 200 basis points. For loans with variable
rates, the bank requires a minimum debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of 1.25x, calculated using a stressed interest rate of
prime + 300 basis points.
The bank also imposes limits on the duration of construction loans. The maximum term for a construction loan is 36 months,
with an option to extend for an additional 12 months subject to CLC approval. Loans that exceed 24 months in duration require
quarterly progress inspections by an independent third-party engineer, at the borrower’s expense. Failure to meet construction
milestones may result in the suspension of disbursements or acceleration of the loan.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 6

6. 6. Approval Authorities and Escalation Paths
Approval authorities for construction loans are tiered based on the loan amount, risk profile, and complexity of the project.
Relationship Managers may approve construction loans up to $5 million, provided the loan meets all underwriting criteria and
the borrower has an existing relationship with the bank. Loans between $5 million and $10 million require approval from the
Regional Credit Officer (RCO) in addition to the Relationship Manager.
Loans exceeding $10 million must be approved by the Construction Lending Committee (CLC). The CLC’s approval is also
required for any loan that involves speculative development, a borrower with a credit rating below BBB-, or a project located in a
market where the bank has limited experience. The CLC’s decision is final, unless overridden by the Chief Credit Officer (CCO)
in exceptional circumstances.
Escalation paths are clearly defined to ensure timely resolution of issues. Any deviations from underwriting criteria, such as LTC
or LTV ratios exceeding policy limits, must be escalated to the RCO for review. The RCO has the authority to approve
exceptions up to 5% above the policy limits, provided the deviation is justified by compensating factors such as strong borrower
financials or pre-leasing commitments.
Material exceptions, defined as deviations exceeding 5% of policy limits or involving high-risk features such as speculative
development in an untried market, must be escalated to the CLC. The CLC will review the exception request, along with any
mitigating factors, and provide a written decision within 10 business days. All exception requests and decisions are documented
in the bank’s exception tracking system and reported to the CCO on a quarterly basis.
In cases where a construction loan exhibits signs of distress, such as cost overruns exceeding 10% of the budget or delays in
construction milestones, the Relationship Manager must immediately escalate the matter to the Construction Risk Officer
(CRO). The CRO will assess the situation and determine whether to place the loan on the watchlist, require additional collateral,
or take other risk mitigation actions. The CRO’s findings and recommendations are presented to the CLC for further action.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 7

7. 7. Monitoring and Controls
Ongoing monitoring of construction loans is critical to identifying and addressing risks in a timely manner. The bank requires
monthly progress reports from the borrower, which must include updated construction budgets, disbursement requests, and
milestone achievements. These reports are reviewed by the Relationship Manager and forwarded to the Construction Risk
Officer (CRO) for validation.
In addition to borrower-provided reports, the bank conducts independent site inspections at least quarterly for all active
construction loans. Inspections are performed by third-party engineers approved by the bank and focus on verifying the physical
progress of the project, the quality of construction, and compliance with building codes and permits. Inspection reports are
submitted to the CRO and retained in the loan file.
The bank employs a series of early warning indicators to proactively identify potential issues. These include: (1) disbursement
requests exceeding 110% of the approved budget for any line item; (2) delays in achieving construction milestones by more
than 30 days; (3) a decline in the borrower’s credit rating or financial condition; or (4) adverse market conditions, such as a 10%
or greater decline in local real estate prices. Triggering any of these indicators requires immediate escalation to the CRO.
Controls are also in place to manage disbursements. Loan funds are disbursed in accordance with a pre-approved draw
schedule, which is tied to the achievement of specific construction milestones. Each disbursement request must be
accompanied by lien waivers from contractors and suppliers, as well as evidence of payment for prior disbursements. The bank
will not release funds for any milestone until all prior milestones have been completed and documented to the bank’s
satisfaction.
The CRO conducts a comprehensive portfolio review on a quarterly basis, which includes an assessment of each construction
loan’s performance against its approved budget, timeline, and financial projections. Loans identified as high-risk are subject to
enhanced monitoring, including more frequent inspections and reporting. The results of the portfolio review are presented to the
CLC and documented in a report to the CCO.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 8

8. 8. Exception Handling
Exceptions to this policy are permitted only under limited circumstances and require formal approval. An exception is defined as
any deviation from the underwriting criteria, quantitative limits, or other requirements outlined in this document. All exceptions
must be documented in writing, justified by compensating factors, and approved by the appropriate authority as defined in
Section 6.
Compensating factors that may justify an exception include, but are not limited to: (1) a borrower with a long-standing
relationship with the bank and a proven track record of successful project completion; (2) pre-leasing or pre-sales commitments
that exceed 70% of the project’s capacity; (3) a project located in a high-demand market with limited supply; or (4) additional
collateral or guarantees provided by the borrower. The presence of compensating factors does not guarantee approval of an
exception request.
The exception request process begins with the Relationship Manager, who must submit a formal request to the RCO or CLC,
depending on the nature and size of the exception. The request must include a detailed explanation of the deviation, the
compensating factors, and the rationale for approval. The RCO or CLC will review the request, along with any supporting
documentation, and provide a written decision.
Approved exceptions are subject to enhanced monitoring and controls. For example, a loan approved with an LTC ratio
exceeding 80% may require monthly inspections instead of quarterly, or additional equity contributions from the borrower. The
terms of the exception, including any additional controls, are documented in the loan approval memo and monitored by the
CRO.
Exceptions that are denied or withdrawn must be documented, along with the reasons for the decision. The bank maintains a
log of all exception requests, including those that are approved, denied, or withdrawn, which is reviewed by Internal Audit as
part of its annual validation process. This log is also reported to the CCO and the Board’s Risk Committee on a semi-annual
basis.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 9

9. 9. Reporting and Documentation
Reporting is a critical component of the bank’s construction lending program, ensuring transparency and accountability. The
Relationship Manager is responsible for preparing a monthly Construction Loan Portfolio Report, which includes a summary of
all active construction loans, their current status, disbursement activity, and any exceptions or issues. This report is submitted to
the CRO and the RCO by the 5th business day of each month.
The CRO prepares a quarterly Construction Lending Risk Report, which provides a more detailed analysis of the portfolio’s
performance, including trends in delinquencies, cost overruns, and market conditions. This report also highlights any loans on
the watchlist, as well as the status of exception requests and approved exceptions. The quarterly report is presented to the CLC
and distributed to the CCO, the Chief Risk Officer, and the Board’s Risk Committee.
Documentation requirements are stringent to ensure a complete audit trail for each construction loan. The loan file must
include, at a minimum: (1) the loan application and all supporting documentation, such as feasibility studies and appraisals; (2)
the underwriting memo, including the analysis of the borrower’s financial condition and the project’s viability; (3) the loan
approval memo, signed by the appropriate authority; (4) the draw schedule and all disbursement requests, along with
supporting documentation; and (5) all inspection reports, progress updates, and correspondence with the borrower.
The bank retains all construction loan documentation for a minimum of seven years after the loan is repaid or charged off.
Documents are stored in the bank’s secure electronic document management system, with access restricted to authorized
personnel. Original hard copies of critical documents, such as signed loan agreements and security instruments, are retained in
a fireproof vault at the bank’s headquarters.
In addition to internal reporting, the bank is required to submit construction lending data to regulators as part of its periodic
filings. This includes information on loan concentrations, delinquencies, and exceptions. The Compliance department is
responsible for ensuring that all regulatory reporting requirements are met and that the data submitted is accurate and
complete.

SEC-CRE-v2.0 §2.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 10

10. 10. Policy Review and Updates
This policy is subject to periodic review to ensure its continued relevance and effectiveness in managing construction lending
risks. The Construction Risk Officer (CRO) is responsible for conducting an annual review of the policy, which includes an
assessment of its alignment with the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory expectations, and industry best practices. The review also
considers feedback from stakeholders, including Relationship Managers, underwriters, and the CLC.
The annual review process begins with a comprehensive assessment of the policy’s performance over the past year. This
includes an analysis of loan defaults, cost overruns, and other losses attributed to construction lending, as well as a review of
any regulatory findings or audit issues related to the policy. The CRO also benchmarks the bank’s construction lending
practices against those of peer institutions to identify areas for improvement.
Based on the findings of the annual review, the CRO may recommend updates to the policy. Proposed changes are
documented in a Policy Update Memo, which includes a summary of the changes, the rationale for each change, and the
expected impact on the bank’s construction lending activities. The memo is submitted to the CLC for review and approval.
Material changes to the policy, such as adjustments to quantitative limits or underwriting criteria, require the approval of the
CCO.
Once approved, updates to the policy are communicated to all relevant stakeholders, including Relationship Managers,
underwriters, and risk managers. Training on the updated policy is provided as necessary, with completion tracked by Human
Resources. The updated policy is published on the bank’s internal policy portal, with the effective date clearly noted. Previous
versions of the policy are archived but remain accessible for reference purposes.
In addition to the annual review, the policy may be updated on an ad hoc basis in response to significant changes in the bank’s
risk appetite, regulatory environment, or market conditions. For example, a downturn in the real estate market may prompt the
CRO to recommend temporary reductions in LTC or LTV limits. Such updates follow the same approval and communication
process as the annual review, ensuring that all stakeholders are informed of changes in a timely manner.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 1
 3.1 Approval Authorities
DEL-v3.3 §3.1 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose
This synthetic credit policy document, designated as Clause 3.1 Approval Authorities under the parent policy DEL-v3.3,
establishes the framework for credit approval authorities within the bank. It is designed for demonstration purposes to illustrate
how a financial institution might structure its credit approval processes, roles, and responsibilities. The policy ensures that credit
decisions are made in a consistent, transparent, and accountable manner, aligning with the bank’s risk appetite and regulatory
requirements.
The primary purpose of this document is to define the hierarchical structure of approval authorities, ensuring that credit
decisions are made at the appropriate level based on the transaction's risk profile, size, and complexity. This policy aims to
prevent unauthorized credit exposures, mitigate risks, and ensure compliance with internal and external guidelines. By clearly
delineating approval authorities, the bank can maintain operational efficiency while safeguarding its financial stability.
This synthetic policy also serves as a training tool for employees, providing a clear reference for understanding the escalation
paths, thresholds, and evidence requirements for credit approvals. It emphasizes the importance of adherence to predefined
limits and the necessity of obtaining proper authorization before committing the bank’s resources. The policy is internally
consistent and reflects industry best practices for credit risk management.
All references to specific roles, thresholds, or processes in this document are fictional and intended solely for demonstration. No
real-world financial institution, individual, or regulatory body is implied or referenced. The policy is structured to simulate a
real-world scenario, enabling users to understand how credit approval authorities might be organized in a banking environment.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope
This synthetic credit policy applies to all credit approval activities conducted within the bank, including but not limited to
corporate lending, commercial lending, retail lending, and treasury operations. It governs the approval of new credit facilities,
renewals, amendments, and any other transactions that expose the bank to credit risk. The policy is applicable to all
employees, officers, and committees involved in the credit approval process.
The scope of this document includes the definition of approval authorities for various credit products, such as term loans,
revolving credit facilities, letters of credit, and derivatives. It also covers the approval of credit limits, collateral requirements, and
pricing decisions. The policy ensures that all credit-related decisions are made within the bounds of the bank’s risk appetite and
regulatory constraints.
Excluded from this policy are non-credit-related activities, such as operational risk management, market risk management, and
liquidity risk management. While these areas may interact with credit risk, they are governed by separate policies and
frameworks. Additionally, this policy does not address the approval of internal administrative expenses or non-credit financial
transactions.
The synthetic nature of this document means that all references to specific products, departments, or jurisdictions are fictional.
The policy is designed to provide a comprehensive example of how a bank might define the scope of its credit approval
authorities, ensuring clarity and consistency across all credit-related activities.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 3

3. 3. Governance
The governance framework for credit approval authorities is structured to ensure accountability, transparency, and alignment
with the bank’s strategic objectives. The Board of Directors retains ultimate responsibility for approving the bank’s credit risk
appetite and delegating authority to senior management. The Chief Credit Officer (CCO) is responsible for overseeing the
implementation of this policy and ensuring compliance with all applicable regulations.
The Credit Committee, chaired by the CCO, is the primary body responsible for reviewing and approving credit transactions that
exceed predefined thresholds. The committee’s composition includes senior representatives from risk management, finance,
and business units to ensure a balanced and independent assessment of credit proposals. The committee meets monthly to
review high-value or high-risk transactions and may convene ad hoc for urgent matters.
Delegated authority is granted to specific roles, such as Relationship Managers, Credit Analysts, and Regional Credit Heads,
based on their expertise and the risk profile of the transactions they oversee. These delegations are documented in the bank’s
Delegation of Authority (DoA) matrix, which is reviewed and updated annually. Any deviations from the DoA matrix must be
escalated to the Credit Committee for approval.
This synthetic governance structure is designed to demonstrate how a bank might organize its credit approval processes to
ensure robust oversight and control. All roles, committees, and processes described herein are fictional and intended for
illustrative purposes only.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 4

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
The underwriting criteria outlined in this synthetic policy are designed to ensure that credit decisions are based on a thorough
assessment of the borrower’s financial health, repayment capacity, and collateral quality. The bank employs a risk-based
approach to underwriting, where the depth and rigor of the analysis are proportional to the size and complexity of the credit
exposure.
For corporate and commercial lending, the underwriting process includes a detailed review of the borrower’s financial
statements, cash flow projections, industry analysis, and management quality. The bank requires a minimum debt service
coverage ratio (DSCR) of 1.25x for term loans and a loan-to-value (LTV) ratio not exceeding 70% for secured transactions.
These thresholds are synthetic and intended for demonstration purposes.
Retail lending underwriting criteria include an assessment of the borrower’s credit score, income stability, and debt-to-income
(DTI) ratio. The bank sets a minimum credit score of 650 for unsecured personal loans and a maximum DTI ratio of 40% for
mortgage applications. These criteria are applied consistently across all retail lending products to ensure fairness and risk
mitigation.
The underwriting criteria are reviewed annually by the Credit Policy Team to ensure they remain aligned with the bank’s risk
appetite and market conditions. Any exceptions to the underwriting criteria must be justified, documented, and approved by the
appropriate authority as defined in the DoA matrix.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 5

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
This synthetic policy establishes quantitative limits to control the bank’s credit exposure and ensure that risks are managed
within acceptable parameters. The limits are defined for various credit products, counterparties, and industries, and they are
enforced through the bank’s credit risk management system.
For corporate lending, the bank sets a single borrower limit of 15% of its Tier 1 capital, with a sub-limit of 10% for unsecured
exposures. Industry concentration limits are set at 25% of Tier 1 capital for any single industry sector, ensuring diversification
and reducing the risk of sector-specific downturns. These limits are synthetic and designed to illustrate how a bank might
manage its credit exposures.
For commercial lending, the bank imposes a maximum exposure limit of $10 million per borrower for small and medium-sized
enterprises (SMEs). This limit may be increased to $20 million with the approval of the Regional Credit Head. Retail lending
limits are set at $500,000 for unsecured personal loans and $1 million for residential mortgages, subject to the borrower’s
creditworthiness and collateral value.
The bank also enforces internal limits for credit approval authorities. For example, Relationship Managers may approve credit
facilities up to $5 million, while approvals for amounts between $5 million and $20 million require the sign-off of a Regional
Credit Head. Transactions exceeding $20 million must be escalated to the Credit Committee for review and approval.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 6

6. 6. Approval Processes
The approval processes defined in this synthetic policy ensure that credit decisions are made in a timely, consistent, and
controlled manner. The processes are tiered based on the size, complexity, and risk profile of the transaction, with clear
escalation paths for higher-risk or larger exposures.
For transactions below the Relationship Manager’s delegated authority (e.g., up to $5 million), the approval process involves a
credit analysis conducted by the Relationship Manager, followed by a review by a Credit Analyst. The proposal is then
submitted to the Relationship Manager for final approval. All approvals must be documented in the bank’s credit management
system, with supporting evidence such as financial statements, collateral valuations, and risk assessments.
Transactions exceeding the Relationship Manager’s authority but within the Regional Credit Head’s limit (e.g., up to $20 million)
require an additional layer of review. The proposal is first assessed by the Relationship Manager and Credit Analyst, then
escalated to the Regional Credit Head for approval. The Regional Credit Head may request additional information or
adjustments to the terms before granting approval.
For transactions exceeding $20 million, the proposal must be submitted to the Credit Committee for review. The committee
evaluates the transaction based on its alignment with the bank’s risk appetite, the borrower’s creditworthiness, and the overall
portfolio risk. The committee’s decision is documented and communicated to the business unit, with any conditions or
requirements for approval clearly outlined.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 7

7. 7. Monitoring and Controls
The bank’s synthetic credit policy includes robust monitoring and control mechanisms to ensure ongoing compliance with
approval authorities and risk limits. The Credit Risk Management Team is responsible for monitoring the bank’s credit portfolio,
identifying emerging risks, and ensuring adherence to the policy’s quantitative and qualitative limits.
Monitoring activities include regular reviews of credit exposures against approved limits, assessments of borrower financial
performance, and evaluations of collateral values. The bank conducts monthly portfolio reviews to identify any breaches of
limits or deterioration in credit quality. Any breaches must be reported to the Credit Committee and addressed through
corrective actions, such as reducing exposure or obtaining additional collateral.
Controls are implemented at various levels to prevent unauthorized credit commitments. The bank’s credit management system
enforces role-based access controls, ensuring that only authorized personnel can approve transactions within their delegated
limits. Additionally, the system automatically flags any transactions that exceed predefined thresholds for escalation to higher
authorities.
Independent audits of the credit approval process are conducted annually by the Internal Audit Team. These audits assess the
effectiveness of the controls, the accuracy of the monitoring reports, and the compliance of the approval processes with the
bank’s policies and regulatory requirements. Findings from the audits are reported to the Board of Directors and addressed
through remediation plans.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 8

8. 8. Exceptions and Escalations
This synthetic policy recognizes that exceptions to the standard approval authorities and underwriting criteria may be necessary
in certain circumstances. However, all exceptions must be justified, documented, and approved through the appropriate
escalation paths to ensure that risks are properly managed and controlled.
Exceptions to the underwriting criteria, such as a DSCR below 1.25x or an LTV ratio exceeding 70%, require a detailed
justification from the Relationship Manager. The justification must include an assessment of the borrower’s mitigating factors,
such as strong cash flows, high-quality collateral, or a long-standing relationship with the bank. The proposal is then escalated
to the next higher authority, as defined in the DoA matrix, for approval.
Exceptions to the quantitative limits, such as exceeding the single borrower limit or industry concentration limit, must be
approved by the Credit Committee. The committee evaluates the exception based on the bank’s overall risk appetite, the
potential impact on the portfolio, and the availability of risk mitigants, such as additional collateral or guarantees. The
committee’s decision is documented and communicated to the relevant stakeholders.
All exceptions and escalations are tracked in the bank’s credit management system, with a clear audit trail of the justification,
approval, and any conditions imposed. The Credit Risk Management Team reviews exception reports quarterly to identify
trends or systemic issues that may require adjustments to the policy or underwriting criteria.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 9

9. 9. Reporting
The synthetic credit policy mandates comprehensive reporting to ensure transparency, accountability, and informed
decision-making. Reports are generated at various frequencies and distributed to relevant stakeholders, including senior
management, the Credit Committee, and the Board of Directors.
Monthly credit reports provide an overview of the bank’s credit portfolio, including new approvals, disbursements, repayments,
and any breaches of limits or underwriting criteria. These reports include key metrics such as portfolio concentration, credit
quality trends, and the status of exceptions and escalations. The reports are prepared by the Credit Risk Management Team
and reviewed by the CCO before distribution.
Quarterly reports focus on the performance of the credit portfolio, including delinquency rates, non-performing loans (NPLs),
and provisions for credit losses. These reports also include an analysis of the effectiveness of the approval authorities and
underwriting criteria, with recommendations for any adjustments or improvements. The quarterly reports are presented to the
Credit Committee and the Board of Directors for review and discussion.
Ad hoc reports are generated as needed to address specific requests from senior management or regulatory bodies. These
reports may focus on particular segments of the portfolio, such as high-risk industries or large exposures, and provide detailed
insights into the associated risks and mitigants. All reports are archived in the bank’s document management system for future
reference and audit purposes.

DEL-v3.3 §3.1 | Synthetic policy data
Page 10

10. 10. Policy Review and Updates
This synthetic credit policy is subject to regular review to ensure its continued relevance, effectiveness, and alignment with the
bank’s strategic objectives and regulatory requirements. The policy review process is designed to identify areas for
improvement, address emerging risks, and incorporate industry best practices.
The Credit Policy Team, led by the CCO, is responsible for conducting an annual review of the policy. The review includes an
assessment of the policy’s adherence to regulatory guidelines, the effectiveness of the approval authorities and underwriting
criteria, and the adequacy of the monitoring and reporting mechanisms. The team also evaluates feedback from business units,
risk management, and internal audit to identify any gaps or inefficiencies.
Proposed updates to the policy are documented in a change log, which includes the rationale for the change, the impact on the
bank’s operations, and the expected benefits. The proposed updates are then submitted to the Credit Committee for review and
approval. Significant changes, such as adjustments to quantitative limits or governance structures, may require the approval of
the Board of Directors.
Once approved, the updated policy is communicated to all relevant stakeholders, including employees, business units, and risk
management teams. Training sessions may be conducted to ensure that all personnel are aware of the changes and
understand their implications. The updated policy is also published in the bank’s policy repository, with the previous version
archived for reference. This synthetic review process ensures that the policy remains a dynamic and effective tool for managing
credit risk.

1. 1. Purpose and Applicability
This document, titled 'Clause 3.2: Escalation Rules,' is a synthetic demonstration policy derived from the parent framework
DEL-v3.3. It establishes the escalation protocols for credit-related decisions within the bank, ensuring that risks are managed
hierarchically and that no single point of failure exists in the approval or review process. The purpose of this clause is to define
clear, actionable pathways for escalating credit decisions that exceed predefined thresholds, involve high-risk counterparties, or
require exceptions to standard underwriting criteria.
The policy applies universally across all business units, subsidiaries, and geographic regions where the bank operates. It
governs the escalation of credit applications, limit increases, risk grade downgrades, and any deviations from established credit
policies. By standardizing escalation procedures, the bank aims to enhance transparency, accountability, and the consistency
of decision-making, while mitigating operational, financial, and reputational risks.
All employees, contractors, and third-party agents involved in credit origination, underwriting, monitoring, or risk management
are required to adhere to these escalation rules. Compliance with this policy is mandatory, and failure to escalate as prescribed
may result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination of employment or contractual relationships. The policy is
designed to complement, not replace, existing governance frameworks such as the bank’s Enterprise Risk Management Policy
and the Credit Risk Appetite Statement.
The synthetic nature of this document is emphasized to clarify that it is intended for demonstration, training, and system testing
purposes only. While the thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are realistic and internally consistent, they do not
reflect the actual credit policies of any real financial institution. Users of this document must treat it as illustrative content and
not as a binding operational directive.
This clause is effective immediately upon issuance and remains in force until superseded by a revised version or explicitly
withdrawn by the Chief Credit Officer (CCO). Any updates or amendments to this policy will be communicated through official
bank channels and will require approval from the Credit Policy Committee (CPC). The CCO retains the authority to interpret this
policy and resolve any ambiguities that may arise during its implementation.

2. 2. Scope of Escalation Requirements
The escalation requirements outlined in this clause apply to all credit exposures, including but not limited to loans, letters of
credit, guarantees, derivatives, and trade finance facilities. Escalation is mandatory for transactions that exceed the delegated
authority limits of the originating business unit or relationship manager, as well as for those that trigger risk-based thresholds
such as high probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), or exposure at default (EAD).
Quantitative thresholds for escalation are defined as follows: any single transaction exceeding USD 10 million in exposure must
be escalated to the next level of authority. For transactions between USD 5 million and USD 10 million, escalation is required if
the counterparty’s internal risk rating is below investment grade (i.e., BB+ or lower). Additionally, any transaction involving a
new counterparty in a high-risk jurisdiction, as defined by the bank’s Anti-Money Laundering (AML) policy, must be escalated
regardless of size.
Qualitative triggers for escalation include transactions involving complex structures, such as multi-jurisdictional collateral
arrangements or non-standard covenants. Escalation is also required for transactions where the borrower’s financial metrics
(e.g., leverage ratios, interest coverage) fall outside the bank’s standard underwriting tolerances by more than 20%.
Furthermore, any request for a waiver of standard credit terms, such as maturity extensions or covenant relief, must be
escalated to the appropriate authority level.
The scope of this policy extends to post-approval monitoring activities. For example, if a borrower’s credit quality deteriorates
such that its risk rating drops by two or more notches within a 12-month period, the relationship manager must escalate the
case to the Portfolio Risk Manager for review. Similarly, any breach of financial or non-financial covenants that is not cured
within the stipulated grace period must be escalated to the Credit Risk Committee (CRC).
Exclusions from this policy are limited to transactions that fall below the USD 1 million threshold and are classified as low-risk
under the bank’s internal risk assessment framework. However, even for such transactions, the relationship manager retains
the discretion to escalate if they deem it necessary based on qualitative factors or market conditions. The CCO may also direct
ad-hoc escalations for specific portfolios or counterparties as part of targeted risk reviews.

 3.2 Escalation Rules
DEL-v3.3 §3.2 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose and Applicability
This document, titled 'Clause 3.2: Escalation Rules,' is a synthetic demonstration policy derived from the parent framework
DEL-v3.3. It establishes the escalation protocols for credit-related decisions within the bank, ensuring that risks are managed
hierarchically and that no single point of failure exists in the approval or review process. The purpose of this clause is to define
clear, actionable pathways for escalating credit decisions that exceed predefined thresholds, involve high-risk counterparties, or
require exceptions to standard underwriting criteria.
The policy applies universally across all business units, subsidiaries, and geographic regions where the bank operates. It
governs the escalation of credit applications, limit increases, risk grade downgrades, and any deviations from established credit
policies. By standardizing escalation procedures, the bank aims to enhance transparency, accountability, and the consistency
of decision-making, while mitigating operational, financial, and reputational risks.
All employees, contractors, and third-party agents involved in credit origination, underwriting, monitoring, or risk management
are required to adhere to these escalation rules. Compliance with this policy is mandatory, and failure to escalate as prescribed
may result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination of employment or contractual relationships. The policy is
designed to complement, not replace, existing governance frameworks such as the bank’s Enterprise Risk Management Policy
and the Credit Risk Appetite Statement.
The synthetic nature of this document is emphasized to clarify that it is intended for demonstration, training, and system testing
purposes only. While the thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are realistic and internally consistent, they do not
reflect the actual credit policies of any real financial institution. Users of this document must treat it as illustrative content and
not as a binding operational directive.
This clause is effective immediately upon issuance and remains in force until superseded by a revised version or explicitly
withdrawn by the Chief Credit Officer (CCO). Any updates or amendments to this policy will be communicated through official
bank channels and will require approval from the Credit Policy Committee (CPC). The CCO retains the authority to interpret this
policy and resolve any ambiguities that may arise during its implementation.

DEL-v3.3 §3.2 | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope of Escalation Requirements
The escalation requirements outlined in this clause apply to all credit exposures, including but not limited to loans, letters of
credit, guarantees, derivatives, and trade finance facilities. Escalation is mandatory for transactions that exceed the delegated
authority limits of the originating business unit or relationship manager, as well as for those that trigger risk-based thresholds
such as high probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), or exposure at default (EAD).
Quantitative thresholds for escalation are defined as follows: any single transaction exceeding USD 10 million in exposure must
be escalated to the next level of authority. For transactions between USD 5 million and USD 10 million, escalation is required if
the counterparty’s internal risk rating is below investment grade (i.e., BB+ or lower). Additionally, any transaction involving a
new counterparty in a high-risk jurisdiction, as defined by the bank’s Anti-Money Laundering (AML) policy, must be escalated
regardless of size.
Qualitative triggers for escalation include transactions involving complex structures, such as multi-jurisdictional collateral
arrangements or non-standard covenants. Escalation is also required for transactions where the borrower’s financial metrics
(e.g., leverage ratios, interest coverage) fall outside the bank’s standard underwriting tolerances by more than 20%.
Furthermore, any request for a waiver of standard credit terms, such as maturity extensions or covenant relief, must be
escalated to the appropriate authority level.
The scope of this policy extends to post-approval monitoring activities. For example, if a borrower’s credit quality deteriorates
such that its risk rating drops by two or more notches within a 12-month period, the relationship manager must escalate the
case to the Portfolio Risk Manager for review. Similarly, any breach of financial or non-financial covenants that is not cured
within the stipulated grace period must be escalated to the Credit Risk Committee (CRC).
Exclusions from this policy are limited to transactions that fall below the USD 1 million threshold and are classified as low-risk
under the bank’s internal risk assessment framework. However, even for such transactions, the relationship manager retains
the discretion to escalate if they deem it necessary based on qualitative factors or market conditions. The CCO may also direct
ad-hoc escalations for specific portfolios or counterparties as part of targeted risk reviews.

3. 3. Governance and Authority Framework
The governance framework for credit escalations is structured hierarchically to ensure that decisions are made at the
appropriate level of seniority and expertise. At the base of the hierarchy, Relationship Managers (RMs) are empowered to
approve transactions up to USD 1 million, provided they comply with all standard underwriting criteria and do not involve
high-risk counterparties or jurisdictions. RMs must document their rationale for approval in the bank’s credit management
system (CMS) and retain evidence of compliance with policy requirements.
The next level of authority resides with the Business Unit Credit Officers (BUCOs), who can approve transactions up to USD 5
million. BUCOs are also responsible for reviewing and endorsing or rejecting escalations from RMs for transactions that exceed
the RM’s delegated authority but fall within the BUCO’s limit. BUCOs must conduct an independent assessment of the credit
risk, including a review of the borrower’s financial statements, industry analysis, and collateral valuation, where applicable.
For transactions exceeding USD 5 million but not exceeding USD 25 million, escalation to the Regional Credit Officer (RCO) is
required. The RCO’s approval is also mandatory for any transaction involving a counterparty rated below BB- or domiciled in a
jurisdiction subject to sanctions or heightened AML scrutiny. The RCO must convene a credit review committee (CRC) for
transactions in this range that involve complex structures or significant policy exceptions.
Transactions exceeding USD 25 million, or those involving policy exceptions that cannot be resolved at the RCO level, must be
escalated to the Chief Credit Officer (CCO). The CCO’s approval is final for all credit decisions, except in cases where the
transaction exceeds USD 100 million or involves a new product type not previously approved by the bank. In such instances,
the CCO must seek ratification from the bank’s Board of Directors or its designated Risk Committee.
The authority framework is supported by a system of checks and balances, including independent risk reviews by the bank’s
Risk Management Division (RMD) and compliance attestations by the Legal and Compliance teams. All escalations must be
documented in the CMS, with clear audit trails showing the rationale for decisions, the evidence reviewed, and the identities of
the approving authorities. The Internal Audit function conducts periodic reviews of escalation compliance as part of its broader
mandate to assess the effectiveness of the bank’s credit risk controls.

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria and Risk Assessment
Underwriting criteria serve as the foundation for determining whether a transaction requires escalation under this policy. The
bank’s standard underwriting framework evaluates counterparties based on five core risk dimensions: financial strength,
industry risk, management quality, collateral coverage, and structural subordination. Each dimension is scored on a scale of 1
to 5, with 1 representing the lowest risk and 5 the highest. A composite risk score is calculated as the weighted average of
these dimensions, with financial strength and industry risk each accounting for 30% of the total score, and the remaining
dimensions accounting for 10% each.
Transactions with a composite risk score of 3.0 or higher must be escalated to the BUCO, regardless of size. Similarly, any
transaction where a single risk dimension scores a 5 must be escalated to the RCO, as this indicates a critical weakness that
could materially impact the bank’s risk exposure. For example, a counterparty with a financial strength score of 5 (e.g., negative
equity or persistent cash flow deficits) would trigger an automatic escalation, even if the other dimensions are scored more
favorably.
In addition to the composite risk score, the bank employs a series of quantitative thresholds to identify transactions requiring
escalation. These include debt service coverage ratios (DSCR) below 1.25x, leverage ratios (total debt to EBITDA) above 4.0x,
and current ratios below 1.0x. Transactions breaching any of these thresholds must be escalated to the next level of authority,
with the escalation path determined by the severity and number of breaches. For instance, a transaction breaching two or more
thresholds would require RCO approval, while a single breach might be addressed at the BUCO level.
Qualitative underwriting criteria also play a critical role in determining escalation requirements. These include assessments of
the borrower’s business model sustainability, competitive positioning, and exposure to environmental, social, and governance
(ESG) risks. For example, a borrower operating in a sector facing significant regulatory disruption (e.g., fossil fuel extraction)
may require escalation to the RCO or CCO, even if its financial metrics are within standard thresholds. Similarly, transactions
involving related-party exposures or complex intercompany guarantees must be escalated to ensure that conflicts of interest are
appropriately managed.
The underwriting criteria are reviewed and updated annually by the Credit Policy Committee (CPC) to reflect changes in market
conditions, regulatory requirements, and the bank’s risk appetite. Any material changes to the criteria must be approved by the
CCO and communicated to all relevant stakeholders through the bank’s policy management system. Relationship Managers
are required to complete annual training on the underwriting framework and pass a competency assessment to retain their
delegated authority.

5. 5. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
Quantitative limits are a cornerstone of the bank’s credit escalation framework, providing objective triggers for when
transactions must be reviewed by higher authorities. The bank employs a tiered system of limits, which are applied at both the
individual transaction and aggregate exposure levels. At the transaction level, the primary limits are as follows: USD 1 million for
Relationship Managers, USD 5 million for Business Unit Credit Officers, USD 25 million for Regional Credit Officers, and USD

100 million for the Chief Credit Officer. Transactions exceeding these limits must be escalated to the next authority level, as
outlined in Section 3.
Aggregate exposure limits are applied to counterparties, industries, and geographic regions to prevent excessive concentration
risk. For example, the bank’s single counterparty exposure limit is set at 10% of its Tier 1 capital, while the aggregate exposure
to any single industry sector cannot exceed 20% of Tier 1 capital. Exposures approaching or exceeding 80% of these limits
must be escalated to the CCO for review, and any breaches must be reported to the Board of Directors within 48 hours. The
bank’s Risk Management Division (RMD) monitors aggregate exposures in real-time and generates automated alerts when
thresholds are approached.
In addition to exposure limits, the bank enforces risk-based thresholds for specific credit metrics. For corporate borrowers,
these include a maximum leverage ratio of 4.5x, a minimum interest coverage ratio of 2.0x, and a minimum current ratio of 1.2x.
For retail portfolios, thresholds include a maximum delinquency rate of 3% and a minimum FICO score of 650 for new
originations. Transactions or portfolios breaching these thresholds must be escalated according to the severity of the breach,
with more significant deviations requiring higher levels of approval.
The bank also applies concentration limits to specific asset classes and products. For example, exposures to commercial real
estate (CRE) cannot exceed 300% of the bank’s total risk-weighted assets, and within the CRE portfolio, no more than 15% of
the total CRE exposure can be concentrated in a single geographic market. Similarly, the bank limits its exposure to
speculative-grade (below BB-) counterparties to 5% of Tier 1 capital. Any transaction that would cause the bank to exceed
these concentration limits must be escalated to the CCO for exception approval.
Quantitative limits and thresholds are reviewed quarterly by the CPC, which may adjust them based on changes in the bank’s
risk appetite, capital position, or macroeconomic outlook. The CCO has the authority to impose temporary, more restrictive
limits in response to emerging risks or market dislocations. All changes to quantitative limits must be documented in the bank’s
policy management system and communicated to relevant stakeholders within 5 business days of approval.

6. 6. Approval Workflows and Delegated Authority
Approval workflows under this policy are designed to ensure that credit decisions are made efficiently while maintaining robust
risk controls. The workflows are automated through the bank’s Credit Management System (CMS), which routes transactions to
the appropriate authority based on predefined rules, including transaction size, counterparty risk rating, and product type. The
CMS also flags transactions that require escalation due to policy exceptions, threshold breaches, or qualitative risk factors,
ensuring that no high-risk transaction is approved without the necessary oversight.
For transactions within a Relationship Manager’s (RM) delegated authority, the workflow requires the RM to complete a credit
application in the CMS, which includes a detailed assessment of the borrower’s creditworthiness, proposed terms, and
supporting documentation (e.g., financial statements, collateral valuations). The CMS automatically validates the application
against the bank’s underwriting criteria and quantitative thresholds. If the transaction complies with all requirements, the RM
may approve it directly. However, if the CMS identifies any issues, the transaction is automatically escalated to the BUCO for
review.
Transactions requiring BUCO approval follow a similar process, with the BUCO conducting an independent review of the RM’s
assessment. The BUCO must document their rationale for approval or rejection in the CMS, including any mitigating factors or
additional controls they deem necessary. If the BUCO approves the transaction, it is automatically routed to the RCO for
information purposes, though RCO approval is not required unless the transaction exceeds the BUCO’s delegated authority.
The CMS maintains a log of all approvals, including timestamps and the identities of the approving authorities, to ensure full
auditability.
For transactions requiring RCO or CCO approval, the workflow includes additional steps to ensure thorough due diligence. The
RCO or CCO must convene a credit review committee (CRC), which includes representatives from Risk Management, Legal,
Compliance, and the relevant business unit. The CRC reviews the transaction in detail, including a presentation by the RM and
a challenge session led by the RCO or CCO. The CRC’s recommendation is documented in the CMS, and the final decision is
recorded with the approving authority’s digital signature. Transactions requiring Board approval follow a similar process, with
the CCO presenting the case to the Board’s Risk Committee for ratification.
Delegated authority may be temporarily suspended or revised by the CCO in cases of repeated policy breaches, significant
credit losses, or changes in the risk profile of a business unit or region. The CCO must notify affected employees in writing and
update the CMS to reflect the changes. Delegated authority is also subject to annual recertification, which requires employees
to demonstrate ongoing competence in credit risk management through training and assessments. Failure to complete
recertification results in the automatic revocation of delegated authority until the requirements are met.

7. 7. Monitoring and Trigger Events
Monitoring is a critical component of the bank’s credit escalation framework, ensuring that risks are identified and addressed
proactively. The bank employs a multi-layered monitoring approach, combining automated surveillance tools with manual
reviews by credit and risk professionals. The primary objective is to detect early warning signals of credit deterioration, policy
breaches, or emerging risks that may require escalation under this policy.
The bank’s Credit Management System (CMS) includes a real-time monitoring module that tracks key credit metrics for all
counterparties, including financial ratios, risk ratings, covenant compliance, and exposure levels. The system generates
automated alerts when predefined thresholds are breached, such as a decline in a borrower’s risk rating, a breach of financial
covenants, or an increase in exposure beyond approved limits. These alerts are routed to the relevant Relationship Manager
and their supervisor, with escalation to higher authorities if the issue is not resolved within the stipulated timeframe.
In addition to automated monitoring, the bank conducts periodic manual reviews of credit portfolios to identify qualitative risks
that may not be captured by quantitative thresholds. For example, the Portfolio Risk Management team performs quarterly
reviews of high-risk industries, such as commercial real estate or leveraged lending, to assess the impact of macroeconomic
trends on credit quality. These reviews may trigger escalations to the RCO or CCO if they identify systemic risks or the need for
portfolio-level actions, such as increased provisions or reduced exposures.
Trigger events that mandate escalation under this policy include, but are not limited to, the following: a borrower’s risk rating
downgrade by two or more notches within a 12-month period; a breach of any financial or non-financial covenant that is not
cured within the grace period; a material adverse change in the borrower’s business, such as a significant loss of market share,
regulatory action, or litigation; or the identification of fraud, misrepresentation, or other integrity issues. The RM must escalate
such events to the BUCO within 24 hours of identification, with further escalation to the RCO or CCO as determined by the
severity of the issue.
The bank’s Internal Audit function conducts independent reviews of the monitoring and escalation processes at least annually.
These reviews assess the effectiveness of automated alerts, the timeliness of escalations, and the adequacy of actions taken to
address identified risks. Findings from these reviews are reported to the CCO and the Board’s Audit Committee, with corrective
actions tracked to completion. The CCO may also commission targeted reviews of specific portfolios or business units in
response to emerging risks or regulatory concerns.

8. 8. Exception Handling and Waivers
Exceptions to the bank’s standard credit policies, including underwriting criteria, quantitative thresholds, or approval workflows,
are permitted only under strictly controlled circumstances. This section outlines the process for requesting, reviewing, and
approving exceptions, as well as the controls in place to ensure that such exceptions do not expose the bank to unacceptable
risks. All exceptions must be justified by compelling business or strategic rationale and must be supported by robust risk
mitigants.
The process for requesting an exception begins with the Relationship Manager (RM), who must submit a formal exception
request through the Credit Management System (CMS). The request must include a detailed business case, an assessment of
the incremental risk introduced by the exception, and a description of the mitigating factors or controls that will be implemented
to offset the risk. The RM must also provide evidence that the borrower or transaction has been subjected to enhanced due
diligence, such as additional financial analysis, third-party risk assessments, or legal opinions.
Exception requests are reviewed by the Business Unit Credit Officer (BUCO), who assesses the merits of the case and the
adequacy of the proposed mitigants. The BUCO may approve exceptions for transactions within their delegated authority,
provided that the incremental risk is deemed acceptable and the mitigants are sufficient. However, exceptions that involve
policy breaches, such as waivers of standard covenants or underwriting criteria, must be escalated to the Regional Credit
Officer (RCO) for approval. The RCO may consult with the bank’s Risk Management Division (RMD) or Legal team to assess
the implications of the exception.
Exceptions that cannot be resolved at the RCO level, or those involving transactions exceeding USD 25 million, must be
escalated to the Chief Credit Officer (CCO). The CCO has the authority to approve exceptions that are consistent with the
bank’s risk appetite and strategic objectives. However, exceptions that involve material deviations from the bank’s credit
policies, such as transactions with counterparties rated below B- or exposures exceeding 15% of Tier 1 capital, require the
approval of the Board’s Risk Committee. The CCO must present such cases to the committee, including a detailed risk
assessment and a recommendation for approval or rejection.
All approved exceptions are documented in the CMS, with clear records of the rationale, the mitigating factors, and the identities
of the approving authorities. The bank’s Internal Audit function conducts periodic reviews of exception handling to ensure
compliance with this policy and to assess the effectiveness of the controls in place. Exceptions are also subject to post-approval
monitoring, with the RM required to provide quarterly updates on the performance of the transaction and the continued validity
of the mitigating factors. If the risk profile of the transaction deteriorates, the RM must escalate the case for reassessment,
which may result in the withdrawal of the exception or the imposition of additional controls.

9. 9. Reporting and Documentation Requirements
Comprehensive reporting and documentation are essential to the transparency, accountability, and auditability of the bank’s
credit escalation processes. This section establishes the requirements for documenting escalations, approvals, exceptions, and
monitoring activities, as well as the reporting obligations for various stakeholders, including senior management, the Board of
Directors, and regulatory authorities.
All escalations, approvals, and exceptions must be documented in the bank’s Credit Management System (CMS) at the time
they occur. The CMS captures key details, including the transaction size, counterparty information, risk ratings, underwriting
criteria, and the rationale for escalation or exception. The system also records the identities of the individuals involved in the
decision-making process, along with timestamps and digital signatures to ensure non-repudiation. Supporting documentation,
such as financial statements, risk assessments, and legal opinions, must be attached to the CMS record and retained for a
minimum of seven years.
The bank produces a series of standard reports to monitor compliance with this policy and to provide visibility into credit risk
exposures. These include daily reports of new escalations and approvals, which are distributed to the relevant Business Unit
Credit Officers (BUCOs) and Regional Credit Officers (RCOs). Weekly reports summarize the status of all open escalations,
including those awaiting approval, those under review, and those that have been rejected or withdrawn. Monthly reports provide
a more comprehensive view of escalation trends, including the volume and value of escalated transactions, the reasons for
escalation, and the average time taken to resolve escalations.
Quarterly, the bank prepares a Credit Escalation and Exception Report for the Chief Credit Officer (CCO) and the Credit Policy
Committee (CPC). This report includes an analysis of escalation patterns, such as the most common triggers for escalation, the
business units or regions with the highest escalation volumes, and the approval rates at each authority level. The report also
highlights any systemic issues or recurring policy breaches, along with recommendations for corrective actions or policy
updates. The CCO presents this report to the Board’s Risk Committee, which uses it to assess the effectiveness of the bank’s
credit risk management framework.
In addition to internal reporting, the bank is required to provide certain information to regulatory authorities as part of its ongoing
supervisory obligations. This includes regular reports on credit risk exposures, policy exceptions, and the bank’s adherence to
regulatory capital and liquidity requirements. The bank’s Regulatory Reporting team is responsible for compiling this
information, with input from the Credit Risk, Finance, and Compliance departments. All regulatory reports are reviewed by the
CCO and the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) prior to submission to ensure accuracy and completeness.
The bank’s Internal Audit function conducts periodic reviews of the reporting and documentation processes to ensure
compliance with this policy and to assess the adequacy of the controls in place. These reviews include testing the accuracy and
completeness of CMS records, the timeliness of reporting, and the effectiveness of the bank’s data governance framework.
Findings from these reviews are reported to the CCO and the Board’s Audit Committee, with corrective actions tracked to
completion.

10. 10. Policy Review and Continuous Improvement
This policy is subject to regular review to ensure that it remains aligned with the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory requirements,
and industry best practices. The review process is designed to identify opportunities for improvement, address emerging risks,
and incorporate lessons learned from the bank’s credit activities and external developments. The Chief Credit Officer (CCO) is
responsible for overseeing the review process, with input from the Credit Policy Committee (CPC), Risk Management Division
(RMD), and other relevant stakeholders.
The policy is reviewed at least annually, or more frequently if triggered by material changes in the bank’s operating
environment. Trigger events for an ad-hoc review include, but are not limited to, significant credit losses, regulatory changes,
mergers or acquisitions, or shifts in the bank’s strategic direction. The CCO may also initiate a review in response to findings
from internal audits, external examinations, or risk assessments that identify gaps or deficiencies in the escalation framework.
The review process begins with an assessment of the policy’s effectiveness, which is conducted by the CPC in collaboration
with the RMD. This assessment includes an analysis of escalation data from the Credit Management System (CMS), such as
the volume and value of escalated transactions, the reasons for escalation, and the outcomes of the escalation process. The
assessment also evaluates the timeliness of escalations, the adequacy of approval workflows, and the effectiveness of
monitoring and reporting mechanisms. Feedback is solicited from business units, risk professionals, and other stakeholders to
identify practical challenges or areas for improvement.
Based on the findings of the assessment, the CPC develops recommendations for updates to the policy. These
recommendations may include revisions to quantitative thresholds, underwriting criteria, or approval workflows, as well as
enhancements to the CMS or other supporting systems. The CPC presents its recommendations to the CCO, who reviews
them for alignment with the bank’s risk appetite and strategic objectives. If the CCO approves the recommendations, they are
formalized into a revised version of the policy and submitted to the Board’s Risk Committee for ratification.
Once approved, the revised policy is communicated to all relevant stakeholders through the bank’s policy management system,
with a clear implementation timeline and any required training or system updates. The CCO is responsible for ensuring that the
revised policy is effectively implemented and that all employees are aware of their obligations under the new framework. The
bank’s Internal Audit function may conduct a post-implementation review to verify compliance with the revised policy and to
assess its effectiveness in addressing the identified issues.
Continuous improvement is a core principle of the bank’s credit risk management framework. The CCO encourages a culture of
open communication and feedback, where employees at all levels are empowered to identify and report potential improvements
to the escalation process. The bank also benchmarks its policies and practices against industry peers and regulatory
expectations to ensure that it remains at the forefront of credit risk management. By fostering a proactive and adaptive
approach to policy review, the bank aims to maintain a robust and resilient credit escalation framework that supports its
long-term success.

 A.1 RWA Treatment
REG-Basel-IV §A.1 · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose and Objectives
This synthetic credit policy document, designated as Clause A.1 under the parent policy REG-Basel-IV, establishes the
framework for Risk-Weighted Asset (RWA) treatment within the bank’s credit risk management operations. The primary
purpose of this policy is to ensure compliance with Basel IV standards while aligning internal credit risk assessments with
regulatory capital requirements. By defining clear methodologies for RWA calculation, this policy aims to enhance the accuracy
of capital adequacy reporting and support prudent risk-taking.
The objectives of this policy include: (i) providing a structured approach to assigning risk weights to credit exposures; (ii)
ensuring consistency in the application of RWA treatments across all business units; (iii) facilitating transparency in the bank’s
capital allocation processes; and (iv) enabling effective monitoring of credit risk concentrations. This policy is designed to be
internally consistent with the bank’s broader risk management framework, including credit underwriting, portfolio monitoring,
and regulatory reporting.
This document is synthetic demonstration data and does not reflect the actual policies, procedures, or practices of any real
financial institution. It is intended solely for illustrative purposes to demonstrate how a bank might structure its RWA treatment
policy under Basel IV. All thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are fictional and should not be interpreted as
operational guidelines.
The policy is grounded in the principle that RWA calculations must reflect the true economic risk of credit exposures. To achieve
this, the bank adopts a combination of the Standardized Approach and the Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) Approach, as
permitted under Basel IV. The choice of approach depends on the nature of the exposure, the availability of historical data, and
the sophistication of the bank’s risk management systems. The policy ensures that all approaches are applied consistently and
are subject to regular validation.
Compliance with this policy is mandatory for all business units involved in credit risk management, including lending, treasury,
and risk control functions. Failure to adhere to the RWA treatment guidelines may result in misalignment with regulatory capital
requirements, potentially leading to reputational, financial, or regulatory risks. The policy is reviewed annually to ensure its
continued relevance and alignment with evolving regulatory expectations.

2. 2. Scope and Applicability
This policy applies to all credit exposures held by the bank, including but not limited to loans, bonds, derivatives, and
off-balance-sheet commitments. It covers both retail and wholesale portfolios, as well as specialized lending such as project
finance, real estate, and trade finance. The RWA treatment methodologies outlined in this policy are applicable to all
jurisdictions in which the bank operates, unless local regulations dictate otherwise.
The scope of this policy includes the calculation of RWA for both performing and non-performing exposures. For performing
exposures, the policy specifies the use of risk weights derived from external credit ratings or internal risk assessments. For
non-performing exposures, the policy mandates the application of a 100% risk weight, in line with Basel IV requirements, unless
a higher risk weight is justified by the bank’s internal analysis.
Exposures exempt from the RWA treatment requirements of this policy include those explicitly excluded under Basel IV, such
as certain sovereign exposures and intraday liquidity facilities. However, such exemptions must be documented and approved
by the bank’s Risk Management Committee (RMC). The RMC is responsible for maintaining a register of all exempt exposures
and ensuring that they are subject to alternative risk management controls.
The policy also applies to the bank’s subsidiaries and branches, regardless of their geographical location. Local
implementations of this policy must be approved by the Group Chief Risk Officer (CRO) to ensure consistency with the parent
policy. Any deviations from the global RWA treatment standards must be justified and documented in a local policy addendum,
which is subject to annual review by the Group Risk function.
This synthetic policy is designed to demonstrate how a bank might define the scope of its RWA treatment framework. It includes
fictional thresholds and applicability rules to illustrate the complexity of managing credit risk across diverse portfolios and
jurisdictions. The policy emphasizes the importance of a unified approach to RWA calculations while allowing for localized
adaptations where necessary.
