sources.quote:
1. 1. Purpose and Applicability
This document, titled RAT-1.0 Credit Rating Standards, establishes the foundational framework for credit rating assignments
within the synthetic demonstration environment of the bank. It is designed to ensure consistency, transparency, and regulatory
compliance in the evaluation of creditworthiness for all counterparties, including corporate, commercial, and retail clients. The
standards outlined herein are aligned with the parent policy RAT-v1.0 and serve as a critical component of the bank’s risk
management infrastructure.
The primary purpose of RAT-1.0 is to define the methodologies, criteria, and governance structures required to assign, validate,
and monitor credit ratings. These ratings are integral to the bank’s decision-making processes, including loan approvals,
risk-based pricing, capital allocation, and portfolio monitoring. By adhering to these standards, the bank aims to mitigate credit
risk, enhance stakeholder confidence, and fulfill its fiduciary responsibilities.
This policy applies to all business units, risk management teams, and personnel involved in the credit assessment process. It is
mandatory for underwriters, credit analysts, relationship managers, and senior management to comply with the provisions of
this document. Third-party vendors or partners engaged in credit-related activities on behalf of the bank must also adhere to
these standards unless explicitly exempted by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO).
The synthetic nature of this document is emphasized to clarify that it is intended for demonstration, training, and internal testing
purposes only. While the thresholds, roles, and processes described are realistic and internally consistent, they do not reflect
actual bank operations or real-world data. Any use of this document for live transactions or external reporting must be explicitly
authorized by the bank’s compliance and legal departments.
The applicability of RAT-1.0 extends to all credit exposures, including but not limited to loans, bonds, derivatives, and trade
finance instruments. It covers both new credit applications and the periodic review of existing exposures. The standards are
designed to be scalable, accommodating the diverse needs of the bank’s global operations while maintaining uniformity in risk
assessment practices.

2. 2. Scope and Exclusions
The scope of RAT-1.0 Credit Rating Standards encompasses all credit rating activities conducted by the bank, including the
initial assignment, periodic review, and ad-hoc reassessment of ratings. This includes ratings for internal risk management
purposes as well as those used for regulatory reporting, such as under the Basel III framework. The policy is global in nature,
applying to all jurisdictions in which the bank operates, unless local regulations impose stricter requirements.
All credit exposures, regardless of size or complexity, fall within the scope of this policy. This includes exposures to corporate
entities, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), retail customers, financial institutions, and sovereign entities. The policy
also covers specialized lending areas such as project finance, leveraged finance, and structured credit products. Each
exposure must be assigned a credit rating in accordance with the methodologies outlined in this document.
Exclusions from this policy are limited and must be explicitly documented and approved by the CRO. Typical exclusions may
include intra-group exposures, where the counterparty is a subsidiary or affiliate of the bank, and exposures that are fully
guaranteed by a sovereign entity with a risk weight of 0% under regulatory capital rules. Additionally, exposures that are
immaterial in size (defined as less than USD 100,000) may be exempted from formal rating assignments, provided they are
subject to alternative risk controls.
The policy also excludes credit ratings assigned by external credit rating agencies (e.g., Moody’s, S&P, Fitch) for the purpose of
regulatory compliance, where such ratings are used directly without internal override. However, the bank reserves the right to
perform its own internal rating assessment for risk management purposes, even when external ratings are available. In such
cases, the internal rating must be documented and justified in accordance with the standards set forth in this policy.
Any deviations from the scope of this policy, including temporary or permanent exclusions, must be documented in the bank’s
Risk Policy Exception Log. Such deviations require the approval of the CRO and must be reviewed at least annually to ensure
they remain appropriate. The bank’s internal audit function will periodically verify compliance with the scope and exclusion
provisions of this policy.

extracted.name: CRM Department Administrative Ownership
extracted.source_quote:
The Credit Risk Management (CRM) department is the primary owner of this policy and is tasked with its day-to-day
administration. The CRM department is responsible for developing and maintaining the credit rating methodologies, tools, and
systems used by the bank. It also oversees the training of personnel involved in the rating process and ensures that all ratings
are assigned in accordance with the established criteria. The Head of CRM reports directly to the CRO and provides regular
updates on the performance and effectiveness of the rating standards.

extracted.name: Underwriter and Analyst Execution and Annual Training Requirement
extracted.source_quote:
Credit analysts and underwriters are responsible for the execution of the rating process, including the collection and analysis of
relevant data, the application of rating methodologies, and the documentation of rating rationales. These individuals must
possess the necessary qualifications and experience, as defined in the bank’s Competency Framework for Credit
Professionals. Analysts and underwriters are required to complete annual training on the RAT-1.0 standards and any updates
thereto.

extracted.name: Independent Risk Validation Oversight Responsibilities
extracted.source_quote:
The Independent Risk Validation (IRV) team plays a critical role in the governance framework by providing an independent
review of the credit rating process. The IRV team is responsible for validating the accuracy and consistency of ratings,
assessing the effectiveness of the rating methodologies, and identifying any potential biases or weaknesses in the process. The
IRV team reports its findings directly to the CRO and the Board’s Risk Committee, ensuring that any issues are addressed
promptly and transparently.

metrics, while qualitative assessments consider factors such as management quality, industry dynamics, and macroeconomic
conditions.

 Credit Rating Standards
RAT-v1.0 · Rating · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose and Applicability
This document, titled RAT-1.0 Credit Rating Standards, establishes the foundational framework for credit rating assignments
within the synthetic demonstration environment of the bank. It is designed to ensure consistency, transparency, and regulatory
compliance in the evaluation of creditworthiness for all counterparties, including corporate, commercial, and retail clients. The
standards outlined herein are aligned with the parent policy RAT-v1.0 and serve as a critical component of the bank’s risk
management infrastructure.
The primary purpose of RAT-1.0 is to define the methodologies, criteria, and governance structures required to assign, validate,
and monitor credit ratings. These ratings are integral to the bank’s decision-making processes, including loan approvals,
risk-based pricing, capital allocation, and portfolio monitoring. By adhering to these standards, the bank aims to mitigate credit
risk, enhance stakeholder confidence, and fulfill its fiduciary responsibilities.
This policy applies to all business units, risk management teams, and personnel involved in the credit assessment process. It is
mandatory for underwriters, credit analysts, relationship managers, and senior management to comply with the provisions of
this document. Third-party vendors or partners engaged in credit-related activities on behalf of the bank must also adhere to
these standards unless explicitly exempted by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO).
The synthetic nature of this document is emphasized to clarify that it is intended for demonstration, training, and internal testing
purposes only. While the thresholds, roles, and processes described are realistic and internally consistent, they do not reflect
actual bank operations or real-world data. Any use of this document for live transactions or external reporting must be explicitly
authorized by the bank’s compliance and legal departments.
The applicability of RAT-1.0 extends to all credit exposures, including but not limited to loans, bonds, derivatives, and trade
finance instruments. It covers both new credit applications and the periodic review of existing exposures. The standards are
designed to be scalable, accommodating the diverse needs of the bank’s global operations while maintaining uniformity in risk
assessment practices.

RAT-v1.0 · Rating | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope and Exclusions
The scope of RAT-1.0 Credit Rating Standards encompasses all credit rating activities conducted by the bank, including the
initial assignment, periodic review, and ad-hoc reassessment of ratings. This includes ratings for internal risk management
purposes as well as those used for regulatory reporting, such as under the Basel III framework. The policy is global in nature,
applying to all jurisdictions in which the bank operates, unless local regulations impose stricter requirements.
All credit exposures, regardless of size or complexity, fall within the scope of this policy. This includes exposures to corporate
entities, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), retail customers, financial institutions, and sovereign entities. The policy
also covers specialized lending areas such as project finance, leveraged finance, and structured credit products. Each
exposure must be assigned a credit rating in accordance with the methodologies outlined in this document.
Exclusions from this policy are limited and must be explicitly documented and approved by the CRO. Typical exclusions may
include intra-group exposures, where the counterparty is a subsidiary or affiliate of the bank, and exposures that are fully
guaranteed by a sovereign entity with a risk weight of 0% under regulatory capital rules. Additionally, exposures that are
immaterial in size (defined as less than USD 100,000) may be exempted from formal rating assignments, provided they are
subject to alternative risk controls.
The policy also excludes credit ratings assigned by external credit rating agencies (e.g., Moody’s, S&P, Fitch) for the purpose of
regulatory compliance, where such ratings are used directly without internal override. However, the bank reserves the right to
perform its own internal rating assessment for risk management purposes, even when external ratings are available. In such
cases, the internal rating must be documented and justified in accordance with the standards set forth in this policy.
Any deviations from the scope of this policy, including temporary or permanent exclusions, must be documented in the bank’s
Risk Policy Exception Log. Such deviations require the approval of the CRO and must be reviewed at least annually to ensure
they remain appropriate. The bank’s internal audit function will periodically verify compliance with the scope and exclusion
provisions of this policy.

Page 3

3. 3. Governance and Roles
The governance framework for RAT-1.0 Credit Rating Standards is designed to ensure accountability, independence, and
oversight in the credit rating process. The Board of Directors retains ultimate responsibility for the approval and periodic review
of this policy, delegating its implementation to the CRO. The CRO, in turn, is responsible for ensuring that the policy is applied
consistently across the bank and that all personnel adhere to its provisions.
The Credit Risk Management (CRM) department is the primary owner of this policy and is tasked with its day-to-day
administration. The CRM department is responsible for developing and maintaining the credit rating methodologies, tools, and
systems used by the bank. It also oversees the training of personnel involved in the rating process and ensures that all ratings
are assigned in accordance with the established criteria. The Head of CRM reports directly to the CRO and provides regular
updates on the performance and effectiveness of the rating standards.
Credit analysts and underwriters are responsible for the execution of the rating process, including the collection and analysis of
relevant data, the application of rating methodologies, and the documentation of rating rationales. These individuals must
possess the necessary qualifications and experience, as defined in the bank’s Competency Framework for Credit
Professionals. Analysts and underwriters are required to complete annual training on the RAT-1.0 standards and any updates
thereto.
The Independent Risk Validation (IRV) team plays a critical role in the governance framework by providing an independent
review of the credit rating process. The IRV team is responsible for validating the accuracy and consistency of ratings,
assessing the effectiveness of the rating methodologies, and identifying any potential biases or weaknesses in the process. The
IRV team reports its findings directly to the CRO and the Board’s Risk Committee, ensuring that any issues are addressed
promptly and transparently.
Escalation paths are clearly defined to resolve disputes or uncertainties in the rating process. If a credit analyst or underwriter
disagrees with a proposed rating, the matter must be escalated to the relevant Credit Committee, which includes senior
representatives from CRM, IRV, and the business unit. The Credit Committee’s decision is final, unless further escalation is
warranted to the CRO. All escalations and their resolutions must be documented in the bank’s Credit Rating Dispute Log.

Page 4

4. 4. Credit Rating Methodologies
The credit rating methodologies outlined in RAT-1.0 are designed to provide a systematic and objective framework for
assessing the creditworthiness of counterparties. The bank employs a dual approach, combining quantitative models and
qualitative assessments to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of credit risk. Quantitative models are used to analyze financial
metrics, while qualitative assessments consider factors such as management quality, industry dynamics, and macroeconomic
conditions.
For corporate and commercial counterparties, the bank utilizes a scoring model that assigns weights to key financial ratios,
including leverage, liquidity, profitability, and interest coverage. The model generates a preliminary score, which is then
adjusted based on qualitative factors. The final score corresponds to a specific rating on the bank’s internal rating scale, which
ranges from AAA (highest credit quality) to D (default). The internal scale is mapped to external rating scales for consistency
and comparability.
Retail counterparties are evaluated using a separate scoring model that incorporates factors such as credit history, income
stability, debt-to-income ratio, and collateral coverage. The model is calibrated to the bank’s historical default data and is
regularly updated to reflect changes in the economic environment. Retail ratings are assigned on a scale from 1 (lowest risk) to

10 (highest risk), with corresponding probability of default (PD) estimates.
Qualitative assessments are conducted using a standardized checklist that evaluates non-financial factors. For corporate
counterparties, this includes an analysis of the industry’s competitive landscape, the counterparty’s market position, the
experience and track record of its management team, and the quality of its risk management practices. For retail counterparties,
qualitative factors may include employment stability, residential status, and behavioral patterns observed in past transactions.
The bank’s credit rating methodologies are subject to annual review and validation by the IRV team. Any material changes to
the methodologies, such as updates to the scoring models or adjustments to the qualitative assessment criteria, must be
approved by the CRO and documented in the bank’s Methodology Change Log. The bank also conducts backtesting exercises
to assess the predictive accuracy of its rating models, with results reported to the Board’s Risk Committee.

5. 5. Underwriting Criteria and Evidence Requirements
The underwriting criteria specified in RAT-1.0 are designed to ensure that credit decisions are based on a thorough and
rigorous analysis of all relevant factors. Underwriters must adhere to these criteria when evaluating new credit applications or
reviewing existing exposures. The criteria are structured to align with the bank’s risk appetite and regulatory expectations,
ensuring that only counterparties meeting the minimum standards are approved for credit facilities.
For corporate and commercial lending, underwriters are required to obtain and analyze a comprehensive set of financial
statements, including audited annual reports, interim financial statements, and management accounts. The financial statements
must cover at least the past three years, unless the counterparty is a startup or has a shorter operating history. Underwriters
must also review the counterparty’s business plan, cash flow projections, and any available market research reports.
In addition to financial data, underwriters must gather qualitative evidence to support their assessment. This includes
conducting site visits, interviewing key management personnel, and reviewing industry reports from reputable sources. For
counterparties operating in high-risk industries or jurisdictions, underwriters must also obtain independent third-party
assessments, such as due diligence reports or environmental, social, and governance (ESG) evaluations.
For retail lending, underwriters must verify the applicant’s identity, income, and employment status using primary sources, such
as government-issued identification, pay stubs, and employer verification letters. Credit reports from at least one major credit
bureau must be obtained and reviewed for all retail applicants. In cases where the applicant’s credit history is limited or
unavailable, underwriters may use alternative data sources, such as utility payment records or rental history, provided these are
documented and justified.
All evidence gathered during the underwriting process must be retained in the bank’s credit file system for a minimum of seven
years from the date of the last action on the credit facility. The evidence must be organized and labeled clearly to facilitate
future reviews or audits. Underwriters are responsible for ensuring that the credit file is complete and accurate before submitting
their recommendation to the appropriate approval authority.

6. 6. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
RAT-1.0 establishes quantitative limits and thresholds to ensure that credit exposures are managed within the bank’s risk
appetite and regulatory constraints. These limits are designed to prevent excessive concentration of risk and to ensure that the
bank maintains adequate capital and liquidity buffers. The thresholds are applied at various levels, including individual
counterparties, industry sectors, geographic regions, and the overall portfolio.
For individual counterparties, the bank sets exposure limits based on the assigned credit rating. The maximum exposure to a
single counterparty is capped at 25% of the bank’s Tier 1 capital for investment-grade counterparties (rated BBB- or higher) and
10% of Tier 1 capital for sub-investment-grade counterparties (rated BB+ or lower). Exposures to retail counterparties are
subject to aggregate limits, with no single retail exposure exceeding 1% of Tier 1 capital.
Industry sector limits are established to prevent over-concentration in any single sector. The bank’s exposure to any one
industry sector may not exceed 20% of its total credit exposures. Sectors are defined using the Global Industry Classification
Standard (GICS), and exposures are aggregated at the two-digit GICS level. Geographic limits are also applied, with no single
country (excluding the bank’s home country) accounting for more than 15% of total credit exposures.
The bank also imposes internal risk-based limits, which are more granular than the regulatory limits. These include limits on the
proportion of the portfolio that can be assigned to each rating grade. For example, the bank targets that no more than 10% of its
total credit exposures should be rated BB+ or lower. Additionally, the bank sets thresholds for watchlist and non-performing
exposures, with the latter not exceeding 3% of total exposures at any time.
Quantitative limits are monitored on a daily basis by the bank’s Risk Monitoring team, which reports any breaches to the CRM
department and the relevant business units. Breaches must be addressed within 30 days, either by reducing the exposure or
obtaining a waiver from the CRO. All waivers must be documented and justified, with a clear action plan for remediation. The
bank’s internal audit function conducts quarterly reviews of limit compliance and breach management processes.

7. 7. Approval Authorities and Delegation
The approval authorities and delegation framework outlined in RAT-1.0 are designed to ensure that credit decisions are made
at the appropriate level of seniority, based on the size, complexity, and risk profile of the exposure. The framework establishes
clear thresholds for approval authority, as well as the circumstances under which delegation or escalation is required.
Credit exposures up to USD 1 million may be approved by a designated Credit Officer within the business unit, provided the
exposure is rated investment-grade (BBB- or higher) and complies with all other underwriting criteria. Exposures between USD

1 million and USD 10 million require the approval of the Head of the relevant business unit, while exposures between USD 10
million and USD 50 million must be approved by the regional Credit Committee.
Exposures exceeding USD 50 million, or those involving sub-investment-grade counterparties (rated BB+ or lower), require the
approval of the Global Credit Committee, which is chaired by the CRO. The Global Credit Committee also reviews and
approves all exposures that breach the bank’s internal risk-based limits or involve new or complex products. The committee
meets weekly to review pending approvals and is empowered to reject or modify any proposal that does not meet the bank’s
risk standards.
Delegation of approval authority is permitted under specific circumstances, such as the temporary absence of a designated
approver or the need to expedite a time-sensitive transaction. Delegation must be formally documented and approved by the
CRO or their delegate. The delegated authority is limited to a maximum of 30 days and may not be further delegated. All
delegations must be recorded in the bank’s Delegation of Authority Log, which is reviewed quarterly by the internal audit
function.
In cases where a credit exposure requires approval from multiple authorities (e.g., due to its size, risk rating, or complexity), the
most senior authority’s approval is required. For example, a USD 60 million exposure to a BB-rated counterparty would require
approval from both the regional Credit Committee and the Global Credit Committee. The approval process must be completed
within 10 business days of submission, unless an extension is granted by the CRO. All approvals and rejections must be
documented in the bank’s Credit Approval System, with clear rationales provided for any deviations from the standard criteria.

8. 8. Monitoring and Trigger Events
The monitoring framework specified in RAT-1.0 is designed to ensure that credit exposures are continuously assessed for
changes in risk profile, and that appropriate actions are taken in response to adverse developments. The bank employs a
combination of automated surveillance tools and manual reviews to monitor its credit portfolio, with the frequency and intensity
of monitoring proportional to the risk rating of the exposure.
All credit exposures are subject to automated monitoring on a daily basis, with the bank’s Risk Monitoring team tracking key
financial and non-financial indicators for signs of deterioration. These indicators include financial ratio trends, payment behavior,
credit rating changes, and adverse news events. Automated alerts are generated when predefined thresholds are breached,
such as a decline in the counterparty’s interest coverage ratio below 1.5x or a downgrade in its external credit rating.
In addition to automated monitoring, the bank conducts periodic manual reviews of its credit exposures. Investment-grade
exposures (rated BBB- or higher) are reviewed at least annually, while sub-investment-grade exposures (rated BB+ or lower)
are reviewed at least quarterly. Retail exposures are subject to ongoing behavioral monitoring, with individual accounts flagged
for review if they exhibit delinquency, over-limit usage, or other signs of stress.
Trigger events are defined as specific occurrences that necessitate an immediate review of the credit exposure. These include,
but are not limited to, a breach of financial covenants, a payment default, a material adverse change in the counterparty’s
financial condition, or a significant negative news event (e.g., regulatory action, litigation, or a natural disaster affecting the
counterparty’s operations). Upon the occurrence of a trigger event, the responsible relationship manager must initiate a review
within 5 business days and submit a recommendation to the appropriate approval authority within 10 business days.
The results of monitoring activities and trigger event reviews are documented in the bank’s Credit Monitoring System, with all
actions and rationales recorded for audit purposes. The Risk Monitoring team provides monthly reports to the CRM department
and the CRO, summarizing the number and nature of alerts, the outcomes of reviews, and any emerging trends or concerns.
The internal audit function conducts semi-annual reviews of the monitoring framework to assess its effectiveness and identify
any gaps or weaknesses.

9. 9. Exception Handling and Waivers
RAT-1.0 recognizes that there may be circumstances where strict adherence to the credit policy is not feasible or appropriate.
In such cases, the bank permits exceptions and waivers, provided they are properly justified, documented, and approved in
accordance with the framework outlined in this section. The exception handling process is designed to balance the need for
flexibility with the bank’s commitment to risk discipline and regulatory compliance.
An exception is defined as a deviation from the standard underwriting criteria, quantitative limits, or approval authorities
specified in this policy. Common examples of exceptions include approving a credit exposure that exceeds the counterparty’s
assigned limit, extending credit to a counterparty that does not meet the minimum financial thresholds, or delegating approval
authority beyond the permitted scope. Exceptions may also arise in cases where the counterparty’s risk profile is mitigated by
factors not fully captured by the standard criteria, such as strong collateral or third-party guarantees.
The process for requesting an exception begins with the submission of an Exception Request Form by the relationship manager
or underwriter. The form must include a detailed rationale for the exception, an assessment of the incremental risk, and a
description of any mitigating factors or controls. The request is then reviewed by the CRM department, which assesses its
compliance with the bank’s risk appetite and regulatory expectations. If the CRM department supports the request, it is
forwarded to the appropriate approval authority, which varies based on the nature and size of the exception.

thresholds. Waivers are typically granted in cases where the bank has a strategic or commercial rationale for accepting the
additional risk, such as supporting a long-standing client through a temporary period of financial stress. Waivers must be
approved by the CRO or the Global Credit Committee, depending on the size and risk profile of the exposure. All waivers are
subject to a maximum term of 12 months and must be reviewed at least quarterly to ensure they remain appropriate.
All exceptions and waivers are recorded in the bank’s Risk Policy Exception Log, which is maintained by the CRM department
and reviewed monthly by the CRO. The log includes details such as the nature of the exception, the rationale, the approval
authority, the date of approval, and the expiration date (if applicable). The internal audit function conducts annual reviews of the
exception handling process to ensure compliance with the policy and to identify any systemic issues or trends. Any exceptions
or waivers that result in a loss or near-miss event are subject to a post-mortem analysis, with findings reported to the Board’s
Risk Committee.

The reporting and review requirements specified in RAT-1.0 are designed to ensure transparency, accountability, and
continuous improvement in the bank’s credit rating processes. The policy establishes a comprehensive framework for internal
and external reporting, as well as periodic reviews of the policy’s effectiveness and relevance.
Internal reporting is conducted at multiple levels, with the frequency and detail of reports tailored to the needs of the audience.
The Risk Monitoring team provides daily dashboards to the CRM department, summarizing key portfolio metrics such as
exposure concentrations, rating migrations, and limit breaches. Weekly reports are provided to the business units, highlighting
new approvals, monitoring alerts, and exception requests. Monthly reports are submitted to the CRO and the Global Credit
Committee, with a focus on emerging risks, trend analyses, and the status of remediation actions.
External reporting is conducted in accordance with regulatory requirements, such as those specified under the Basel III
framework and local banking regulations. The bank’s regulatory reports include detailed information on its credit portfolio, such

exposures, and loan loss provisions. The CRM department is responsible for ensuring the accuracy and timeliness of all
external reports, which are subject to independent validation by the IRV team prior to submission.
The RAT-1.0 policy itself is subject to periodic review to ensure it remains aligned with the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory
expectations, and industry best practices. The policy is reviewed at least annually by the CRM department, with input from the
IRV team, internal audit, and the business units. The review process includes an assessment of the policy’s effectiveness in
mitigating credit risk, as well as an evaluation of any gaps or weaknesses identified through monitoring, audits, or loss events.
Material changes to the policy, such as updates to the credit rating methodologies, underwriting criteria, or quantitative limits,
require the approval of the CRO and the Board’s Risk Committee. The CRM department is responsible for communicating any
changes to the relevant stakeholders and ensuring that all personnel are trained on the updated provisions. The policy review
process is documented in the bank’s Policy Review Log, which includes details such as the date of the review, the key findings,
and the actions taken.
In addition to the annual review, the RAT-1.0 policy is subject to ad-hoc reviews in response to significant events, such as a
major loss, a regulatory change, or a shift in the bank’s strategic direction. The results of all reviews are reported to the Board of
Directors, with recommendations for any necessary updates or enhancements to the policy. The bank’s internal audit function
conducts an independent review of the policy at least once every three years, with findings and recommendations reported
directly to the Board’s Audit Committee.

 Industry Risk Assessment Policy
SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose and Objectives
The purpose of the IND-1.0 Industry Risk Assessment Policy is to establish a structured framework for evaluating, categorizing,
and mitigating industry-specific risks within the bank’s credit portfolio. This policy ensures that credit exposures are aligned with
the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory requirements, and strategic objectives. By systematically assessing industry risks, the bank
aims to proactively identify emerging threats, capitalize on opportunities, and maintain a resilient credit portfolio.
This policy is designed to complement the parent policy, SEC-IND-v1.0, by providing detailed guidelines for industry risk
assessment. It ensures consistency in risk evaluation across all business units and geographies, fostering a unified approach to
credit risk management. The policy also supports compliance with internal and external audit requirements, as well as
regulatory expectations for industry risk management.
The primary objectives of this policy include: (1) defining clear criteria for industry risk classification; (2) establishing thresholds
for industry concentration limits; (3) outlining roles and responsibilities for risk assessment and monitoring; (4) providing
mechanisms for escalation and exception handling; and (5) ensuring regular review and updates to reflect evolving industry
dynamics.
This document is synthetic demonstration data and is intended for illustrative purposes only. It does not reflect the actual
policies, procedures, or risk appetites of any real financial institution. All thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are
fictional and should not be interpreted as binding or actionable in a real-world context.
The policy applies to all credit exposures, including loans, lines of credit, and other financial instruments, across all industries. It
is the responsibility of all relevant personnel, including credit officers, risk analysts, and senior management, to adhere to the
guidelines outlined in this document. Failure to comply with this policy may result in increased risk exposure and potential
regulatory non-compliance.

SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry | Synthetic policy data

2. 2. Scope and Applicability
The IND-1.0 Industry Risk Assessment Policy applies to all business units, subsidiaries, and geographic regions under the
bank’s operational umbrella. It governs the assessment of industry risk for all credit exposures, regardless of size, complexity,
or tenure. This includes corporate lending, commercial real estate, project finance, and other credit products where
industry-specific risks are material.
The policy is applicable to both new credit applications and the ongoing monitoring of existing exposures. It covers all stages of
the credit lifecycle, from initial underwriting to portfolio management and risk reporting. The policy also extends to third-party
relationships, such as syndicated loans or participations, where the bank retains credit risk.
Exclusions from this policy include consumer lending products, such as mortgages, personal loans, and credit cards, which are
governed by separate risk assessment frameworks. Additionally, sovereign and supranational exposures are not covered under
this policy, as they are subject to distinct risk evaluation criteria.
The policy is binding for all employees, contractors, and agents involved in credit underwriting, risk management, and portfolio
monitoring. Compliance with this policy is mandatory, and deviations require explicit approval through the exception
management process outlined in Section 9.
This synthetic policy is designed to demonstrate a comprehensive approach to industry risk assessment. All references to
specific industries, thresholds, or organizational structures are fictional and intended solely for illustrative purposes. Real-world
applications would require customization to align with the bank’s actual risk appetite and regulatory environment.

SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry | Synthetic policy data
Page 3

3. 3. Governance and Roles
The governance framework for the IND-1.0 Industry Risk Assessment Policy is structured to ensure accountability,
transparency, and effective risk management. The Board of Directors retains ultimate responsibility for approving the policy and
overseeing its implementation. The Board delegates operational oversight to the Chief Risk Officer (CRO), who is responsible
for ensuring adherence to the policy across all business units.
The Credit Risk Committee (CRC), chaired by the CRO, is responsible for reviewing and approving industry risk assessments,
concentration limits, and exceptions. The CRC meets quarterly to evaluate industry risk trends, approve policy updates, and
address escalated issues. The committee includes representatives from Credit, Risk Management, Finance, and Business
Units to ensure a balanced perspective.
The Industry Risk Team, reporting to the Head of Credit Risk, is tasked with conducting industry risk assessments, monitoring
portfolio concentrations, and developing industry-specific risk metrics. This team collaborates with Business Unit Risk Officers
(BUROs) to ensure that industry risk considerations are integrated into underwriting and portfolio management processes.
Business Unit Heads are accountable for implementing the policy within their respective units. They must ensure that credit
officers and relationship managers adhere to industry risk guidelines and escalate potential breaches or exceptions to the CRC.
Additionally, the Internal Audit function conducts periodic reviews to validate compliance with the policy and the effectiveness of
industry risk controls.
This synthetic governance structure is designed to illustrate a robust framework for industry risk management. The roles,
committees, and responsibilities described are fictional and should not be interpreted as reflective of any real organization’s
governance model.

SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry | Synthetic policy data
Page 4

4. 4. Industry Classification and Risk Rating Methodology
The IND-1.0 Policy establishes a standardized industry classification system to ensure consistency in risk assessment.
Industries are categorized using a combination of the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) and internal bank-specific
groupings. Each industry is assigned a unique identifier and mapped to a risk tier based on its inherent risk characteristics.
The industry risk rating methodology employs a multi-factor approach, incorporating qualitative and quantitative assessments.
Key factors include industry volatility, cyclicality, regulatory environment, competitive landscape, and macroeconomic
sensitivity. Each factor is scored on a scale of 1 to 5, with 1 representing the lowest risk and 5 the highest. The weighted
average of these scores determines the overall industry risk rating.
Industries are classified into four risk tiers: Low (Tier 1), Moderate (Tier 2), High (Tier 3), and Very High (Tier 4). Tier 1
industries exhibit stable cash flows, low volatility, and strong regulatory protections. Tier 4 industries are characterized by high
volatility, significant cyclicality, and exposure to disruptive forces such as technological change or regulatory shifts.
The Industry Risk Team is responsible for conducting annual reviews of industry classifications and risk ratings. Ad-hoc reviews
may be triggered by material changes in industry dynamics, such as mergers and acquisitions, regulatory shifts, or
macroeconomic events. All industry risk ratings must be approved by the CRC before implementation.
This synthetic methodology is intended to demonstrate a structured approach to industry risk assessment. The classification
system, scoring factors, and risk tiers are fictional and designed for illustrative purposes only.

SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry | Synthetic policy data
Page 5

5. 5. Underwriting Criteria and Industry-Specific Considerations
The IND-1.0 Policy mandates that all credit underwriting incorporate industry-specific risk assessments to ensure that
exposures are consistent with the bank’s risk appetite. Underwriting criteria are tailored to the risk tier of the industry in
question, with more stringent requirements applied to higher-risk industries.
For Tier 1 (Low Risk) industries, standard underwriting criteria apply, with a focus on borrower financial strength, collateral
quality, and repayment capacity. Credit facilities for these industries may benefit from streamlined approval processes and
higher delegation limits for credit officers.
For Tier 2 (Moderate Risk) industries, underwriting must include additional due diligence, such as industry-specific financial
ratios, stress testing, and sensitivity analysis. Approval authority for these exposures is typically limited to senior credit officers
or the CRC, depending on the exposure size.
Tier 3 (High Risk) and Tier 4 (Very High Risk) industries require enhanced underwriting standards, including mandatory CRC
approval for all new exposures. Underwriting for these industries must incorporate scenario analysis, contingency planning, and
robust covenant structures. Exposure to Tier 4 industries is subject to strict concentration limits, as outlined in Section 6.
All underwriting decisions must be documented with clear justification for industry risk considerations. The Industry Risk Team
must be consulted for exposures to Tier 3 and Tier 4 industries, and their input must be reflected in the credit memorandum.
This synthetic underwriting framework is designed to illustrate how industry risk assessments integrate with credit
decision-making.

SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry | Synthetic policy data
Page 6

6. 6. Quantitative Limits and Concentration Thresholds
The IND-1.0 Policy establishes quantitative limits to control industry concentration risk and ensure portfolio diversification.
These limits are designed to prevent excessive exposure to any single industry or group of related industries, thereby mitigating
the potential for significant losses due to industry-specific downturns.
The policy defines concentration limits at two levels: (1) Individual Industry Limits, which cap exposure to a single industry as a
percentage of the bank’s total credit portfolio; and (2) Industry Group Limits, which cap exposure to a group of related
industries. Individual Industry Limits are set at 5% for Tier 1 industries, 3% for Tier 2 industries, 2% for Tier 3 industries, and 1%
for Tier 4 industries.
Industry Group Limits are set at 15% for groups comprising Tier 1 and Tier 2 industries, 10% for groups including Tier 3
industries, and 5% for groups including Tier 4 industries. These limits are applied at the consolidated bank level and are
monitored on a monthly basis by the Industry Risk Team.
Breaches of concentration limits must be escalated to the CRC within five business days of identification. The CRC will evaluate
the breach and determine whether corrective action, such as risk mitigation or portfolio rebalancing, is required. Exceptions to
concentration limits require CRC approval and must be justified by compelling strategic or risk-adjusted return considerations.
This synthetic framework for quantitative limits is intended to demonstrate how concentration risk is managed within a credit
portfolio. The specific thresholds and escalation paths described are fictional and should not be applied in a real-world context
without customization.

SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry | Synthetic policy data
Page 7

7. 7. Approval Authorities and Delegation
The IND-1.0 Policy defines clear approval authorities and delegation limits to ensure that credit decisions are made at the
appropriate level of seniority, commensurate with the risk involved. Approval authorities are structured to align with the industry
risk tier and the size of the exposure.
For Tier 1 industries, credit officers with delegation limits up to $10 million may approve exposures without additional escalation,
provided all underwriting criteria are met. Exposures between $10 million and $50 million require approval from a Senior Credit
Officer, while exposures exceeding $50 million require CRC approval.
For Tier 2 industries, credit officers may approve exposures up to $5 million. Exposures between $5 million and $25 million
require Senior Credit Officer approval, and those exceeding $25 million require CRC approval. All exposures to Tier 3 industries
require Senior Credit Officer approval for amounts up to $10 million, with CRC approval required for larger exposures.
Exposures to Tier 4 industries require CRC approval regardless of size. Additionally, all new exposures to Tier 4 industries must
be accompanied by a detailed industry risk assessment and a risk mitigation plan, both of which must be approved by the CRC.
Delegation limits are reviewed annually by the CRC and adjusted as necessary to reflect changes in risk appetite or market
conditions.
This synthetic approval framework is designed to illustrate how authority and accountability are structured within a credit risk
management system. The delegation limits and approval paths described are fictional and intended for demonstration purposes
only.

SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry | Synthetic policy data
Page 8

8. 8. Monitoring and Early Warning Indicators
The IND-1.0 Policy mandates continuous monitoring of industry risk exposures to identify emerging risks and ensure
compliance with concentration limits. The Industry Risk Team is responsible for developing and maintaining a dashboard of key
industry risk metrics, which are reviewed monthly by the CRC.
Early Warning Indicators (EWIs) are used to detect potential deterioration in industry risk profiles. EWIs include financial metrics
such as declining profitability, increasing leverage, or deteriorating liquidity within an industry. Non-financial EWIs may include
regulatory changes, technological disruptions, or shifts in consumer demand.
The Industry Risk Team conducts quarterly deep-dive reviews of industries exhibiting EWI breaches or approaching
concentration limits. These reviews include an assessment of the root causes of the EWI breaches, the potential impact on the
bank’s portfolio, and recommended actions to mitigate risk. Findings are presented to the CRC for discussion and approval.
In addition to internal monitoring, the bank subscribes to external industry risk reports and macroeconomic analyses to
supplement its assessments. The Industry Risk Team integrates these external insights into its monitoring framework and
escalates material findings to the CRC as needed.
This synthetic monitoring framework is intended to demonstrate how industry risk is tracked and managed on an ongoing basis.
The EWIs, review processes, and escalation paths described are fictional and designed for illustrative purposes.

SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry | Synthetic policy data
Page 9

9. 9. Exception Management and Escalation
The IND-1.0 Policy establishes a formal exception management process to address instances where credit exposures deviate
from industry risk guidelines. Exceptions may arise due to strategic opportunities, client relationship considerations, or other
justifiable reasons, but they must be carefully evaluated and approved to ensure that risk is appropriately managed.
All exceptions to industry risk guidelines, including concentration limit breaches, underwriting criteria waivers, or approval
authority overrides, must be documented in the Exception Log. The log captures the nature of the exception, the rationale for
the deviation, the risk mitigation measures in place, and the approval authority. The Exception Log is maintained by the Industry
Risk Team and reviewed quarterly by the CRC.
Exceptions to concentration limits or underwriting criteria for Tier 3 and Tier 4 industries require CRC approval. For Tier 1 and
Tier 2 industries, exceptions may be approved by the Head of Credit Risk or a Senior Credit Officer, depending on the
materiality of the deviation. All exceptions must include a risk-adjusted return analysis to justify the deviation from policy.
Escalation paths are clearly defined to ensure timely resolution of exceptions. Credit officers or BUROs must escalate potential
exceptions to the Industry Risk Team within two business days of identification. The Industry Risk Team then evaluates the
exception and presents it to the appropriate approval authority. Urgent exceptions, such as those posing immediate risk to the
portfolio, must be escalated to the CRO within 24 hours.
This synthetic exception management process is designed to illustrate how deviations from policy are handled in a structured
and controlled manner. The escalation paths, approval authorities, and documentation requirements described are fictional and
intended for demonstration purposes.

SEC-IND-v1.0 · Industry | Synthetic policy data

10. 10. Reporting and Review
The IND-1.0 Policy requires comprehensive reporting to ensure transparency and accountability in industry risk management.
The Industry Risk Team is responsible for preparing and distributing regular reports to key stakeholders, including the CRC,
senior management, and the Board of Directors.
Monthly Industry Risk Reports provide an overview of industry concentrations, EWI breaches, and exceptions. These reports
include trend analyses, emerging risk themes, and recommendations for portfolio adjustments. The reports are distributed to
the CRC and senior management within 10 business days of the end of each month.
Quarterly Industry Risk Reviews are conducted by the Industry Risk Team and presented to the CRC. These reviews provide a
deeper analysis of industry risk trends, the effectiveness of risk mitigation measures, and the impact of external factors on the
bank’s portfolio. The reviews also include updates on industry classifications and risk ratings, as well as any proposed changes
to the policy.
Annual Policy Reviews are conducted to ensure that the IND-1.0 Policy remains aligned with the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory
requirements, and industry best practices. The review process includes a comprehensive assessment of the policy’s
effectiveness, gaps, and areas for improvement. The CRC approves any updates to the policy, which are then communicated to
all relevant personnel.

2. 2. Scope
The Foreign Currency Credit Risk Policy (CUR-1.0) applies to all business units, subsidiaries, and branches of the bank that
engage in transactions denominated in foreign currencies. This includes but is not limited to corporate lending, trade finance,
project finance, syndicated loans, and derivative transactions where the bank assumes credit risk in a currency other than its
functional currency. The policy covers both on-balance-sheet assets (e.g., loans, bonds) and off-balance-sheet exposures (e.g.,
guarantees, letters of credit, derivatives).
The scope of this policy extends to all counterparties, including corporate clients, financial institutions, sovereign entities, and
multilateral organizations. It applies regardless of the counterparty’s domicile or the jurisdiction in which the transaction is
booked. The policy is particularly relevant for transactions involving currencies that are not freely convertible or are subject to

 Foreign Currency Credit Risk Policy
RAF-CUR-v1.0 · Currency · Effective 2026-09-10

1. 1. Purpose
The purpose of the Foreign Currency Credit Risk Policy (CUR-1.0) is to establish a comprehensive framework for identifying,
assessing, mitigating, and monitoring credit risks arising from transactions denominated in foreign currencies. This policy
ensures that the bank’s exposure to foreign currency-denominated assets, liabilities, and off-balance-sheet items is managed
within acceptable risk parameters, aligned with the bank’s overall risk appetite as defined in the parent policy RAF-CUR-v1.0.
The policy is designed to address the unique challenges posed by currency fluctuations, sovereign risks, and cross-border
regulatory complexities, which can significantly impact the bank’s creditworthiness and financial stability.
Foreign currency credit risk encompasses the potential for losses due to a counterparty’s failure to meet its obligations in a
foreign currency, as well as the risk of adverse exchange rate movements between the time a credit exposure is initiated and
when it is settled. This policy explicitly addresses both types of risk, ensuring that the bank maintains a robust control
environment to protect its capital and earnings. The policy is synthetic demonstration data and does not reflect the actual
practices or risk exposures of any real financial institution.
The policy seeks to balance the bank’s strategic objectives of expanding its international footprint and serving global clients with
the need to maintain prudent risk management practices. By clearly defining roles, responsibilities, and controls, the policy
ensures that foreign currency credit exposures are entered into only after a thorough assessment of the counterparty’s
creditworthiness, the economic and political stability of the relevant jurisdictions, and the bank’s ability to hedge or mitigate the
associated risks.
This document also serves as a reference for internal stakeholders, including credit officers, risk managers, and compliance
teams, to ensure consistent application of foreign currency credit risk principles across all business lines. It provides the
necessary guidance to evaluate, approve, and monitor foreign currency-denominated transactions, while ensuring compliance
with applicable laws, regulations, and internal policies. The policy is reviewed annually or as required by material changes in the
bank’s risk profile or external environment.
The policy is grounded in the principle that foreign currency credit risk must be managed proactively, with a focus on early
identification of potential issues and timely intervention to prevent losses. It emphasizes the importance of collaboration
between front-office, risk management, and finance teams to ensure that foreign currency exposures are accurately measured,
reported, and controlled. This collaborative approach is essential to maintaining the bank’s financial health and reputation in the
global marketplace.

RAF-CUR-v1.0 · Currency | Synthetic policy data
Page 2

2. 2. Scope
The Foreign Currency Credit Risk Policy (CUR-1.0) applies to all business units, subsidiaries, and branches of the bank that
engage in transactions denominated in foreign currencies. This includes but is not limited to corporate lending, trade finance,
project finance, syndicated loans, and derivative transactions where the bank assumes credit risk in a currency other than its
functional currency. The policy covers both on-balance-sheet assets (e.g., loans, bonds) and off-balance-sheet exposures (e.g.,
guarantees, letters of credit, derivatives).
The scope of this policy extends to all counterparties, including corporate clients, financial institutions, sovereign entities, and
multilateral organizations. It applies regardless of the counterparty’s domicile or the jurisdiction in which the transaction is
booked. The policy is particularly relevant for transactions involving currencies that are not freely convertible or are subject to
exchange controls, as these introduce additional layers of risk that must be carefully managed.
Excluded from the scope of this policy are transactions denominated in the bank’s functional currency, as these are governed
by the bank’s domestic credit risk policies. Additionally, foreign exchange (FX) risk arising from non-credit transactions (e.g., FX
trading for proprietary purposes) is managed under the bank’s Market Risk Policy and is not addressed here. However, the
policy acknowledges the interplay between credit risk and FX risk and requires that both be considered holistically where
applicable.
The policy is binding on all employees, contractors, and third-party service providers acting on behalf of the bank in the
origination, execution, or management of foreign currency-denominated credit exposures. Compliance with this policy is
mandatory, and any deviations must be approved through the formal exception process outlined in Section 9. The policy is
synthetic demonstration data and is not intended to reflect the actual scope of any real financial institution’s operations.
The bank reserves the right to expand or contract the scope of this policy as its business activities evolve. Any material changes
to the scope will be communicated to all relevant stakeholders and will require approval from the bank’s Risk Policy Committee
(RPC). The policy is designed to be flexible enough to accommodate new products, markets, or counterparty types while
maintaining a consistent and rigorous approach to foreign currency credit risk management.

RAF-CUR-v1.0 · Currency | Synthetic policy data

3. 3. Governance and Roles
The governance framework for the Foreign Currency Credit Risk Policy (CUR-1.0) is designed to ensure clear accountability,
effective oversight, and robust controls at all levels of the organization. Ultimate responsibility for the policy rests with the bank’s
Board of Directors, which delegates day-to-day oversight to the Risk Policy Committee (RPC). The RPC is responsible for
approving the policy, monitoring its effectiveness, and ensuring that it remains aligned with the bank’s overall risk appetite and
strategic objectives.
The Chief Risk Officer (CRO) is accountable for the implementation and enforcement of this policy across the bank. The CRO is
supported by the Credit Risk Management (CRM) team, which is responsible for developing the methodologies, tools, and
processes required to identify, measure, and monitor foreign currency credit risk. The CRM team also provides guidance and
training to business units to ensure consistent application of the policy.
Business unit heads are responsible for ensuring that their respective teams adhere to the policy and that all foreign currency
credit exposures are originated, approved, and managed in accordance with its provisions. Credit officers within each business
unit are tasked with conducting the initial assessment of counterparty creditworthiness and transaction-specific risks, while risk
managers perform independent validation and ongoing monitoring. The separation of duties between front-office and risk
management functions is a critical control to prevent conflicts of interest and ensure objective risk assessment.
The Finance and Treasury departments play a key role in managing the bank’s foreign currency liquidity and funding risks,
which are closely linked to credit risk. These departments are responsible for ensuring that the bank maintains adequate
liquidity buffers in each currency to meet its obligations and that FX hedging strategies are in place to mitigate the impact of
adverse currency movements on the bank’s credit exposures. Collaboration between Finance, Treasury, and CRM is essential
to ensure a comprehensive approach to foreign currency risk management.
Internal Audit is responsible for periodically reviewing the effectiveness of the policy and the bank’s adherence to its provisions.
Audit findings and recommendations are reported to the RPC and the Board of Directors, and corrective actions are tracked to
ensure timely resolution. The governance structure is designed to foster a culture of risk awareness and accountability, with
clear escalation paths for issues or exceptions. This policy is synthetic demonstration data and does not reflect the actual
governance structure of any real financial institution.

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
The underwriting criteria for foreign currency credit exposures are designed to ensure that the bank only assumes risks that are
fully understood, appropriately priced, and consistent with its risk appetite. All foreign currency-denominated transactions must
undergo a rigorous credit assessment process, which includes an evaluation of the counterparty’s financial strength, industry
and country risks, and the transaction’s structure and terms. The assessment must be documented in a credit memo that is
approved by the appropriate authority as defined in Section 6.
Counterparty creditworthiness is evaluated using a combination of internal credit ratings and external ratings from recognized
credit rating agencies (e.g., Moody’s, S&P, Fitch). For counterparties without external ratings, the bank’s internal rating
methodology must be applied. The minimum acceptable credit rating for foreign currency exposures is BBB- (or equivalent) for
corporate counterparties and BBB (or equivalent) for sovereigns. Counterparties rated below these thresholds may be
considered only with additional mitigants, such as collateral, guarantees, or credit derivatives, and must receive approval from
the RPC.
Country risk is a critical component of the underwriting process for foreign currency exposures. The bank uses a proprietary
country risk rating model, which considers factors such as political stability, economic fundamentals, external debt levels, and
the presence of exchange controls. Transactions involving countries rated below the bank’s internal threshold of ‘Moderate
Risk’ (or equivalent) require additional due diligence, including an assessment of the counterparty’s ability to access foreign
currency to service its obligations. Exposures to high-risk countries are subject to stricter limits and more frequent monitoring.
The transaction structure and terms must be carefully evaluated to ensure that they do not introduce unnecessary risks. Key
considerations include the currency of denomination, the tenor of the exposure, the presence of embedded options (e.g., early
repayment clauses), and the availability of hedging instruments. The bank must also assess the legal and regulatory risks
associated with the transaction, including the enforceability of contracts and the ability to perfect security interests in the
relevant jurisdiction. Legal opinions may be required for complex or high-value transactions.
The underwriting criteria are reviewed annually by the CRM team to ensure that they remain relevant and effective in light of
changing market conditions, regulatory requirements, and the bank’s risk appetite. Any material changes to the criteria must be
approved by the RPC. This policy is synthetic demonstration data and does not reflect the actual underwriting standards of any
real financial institution.

RAF-CUR-v1.0 · Currency | Synthetic policy data

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
The Foreign Currency Credit Risk Policy (CUR-1.0) establishes a series of quantitative limits to control the bank’s exposure to
foreign currency credit risk. These limits are designed to ensure that the bank’s aggregate and individual exposures remain
within acceptable risk parameters, as defined by the bank’s risk appetite statement. The limits are set at multiple levels,
including counterparty, country, currency, industry, and portfolio, to provide a comprehensive framework for risk management.
Counterparty limits are the maximum exposure the bank is willing to assume to a single counterparty or group of connected
counterparties in any foreign currency. These limits are expressed as a percentage of the bank’s Tier 1 capital and are
calibrated based on the counterparty’s credit rating, country risk, and the nature of the exposure. For example, the maximum
exposure to a single corporate counterparty rated BBB+ is 2% of Tier 1 capital, while the limit for a counterparty rated A- is 5%.
Exposures to sovereigns are subject to separate limits, with a maximum of 10% of Tier 1 capital for investment-grade
sovereigns and 5% for non-investment-grade sovereigns.
Country limits cap the bank’s aggregate exposure to counterparties domiciled in or with significant operations in a particular
country. These limits are based on the country’s risk rating, with higher limits for lower-risk countries and stricter limits for
higher-risk jurisdictions. For example, the country limit for a ‘Low Risk’ country is 15% of Tier 1 capital, while the limit for a ‘High
Risk’ country is 2%. Country limits are reviewed quarterly by the CRM team and adjusted as necessary based on changes in
the country’s risk profile or the bank’s risk appetite.
Currency limits restrict the bank’s net exposure to a particular foreign currency, considering both assets and liabilities. These
limits are designed to manage the bank’s FX risk and ensure that it maintains a balanced currency portfolio. The net exposure
to any single foreign currency must not exceed 10% of Tier 1 capital, and the aggregate net exposure to all foreign currencies
must not exceed 50% of Tier 1 capital. Currency limits are monitored daily by the Treasury department, and breaches must be
reported immediately to the CRM team and the RPC.
Portfolio limits are set to control the bank’s aggregate exposure to foreign currency credit risk across all business units. The
total foreign currency credit exposure must not exceed 150% of Tier 1 capital, and the exposure to any single industry sector
(e.g., energy, real estate) must not exceed 25% of Tier 1 capital. Portfolio limits are reviewed annually by the RPC and may be
adjusted based on changes in the bank’s risk appetite or market conditions. All limits are synthetic demonstration thresholds
and do not reflect the actual risk limits of any real financial institution.

6. 6. Approval Authorities and Process
The approval process for foreign currency credit exposures is designed to ensure that all transactions are reviewed and
authorized by individuals with the appropriate level of authority and expertise. The process is tiered based on the size,
complexity, and risk profile of the exposure, with higher-risk transactions requiring approval from more senior levels of
management. The approval authorities and thresholds are defined in the bank’s Delegated Authority Matrix (DAM), which is
maintained by the CRM team and approved by the RPC.
For standard foreign currency credit exposures with a total exposure of up to 1% of Tier 1 capital and involving counterparties
rated BBB- or higher, approval authority is delegated to the relevant business unit’s credit committee. The credit committee
must include at least one independent risk manager and must document its decision in a credit approval memo, which is stored
in the bank’s central credit repository. The memo must include a detailed assessment of the counterparty’s creditworthiness,
country risk, transaction structure, and compliance with the bank’s quantitative limits.
Exposures exceeding 1% of Tier 1 capital or involving counterparties rated below BBB- require approval from the bank’s Group
Credit Committee (GCC). The GCC is chaired by the CRO and includes representatives from CRM, Finance, Treasury, and the
relevant business units. The GCC reviews the credit memo and may request additional information or analysis before making a
decision. Approvals from the GCC are valid for a maximum of 12 months, after which the exposure must be re-reviewed and
re-approved.
Transactions involving high-risk countries, complex structures, or novel products require approval from the RPC. The RPC
reviews the transaction’s alignment with the bank’s risk appetite, the adequacy of the risk assessment, and the effectiveness of
the proposed mitigants. The RPC may impose additional conditions or limits on the transaction as a prerequisite for approval.
All RPC approvals must be documented in a formal resolution and communicated to the relevant business units and control
functions.
The approval process includes a mandatory second-line review by the CRM team for all foreign currency credit exposures
exceeding 0.5% of Tier 1 capital. The CRM team’s review focuses on the accuracy of the risk assessment, the appropriateness
of the proposed limits and mitigants, and compliance with the bank’s policies and regulatory requirements. Any discrepancies or
concerns identified during the review must be resolved before the transaction can proceed. The approval authorities and
thresholds are synthetic demonstration data and do not reflect the actual delegation of authority in any real financial institution.

RAF-CUR-v1.0 · Currency | Synthetic policy data
